items.body:
Written for four Ebow-ed guitars, 'Avaeken' preserves a site-specific piece that O'Malley used to accompany an exhibition by Banks Violette. It's a microtonal symphony dedicated to Alvin Lucier and Kali Malone that's almost physically disorienting - RIYL Eleh, Phill Niblock, Pauline Oliveros et al.

It must be difficult to strike a balance when you're best known for creating some of the heaviest, most chest-pummeling drone music to ever vibrate from a stack of Sun amplifiers. But O'Malley's risen to the challenge; 'Avaeken' is relatively minimal, for him at least, but smacks with an intensity that you don't really see coming until your body starts feeling it. Made using four vibrating strings, he tunes the instruments to create that unsettling beating sound that seems to whirl around the noggin as the resonances interfere with each other. O'Malley wrote the piece following a commission from Belgium's ZWERM electric guitar quartet in 2020, performing it a handful of times before they knuckled down and recorded it in Gent's Muziekcentrum De Bijloke, a medieval hospital that's been fitted out with the proper acoustic treatments. 

And if you've been studying O'Malley's output carefully, you'll already know that he's frequently been spotted alongside Violette, the American artist best known for his huge sculptures and installations. The two have been friends for two decades at this point and have worked together multiple times, so when Violette was describing his show 'Wish You Were Here', an exhibition that tears at the fabric of America's subcultural underground, O'Malley immediately thought about this piece. The link might not be obvious, but O'Malley's use of phase cancellation - when "sound energy is eating itself", in O'Malley's own words - reaps ample rewards here. The effect is unsubtle, penetrating oscillations so disorienting that Violette's themes of societal rot emanate from every skewed tone.

O'Malley presents two takes of the same piece, fixing Violette's striking artwork - of a cracked mirror ball - to the cover. And it's incredible to hear him working as a composer for a change, letting the ZWERM quartet do the heavy lifting. Their expertise helps elevate the piece; it's precise, expertly rendered gear, the kind of thing you need to give your full attention to. Surprisingly, it's also got more in common with those Sunn O))) records than you might expect - play at high volume and you'll know exactly what we mean.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由四把Ebow电吉他演奏，是奥马利为艺术家班克斯·维奥莱特展览创作的特定场域作品，献给阿尔文·露西尔和凯莉·莫龙。乐曲利用微音程调弦制造出相位抵消效应，产生环绕头部旋转的不稳定拍频，以极简编制构建出具有物理压迫感的声响体验。两个版本的录音由比利时ZWERM四重奏在根特经过声学处理的 medieval 医院中完成，演奏精准且层次清晰。作品虽相对克制，但延续了奥马利在Sunn O)))时期对极端音量与低频振动的探索，高音量播放时能明显感受到其与早期重型Drone谱系的关联。维奥莱特的镜面球破损图像作为封面，与音乐中渗透的社会溃败主题形成呼应。

items.body:
Revisiting their debut album '.After', Tujiko Noriko and Adrian Corker commission a suite of remixes, bringing in Koshiro Hino ov YPY, goat (JP) and KAKUHAN fame, Tashi Wada, DJ Trystero, Shojiro Nakaoka and DJ ojo to put their spin on the source material.

The original album only took Noriko and Corker a couple of days in the studio, but they wired the results to percussionist and arranger George Barton, who took it to the next level. They continue the thought on '.After Again', dishing out the stems to a carefully pruned list of collaborators - artists whose distinctive sounds only extend the original album's sonic universe. And of course it's the YPY version of the album's opening track 'Yasashii Sayonora' that'll have most of y'all chomping at the bit; Hino turns Corker and Noriko's source material to dust, time-stretching Noriko's vocal and zeroing in on the stuttering percussion and rusted turntable loops. Adding his signature jerks, he fills the track with clattering metallic clangs, twisting the voices into downsampled groans from a neighboring cyber-reality.

Tokyo's DJ Trystero opts for a different but similarly unique approach on his two reworks, the "All Frills" remix of 'Toku No Minato' and his "Naive Declension" version of the same track. On the former, he isolates almost indistinguishable elements of the original, setting the ghost traces to a typically deep, dubby groove and on the latter, creates a rugged, gear-heavy jam from the remains. It's actually Nakaoka who provides the weirdest - yet strangely most recognisable - versions, using his custom generative code to match Noriko's voice with whirring interference and warbling digital detritus.
items._genre: experimental electronic / remix / glitch / IDM / avant-pop
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是 Tujiko Noriko 与 Adrian Corker 邀请多位艺术家对其首张专辑进行的再创作合集。原版录音被拆解为独立音轨分发给 Koshiro Hino (YPY)、DJ Trystero、Shojiro Nakaoka 等六位制作人，每位以截然不同的手法重塑素材。Hino 将人声拉伸、采样率降低，配合金属敲击与锈蚀的唱机循环，营造出赛博空间的呻吟质感；DJ Trystero 在两版混音中分别以幽灵般的碎片配以 dub 向律动，以及粗粝的机械节拍展开；Nakaoka 则使用自生成代码匹配人声与数字干扰。整张作品从原专辑的简约声学基底出发，延伸出包含 glitch、IDM、dub 与生成式电子的丰富声景，体现出对原始素材的高度开放性以及对声音解构与重建的实验态度。

items.body:
HTRK slickly seduce with the unheimlich sensuality on 'Work (Work, Work)', on a new pressing for 2026.

While it may be gauche to attribute the lightless mood of this LP to the departure of Sean Stewart in 2010, it certainly lends some inescapable context. It's hardly like HTRK were doing tween-pop previously, but the sense of gloom and dystopia is almost suffocatingly closer to the edge, from the crawling-on-all-fours pacing, to the detached, androgynous vocals of Jonnine Standish and their perversely detailed production values.

They've got our attention instantly with the sideroom synth eurotica of 'Ice Eyes Eis', and sustain the mood beautifully into the pinging metallic delays and seeping reverb of 'Slo Go', sounding like Atelecine produced by a young Geoff Barrow after a Birthday Party binge. Dragging us further down into the abyss, on 'Eat Yr Heart' the drums become clammier while Jonnine's vocals drift like ghostly vapour trail. At the album's apex, 'Skinny', the beats feel like a dystrophied version of something from Mika Vainio's 'Life, It Eats You Up…' album, and 'Synthetik' serves a tangibly textured taste of steely Techno pulses and opiated post-punk guitar drifts into 'Poison'.

To close, the atmopshere weighs heavier still on 'Work That Body', tracing anaesthetic connections with their Melbourne forefathers, Pelican Daughters, before the bleak romance of 'Love Triangle' and the blank-eyed writhe of 'Body Double'.

For fans of occluded sonics from Pump to Atelecine or Mika Vainio, it's as good as it gets.
items._cn_summary: HTRK在《Work (Work, Work)》中延续其阴郁、疏离的美学路线，专辑笼罩在近乎窒息的黑暗与末世氛围中。制作上注重细节质感，合成器延迟与混响层层渗透，节拍缓慢爬行般推进，人声冰冷中性、飘忽如幽灵。评论将其与Atelecine、Mika Vainio等声音艺术家并置，并提及Birthday Party、Pelican Daughters等墨尔本后朋克传统的影响。整张作品在暗潮、合成器工业与后朋克之间游走，声音设计考究，情感表达克制而深沉，是面向小众听众的实验性暗潮佳作。2026年的新版压制为这张已有的氛围之作提供了再次被聆听的机会。

items.body:
The spirit of legendary film score composer Toru Takemitsu looms large over Kotaro Maruyama’s economical yet lush studies, ranging from sublime echoes of Japanese environmental ambient to beatific pulse poems edging on weightless Heinrich Mueller works.

"Composing primarily with the piano, Kotaro Maruyama creates music for a variety of visual media, including commercials and short films. Influenced by the composer Toru Takemitsu, he places importance on the “silence” and "ambience" of sound, aiming to create works where the music quietly depicts a scene.

Kotaro Maruyama's first solo album, "Vapor Curve," is constructed entirely from the sound source of the OP-Z digital synthesizer. Notably, he avoids the concept of harmony for a single tone, instead pursuing a unique "woven harmony" created by intricately layering multiple independent melodies. Using only the OP-Z, and recording everything in a single take without using a computer, Kotaro Maruyama's "Vapor Curve" is distinguished by its uncompromising production style. The minimalist melodies that are layered to create an ambient soundscape, along with the incidental noise that gives an organic texture to the inorganic electronic sound, showcase the raw appeal of sound that is imperfect."
items._cn_summary: Kotaro Maruyama的首张个人专辑完全以OP-Z数字合成器为音源，不借助电脑、一次性录制完成，展现出高度自律的制作方式。音乐深受武满彻影响，强调声音中的“留白”与氛围感，避免传统和声结构，转而通过多条独立极简旋律的精细叠加，形成独特的“编织和声”。环境音景中穿插的偶然噪音，为冰冷的电子声响注入了有机质感，使整张作品在环境电子与实验极简之间取得平衡，呈现出对声音材质与空间层次的深入探索。

items.body:
Required listening for computer music freaks, 'Synthesized Voices' originally appeared in 1976, collecting innovative composer Charles Dodge's prophetic vocal experiments - recordings of Mark Strand's surrealist poems recreated on Bell Laboratories' uncanny synthetic speech tech. If you're into Anton Bruhin's deranged 'Speech Poems', this'll hit the spot.

You've got to applaud DINTE for the timing of this one. Right now, it's hard to tell what's a real voice and what's been cobbled together using LLM tech, Frankensteined from decades of scraped voiceovers and newsreels. Synthesized voices are stapled to short form content and used to provide an air of humanity to mass-generated robo-slop. And listening to Dodge's set of pioneering studies, it's remarkable how the technology has evolved in such a short period of time. In the early '70s, when Dodge began his investigations, heavily synthesised voices were terrifyingly mechanical, usually used to depict malign forces - just cop any of those vintage Doctor Who episodes that feature Cybermen. What's fascinating is that Dodge seems to understand its crucial limitation; he doesn't attempt to make the voice sound more human (and therefore more tolerable), but mirrors Strand's absurdist logic instead, going beyond the limit of the larynx.

Dodge explains that he labels it computer music because it's the Bell Labs computer setup that analysed and synthesised the voices, but he's quick to say that it's not generative music. Each poem was recorded to tape first then fed into the mainframe, that was then able to recreate the language using a pre-loaded archive of words and phrases. This would have resulted in a dry study, so Dodge tested the limits of the system by reconfiguring the parameters beforehand, shifting the pitch contour, the formants and duration of the syllables to radically diverge from the way we actually speak. The eight-minute 'In Celebration' is a great starting point. Composed in 1975, it seemingly shreds Strand's poem of the same name, in actuality locating its spirit, hanging on the word "you" just like Strand does. Dodge works with speed and pitch radically, twisting the phrases into machine-gunned barrages or disorienting decelerated harmonies. The words are still there - "your lungs prepare themselves for an ashen feeling" is a banger - but they've become hoarse, noisy growls or synthetic cries. 

The four part 'Speech Songs' is lighter, rooted in poems that were intended to invite audiences to respond with laughter, yet there's something even more disturbing about a computerised voice noisily bellowing out the same word, stuttering and getting stuck on throwaway rhymes. Really, Dodge hits his stride with the ambitious 'The Story of Our Lives', an "operatic dialogue for male and female synthetic voices" that we'd love to think Robert Ashley heard. There's a similar commitment to breaking down the formula of theater and opera on display here as Dodge corrupts these mundane utterances, forcing out near-songs and high drama from soap opera-ready domestic situations. With Dodge at the controls, the words shift haphazardly from recognizable to horrifyingly alien for almost no reason whatsoever, adding a sense of danger to what might regularly be daytime telly. It's an astute skewering of American culture that's maybe more relevant now than it ever was.
items._genre: electroacoustic / computer music / vocal synthesis / experimental composition
items._cn_summary: 这张1976年的专辑收录了查尔斯·道奇在贝尔实验室利用早期语音合成技术对超现实主义诗人马克·斯特兰德诗作的重新演绎。创作流程并非生成式算法：诗人朗诵先录至磁带，再输入主机，系统依据预存词库重组语言。道奇刻意不追求人声拟真，而是通过改变音高轮廓、共振峰与音节时长，让合成声音偏离自然发声机制，走向嘶哑、咆哮与机械嘶鸣。收录的《庆祝》以八分钟篇幅展现激进变形，《Speech Songs》四首则更具荒诞喜感，《我们生活的故事》以男女合成声构建歌剧式对话，解构传统戏剧结构。专辑作为计算机音乐史上的先驱文献，对理解语音合成从恐怖符号到日常工具的演变提供了关键参照。

items.body:
Picking up where 2024's 'Trash Can Lamb' left off, Keith Freund blurs the line between acoustic instrumentation and DIY electronics on his latest full-length, unraveling his gentle, jazzy sessions with 8-bit beats and oddball FX.

Since the beginning, Freund has been fixated on the character of a sound rather than what that sound, on its own, might represent. His piano parts rarely come off as if they've been played by hand; after chopping them to shreds, he inevitably reconstitutes them into player-piano style impossible sequences, re-organizing the notes and re-sculpting the tone completely. On 'Over Sidewalk Bryum', for example, it's the piano that provides the track's rhythm, accented by radio interference and bit-crushed oscillations. And although Freund does less chipping at his horn parts, letting the sax soar over the chattering electronics, it's still subtly tweaked - nothing's ever quite what it seems.

A swamp of discarded blips and glitches help prop up 'I'll Find a Place for Us', and Freund's soft woodwind tones make their way through the noise initially - or at least that's what we're supposed to think. In time, Freund's sax emerges and the soft-hued, woodwind-like sound is revealed to be a red herring. But that's the kind of sleight of hand that Freund seems to revel in, creating glitchy, unstable music from soft, placid sound sources, not the harsh digital detritus you'd expect to find on a Mille Plateaux disc.
items._cn_summary: Keith Freund延续前作手法，将原声爵士乐器与DIY电子融合。钢琴被切碎重组为自动钢琴式的不可能序列，在《Over Sidewalk Bryum》中成为节奏骨架，叠加无线电干扰与bit-crushed振荡。萨克斯部分保留即兴呼吸感，但经微妙处理，在故障噪声中穿行。《I'll Find a Place for Us》以废弃音效与glitches为基底，木管般的音色实为萨克斯的伪装，展现其声学错觉手法。整张专辑从柔和声源中提炼不稳定、故障化的声响，区别于典型数字噪音，呈现细腻而难以捉摸的实验气质。

items.body:
Returning to Jabu's do you have peace? imprint, Bristol-based Ukrainian artist Regina Collage reflects on global and personal instability, infusing her haunted, lo-fi songs with tentative passion. It's gorgeous, fragile and deeply personal pop - somewhere between HTRK, Broadcast and Cukor Bila Smert’.

Hailing from Kharkiv where her parents still live, Collage is acutely aware of the lasting impacts of war - the severed relationships, the daily, ongoing trauma. In Bristol, she's away from the front line, but carries it with her, a feeling of "quiet shame" that grounds her latest album's subtle, minimal arrangements. Because although her voice is at the centre of the album, she rarely raises it to more than a distant whisper, sounding as if she's trapped in a liminal space between realities. On 'It Should Be Something', she drowns her moans in reverb, harmonising with echo trails, bass guitar plucks and languid riffs; it's music that won't come as a complete surprise to anyone familiar with Jabu's output, but Collage's outlook is slower, sadder and more exposed. Sure, she plays fast and loose with effects, but the processes never obscure the album's core emotions - heart-melting feelings we haven't heard rendered quite so perfectly since we locked in with Jonnine's 'Southside Girl'. 

'Horizont' is rooted in a kind of bedroom-recorded post-punk that's so slow and gummed up with noise you'd think it was some STROOM-related archival discovery. On 'Davno', her voice seems to float around a simple, distorted drum machine and ebbing analog synths, molded into casual moans that betray Collage's sobering, vulnerable themes. But she's almost in a different headspace altogether on 'I Hope', curling her words around a Hooky-style staccato bassline and anticipating a beat that never actually comes. Each song sounds as if it's a torn page from her scrapbook, not exactly half-finished, but certainly not polished - and it's this aesthetic that gives the album so much emotional weight. We get to reach into Collage's psyche, hearing her own instability as she wonders about a world that's been thrown into chaos. As she reconciles with the situation, figuring out her life in Bristol at the same time, she constructs a sound that's similarly dualistic - unashamedly displaying its roots in the Ukrainian underground while absorbing ideas from her new home.
items._genre: post-punk / darkwave / lo-fi / experimental pop / electronic
items._cn_summary: 乌克兰艺术家Regina Collage在布里斯托尔创作的作品，以卧室录音美学承载战争创伤与流离失所的个人情感。她的嗓音始终压得很低，仿佛在现实与记忆的夹缝中低语，混响与回声拖曳出缓慢、黏稠的后朋克肌理。模拟合成器、失真鼓机与断续的贝斯线构成极简而沉浸的声响空间，每首歌都像从私人剪贴簿中撕下的残页，保留着未完成的粗粝感。专辑同时扎根于乌克兰地下音乐传统，并吸收新居地的声音养分，在双重文化视角下形成独特的抒情气质。乐评认为其情感表达直接而脆弱，在同类暗潮系创作中具有罕见的坦诚与感染力。

items.body:
On Kirk Barley’s definitive solo gem, alternative tunings and a tactile feel for pitching rhythms generate their gentlest and most absorbing work, twinkling amid a microcosm of similar, exploratory productions from Mark Fell & Rian Treanor thru to Aleksi Perälä, Beatrice Dillon, Terry Riley & Jon Hassell.

Building on a decade of work spanning cuts for Brownswood thru to jams with Matthew Herbert and Matt Davies, ‘Arc’ finds Yorkshire-bred artist Barley fully indulge formative passions for microtonal just intonation - as seeded in Terry Riley’s ‘Shri Camel’ - and slippery syncopation to the fullest. Half solo, proper, and half peppered with percussion by regular spar, Matt Davies, it follows his nose for open frontiers of alternative tunings and wonky meter with the blend of low key modesty and prism-pushing tekkerz that have long endeared his work to lovers of lower case experimental music. 

Sweetly balanced between timeless, folk-soul-wise and futurist sensibilities, the half hour suite knits hyaline synths and rippling gamelan metallophonics with clarinet and guitar in lissom, sloshing shapes that effortlessly seduce, rather than demand, the listener’s attention. In particular we are drawn to the bits in duo with Davies, floating sublime ideas in the dreamlike, inverted dub architexture of ‘Ion’, settling on mind like a strangely bucolic Incus work on ’Sundry’, and thru the exquisite, tip-toed rhythms of ‘Ecstatic’, to a trippier, bittersweet type of ante-chamber music on ‘Fret (Hear)’.

He’s also deeply charming when left to his own devices. Ambient opener ‘Billow’ calls to mind the tenderness of Cotton Goods works, and ‘Knead’ chases a certain geist of Irdial or Plaid-esque gamelantronica into the sublime title tune, while ‘Prism’ most beautifully ties all his interests in a melting dream sequence which he caps with the harmonic nightlight glow of ‘Column’.
items._cn_summary: Kirk Barley的《Arc》是其个人创作中的代表之作，基于十年间从Brownswood到与Matthew Herbert合作的广泛实践，深入探索微分音纯律与另类调弦。专辑半数为独奏，半数与打击乐手Matt Davies合作，将透明质感的合成器、涟漪般的甘美兰金属打击乐、单簧管与吉他编织成流畅而摇摆的声响形态。曲目如《Ion》《Sundry》《Ecstatic》在梦幻倒置的混响结构中呈现精致步点，兼具田园气息与实验前卫的室内乐质感。独奏部分如《Billow》《Knead》《Prism》《Column》则展现温柔旋律与和声夜光，呼应Terry Riley、Plaid等谱系。整张作品在低调谦逊与棱镜式技术探索之间取得平衡，以不强迫聆听的方式自然吸引注意力，将民谣般的感性、未来主义视野与微妙的节奏错位融为一体，是实验电子与当代极简传统中值得细品的佳作。

items.body: In April 2025, Argentinian, Brooklyn-based pianist Leo Genovese just finished a concert with The Mars Volta at Madison Square Garden and had ninety free minutes before the tour bus would move on. He called his friends - Japanese, Tokyo-based double bass player (and cellist) Takeshi Sugawa, one of the busiest musicians in the Japanese scene, leader of his Banksia trio, who hosted Genovese in his debut album as bandleader ( Outgrowing , 2018, with drummer Tom Rainey), who was in New York as part of the Satoko Fujii Tokyo Trio North American tour, and Australian drummer Alfred Vogel, of How Noisy Are the Rooms? And Vanish trios, the founder of Boomslang Records and the Bezau Beatz festival, who was visiting New York and had previously recorded with Genovese ( Eyes to the Sun , Boomslang, 2024, with fellow Argentinian sax player Camila Nebbia). Sugawa and Vogel did not know each other, and the ad hoc trio met for dinner in a small restaurant and immediately felt the need to play together. Genovese, Sugawa, and Vogel promised each other that they had to repeat this experience. It did not take long. In May 2025, Genovese played in Berlin with Esperanza Spalding, Sugawa was touring in Europe, and Vogel booked the Bonello Studio in Berlin for an all-night, free-improvised recording session that produced Unleashed . The music is quite spacious and understated, sketching its movement with delicate, skeletal strokes, without a plan and with no aim of reaching cohesive structures or grooves, as if asking the listener to be an active part of its creation and imagine where it can land. Genovese, Sugawa, and Vogel are attuned to every sound and gesture, as each one opens more sonic threads, but without attaching themselves to any of them. Melodic veins rise and dissolve organically, but the deep listening, deeply poetic, spontaneous, primal, and collective, egalitarian process is the essence of this trio. The trio distills its dynamics on the poetic, 13-minute “A World of One Colour”. Letting go and just being in the moment when everything opens, or, as Sugawa puts it, “A spirit that wanders, that lives across times and places.” Hopefully, Genovese, Sugawa, and Vogel would find time in their busy schedules to take this trio on the road, letting it blossom even more on a tight tour. UNLEASHED by Leo Genovese, Takashi Sugawa, Alfred Vogel Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑源自三位乐手在柏林的一次即兴录音，钢琴、低音提琴与鼓在无预设框架下展开对话。音乐以疏朗、克制的笔触勾勒轮廓，不追求完整的结构和律动，而是让声音线索自然浮现又消散，留白与聆听成为核心。三位乐手对彼此声响高度敏感，在集体即兴中保持平等的互动关系，尤其以13分钟的《A World of One Colour》凝聚了全碟的诗意气质。这种即兴并非炫技，而是强调当下性与开放性，邀请听众参与声音的未完成叙事。阿根廷钢琴家、日本贝斯手与澳大利亚鼓手的跨国组合，也为自由即兴注入了多元文化背景下的默契与流动性。

items.body: Improvisations for the Land proceeds with unusual patience. Alessandro Ciccarelli and Milena Punzi Anfossi never seem in a hurry to introduce new material. Instead, they linger over individual sounds, allowing them to exhaust their possibilities before searching for another direction. At several points the music appears to reach an impasse, only for one of the musicians to uncover an entirely new path from within the same sonic terrain. The three improvisations share this quality of persistence, probing ever deeper where it might seem there is nothing left to uncover. The relationship between analogue synthesizer and electric cello is one of constant adjustment. Neither instrument occupies a permanent foreground. Sometimes the synthesizer holds a low-frequency plateau almost stubbornly while the cello slowly alters its pressure, grain and register around it. Elsewhere the electronics recede almost completely, leaving bowed textures to define the pace before quietly reclaiming the space through sustained drones and subtle shifts in colour. The music rarely advances through contrast. It moves by patiently examining the consequences of each gesture. Trial-and-error and risk-taking shape the entire album. High frequencies are sometimes sustained long enough to become physically demanding, forcing the listener to remain inside their unsettling presence instead of treating them as fleeting accents. Low drones establish a bodily weight that occasionally feels architectural rather than harmonic. Even when the texture thickens, each sound retains its own presence, allowing the ear to follow the gradual redistribution of energy across the spectrum. Listening repeatedly, one becomes increasingly aware of how carefully the musicians resist resolution. Electronic textures are allowed to stall. Bowed sounds lose energy without being replaced. Instead of smoothing over moments of uncertainty, Ciccarelli and Punzi Anfossi remain with them, allowing hesitation and suspension to become productive musical states. There is a quiet confidence in this willingness to stay with a sound after it has apparently reached its destination. The titles inevitably invite historical associations. Named after Palestinian villages destroyed during the Nakba, the three improvisations carry an emotional and political charge that extends beyond the music itself. Yet, as the musicians explain in the accompanying interview, the names were chosen only after the recordings had been completed. They do not function as narratives but acknowledge a state of mind that accompanied the project. The music retains its autonomy while remaining inseparable from the experiences that shaped its creation. The cover artwork quietly reinforces this idea. Its layered aerial image shows a fractured landscape at different degrees of resolution and density. Surfaces overlap, traces emerge only to disappear beneath new textures, and the eye is left to make sense of the jagged terrain. It mirrors the music’s own behaviour: sounds accumulate through successive layers, preserving earlier gestures without ever allowing them to become fixed. There is no attempt to overwhelm the listener through density or technical display. The album asks for a different kind of attention, one willing to remain inside slowly evolving textures and to follow sounds beyond their apparent destination. The longer one spends with these improvisations, the more they reveal through the patient excavation of what was already there. That patient search gives Improvisations for the Land its own voice. photo by Leonardo Chiarabini – The Factory PRD To explore things further, we have reached out to Alessandro Ciccarelli and Milena Punzi Anfossi. Improvisations for the Land is rooted in free improvisation, yet the album is also explicitly dedicated to Palestine, with each piece named after a village destroyed during the Nakba in 1948. Rather than illustrating specific events, the music seems to inhabit a space of tension, absence, and attentive listening. How did the decision to name the pieces after Isdud, Jusayr, and Hulayqat shape the improvisations themselves? Were you thinking about these places while performing, or did their historical weight become part of the music retrospectively? We believe that instrumental music — and, more specifically, the kind of improvisational practice we pursue — belongs to a process of abstraction in which music both can and should represent nothing but itself, rather than describing or illustrating events, images, or narratives. This autonomy, however, does not justify the notion of an art detached from life. On the contrary, life itself, the events that surround us, and the history we live through inevitably permeate our being, our sensibilities, and our actions as individuals and as musicians. For this reason, although sound does not represent anything, it is never a neutral or sterile space. As John Cage famously said, “Everything we do is music.” The world therefore does not remain outside music; it inevitably enters it through those who create it and those who listen. In his writings on music, Edward Said consistently defended the formal rigor of classical music without ever separating it from his condition as a Palestinian intellectual living in exile. For him, these two dimensions were never in conflict; they coexisted within the same gesture. The autonomy of form does not entail amnesia on the part of those who practice it. With this in mind, the titles of these pieces are neither captions nor interpretative keys, nor do they ask the listener to search within the music for references to a place or event. In her essay “Against Interpretation,” Susan Sontag argued that interpretation can become a way of taming a work of art — reducing it to its content and then interpreting that, making it manageable. At a time when criticism tended to approach every work as something to decode, the first question became, “What does it mean?”— as though its value lay in some hidden message waiting to be extracted and restated elsewhere. For Sontag, this is precisely what taming means: neutralizing what is intrinsic to a work, what cannot be reduced to a concept, in order to render it harmless. At bottom, this is what she calls “the philistine refusal to leave the work of art alone.” Interpretation risked extinguishing the immediate, sensory impact that a work has on those who hear or see it — an experience that is essential and prior to any content one might later extract from it. We therefore conceive these titles not as content to be extracted from the music, but as biographical traces of ourselves. They do not assign meaning to the listening experience; rather, they point to those who made the music. The decision to title and dedicate these pieces to villages destroyed during the Nakba came only afterward, once the music already existed, but not in order to impose an external meaning upon it. Rather, it was an acknowledgment that those improvisations had already been traversed by our own anxieties, by the anger and grief we felt in the face of the unspeakable. The title does not explain the music; it names the condition of those who created it. Isdud 1930 In the liner notes you write that, while art cannot stop violence, it also cannot remain isolated from the world. That raises a broader question about artistic responsibility. When working on an entirely improvised album, how do you negotiate the relationship between political intention and musical openness? Were there moments where you felt the music itself resisted the conceptual framework you had established, or did improvisation become precisely the right language for responding to events that seem almost impossible to represent? Free improvisation is probably the musical practice in which the performer’s life, emotions, thoughts, and memories enter the musical act most directly. Not by narrating events, but by allowing the sound itself to reveal a presence of one’s inner world that precedes any explanation. Unlike composed music, the outcome of improvisation is always bound to the hic et nunc of the self, and of the self in relation to the other. The environment, one’s state of mind, one’s thoughts, and interpersonal relationships are all integral to the construction of the music. They do not constitute an external context; they are among the very materials of improvisation. For Christopher Small, music is not so much an object as a shared activity — a process of musicking that encompasses performers, listeners, and the relationships that emerge between them in the moment of performance. If there is a political dimension, it is enacted within this network of relationships that comes into being every time people make music together. Pauline Oliveros described Deep Listening as the practice of “listening in every possible way to everything possible to hear.” For us, this means that improvisation is not merely about producing sounds, but about assuming the responsibility of being fully present: listening to one another, to the space, and to the world. It is a mode of listening that precedes expressive intention and also entails a willingness to be transformed by whatever unfolds. For this reason, we have never experienced any tension between political commitment and musical openness. As we suggested earlier, lived experience inevitably enters the sound itself, and precisely for that reason we believe free improvisation is the language best suited to engaging with events that exceed every possibility of representation. Faced with tragedies of this magnitude, music neither can nor should claim to narrate, explain, or stand in for history. What it can do is become a space in which such experiences continue to question both those who perform and those who listen. According to Jacques Rancière, the politics of art does not reside in the message it conveys, but in the way it reconfigures the distribution of the sensible — that is, what can be seen, heard, and shared. In a complementary sense, Jacques Attali argued that music is prophecy: rather than merely reflecting society, it heralds forms that have not yet become visible elsewhere, in a movement he calls annunciatory. If this is true, then a record such as this does not simply “comment” on tragedy through its titles. Rather, in the very way it is organized and experienced, it attempts to imagine a different configuration of reality. For this reason, we do not believe in the possibility of neutral art. The autonomy of music does not mean isolation from history. Every sonic gesture emerges within a network of relationships, experiences, and responsibilities. In this sense, it is not so much that music “speaks about politics”; rather, sound itself, as a human gesture situated in the world, inevitably possesses a political dimension. Sound is political. Hulayqat 1940s map Compared to your previous duo album All’improvviso, the instrumentation here has been reduced to its bare essentials: electric cello and analogue synthesizer. Yet that apparent limitation produces an extraordinarily rich sonic vocabulary, where it often becomes difficult to distinguish which sounds belong to the cello and which emerge from the synthesizer. How has your musical dialogue evolved since your first collaboration, and what possibilities did this more austere instrumental setup open up for both of you? We both share the need to constantly question ourselves and to explore new ways of discovering sound within sound. This happens both individually, through our own personal research, and collectively in our work as a duo. By “new means” we do not simply refer to different devices or instruments, as was the case with our first album, All’Improvviso, but also to new expressive possibilities that emerge from a deeper exploration of each instrument itself. Sometimes, innovation does not come from adding new elements, but from looking more deeply at what is already available to us and questioning our habitual ways of using it. Our decision to reduce the instrumentation to an electric cello and an analogue synthesizer was therefore not an act of renunciation, but part of this very process: a way of focusing our attention on sonic material itself. Limiting our means — both in terms of instruments and musical materials — has never felt like a constraint. On the contrary, it creates a deeper space for exploration, where every timbral variation, every resonance, and every subtle detail acquires greater significance. Giacinto Scelsi spoke of the profondeur du son — the depth of sound — conceiving sound not merely as a vehicle for music but as an autonomous universe to be explored in its own internal complexity. From this perspective, our interest is not simply in combining the electric cello and the analogue synthesizer as two distinct instruments, but in exploring the point at which their identities begin to dissolve and sound becomes a shared space, a material in continuous transformation. This exploration unfolds through a process of exchange and reciprocity, ideally reaching a point where the distinction between the two sound sources no longer matters. The fact that it is often difficult to tell whether a particular sound originates from the cello or the synthesizer is therefore not merely the result of each of us pursuing our own timbral research. Rather, it is the outcome of an encounter between two depths: both instruments become generators of a shared sonic material, continuously transformed through listening, interaction, and mutual responsiveness. Jusair 1940s map Listening to Improvisations for the Land, I was struck by how much the music relies on restraint. Silence, resonance, and microscopic changes in timbre often carry as much expressive weight as the more overt musical gestures, while the dialogue between electric cello and analogue synthesizer unfolds with remarkable patience and responsiveness. At many points it becomes difficult to tell where one instrument ends and the other begins, as both seem to inhabit the same evolving sonic space. How do you cultivate that degree of mutual listening during improvisation? Is it something that develops over years of playing together, or do you deliberately create conditions that allow unexpected musical relationships to emerge in the moment? Although a musical relationship can certainly be built and deepened over time through shared experience and growing familiarity, there are also rare encounters in which something seems to happen immediately, before words and without the need for any particular preparation. These are the moments when a musical dialogue emerges from the very first sound, as a form of mutual recognition. That epiphany is exactly what happened the first time we played together as a duo. All’improvviso, our first album, grew out of that experience: a first meeting, with no rehearsal, no predetermined structures, and no direction established in advance. We simply brought our willingness to listen and to respond to whatever unfolded in the present moment. Ever since that first encounter, we have had the feeling that our shared sound has always found its own continuity, its own direction, while remaining completely open. Of course, this sense of affinity does not imply the absence of research or risk. On the contrary, within such a deep mode of listening, the unexpected becomes an essential source of creative energy. What we do not know is not an obstacle but an opportunity for transformation. Improvisation ultimately lives within this tension between familiarity and the unknown. Writing about non-idiomatic improvisation, Derek Bailey argued that the value of this practice lies precisely in not knowing in advance what will happen. It is not defined by the absence of an idiom, but by the decision to relinquish any pre-existing idiom in order to remain in the position of discovering something together with another person. We recognize the foundation of our own listening to one another in that condition, more than in any acquired technique. For us, improvisation means exposing ourselves to the risk of losing what we already know, accepting that control can never be total, and allowing space for something that can emerge only through the relationship itself. It is precisely this dimension of risk that keeps the musical dialogue alive and vital. In this sense, listening is not simply the ability to follow the other; it is also the willingness to allow the other to change the course of our own path. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以罕见的耐心展开三首即兴作品，模拟合成器与电大提琴之间持续调整，彼此都不占据固定前景。音乐不通过对比推进，而是细致考察每个声音手势的后果，允许纹理停滞、能量衰减，甚至将犹豫与悬置转化为具有生产性的音乐状态。高频率有时被延长至令人不适的强度，低音 drone 则带有近乎建筑般的重量感。三首曲目以 Nakba 中被摧毁的巴勒斯坦村庄命名，但标题在录音完成后才确定，并非叙事，而是对伴随创作的心境的一种承认。封面分层航拍图像呈现破碎地貌的叠加与消隐，与音乐中声音的浮现和消失形成呼应。整体上，这张专辑在即兴的不可预测性与声音材料的深度勘探之间取得了平衡。

items.album: Dean De Benedictis :: Salvaging The Future (Spotted Peccary Music)

items.body: With the completion of this trilogy, we acknowledge our part as a remote viewer of Dean’s life over three decades. Salvaging The Future—perhaps more than the prior two albums—is a restless collage, yet it is so well mixed that it lends itself to uninterrupted full-album listening. This listener is tuning in about 2x per day at the moment. Despite the challenges these decades have wrought, the trilogy’s close with “Our Story Survives Collectively” leaves us with a sense of hope. This is music for visioning. Revolutionizing the human listening experience Salvaging The Future by Dean De Benedictis Salvaging the Future utilizes electronic mastery alongside sparse traditional acoustic instruments and vocals to revolutionize the human listening experience. There will be no undisturbed sleeping, only optional vivid, deep-set dreaming. Music that completely upends your expectations can feel like a sensory assault on the first spin, but the feeling soon becomes mostly energizing and sustaining, including a wispy blend of limitless and beatless space signatures, as well as beat inspired enchantment. This is Art, intending to allow the unconscious mind to somehow express itself, often resulting in the depiction of illogical or dreamlike scenes and ideas. “Moving forward with mindfulness would quite literally mean salvaging the future,” offers De Benedictis. We may expect The Future to bring about profound changes in our listening arts through universal joyfulness, mindful that nothing is forever. As for dancing, that is up to you. I seek a collage shifting into every new world imaginable, or mostly never before imagined. Southern California-based artist Dean De Benedictis has delivered an absolute masterpiece for your collection of auditory journeys that completely bypass conventional reason and transport your mind into uncharted, supernatural territories. He ​is widely recognized in the electronic ambient community as Surface 10. Surface 10 has a long history with performing at galactic electronic music festivals as well as releasing his solo and collaborative recordings internationally, such as on the DiN label, Hypnotic, Space For Music, as well as some self-released works. His previous work with Spotted Peccary Music includes a collaborative project called Desensitized, with Deborah Martin (Hemispherica Portalis, 2020, and Chaos In Premonition, 2022) as well as two solo albums, Salvaging the Past (2005) and Salvaging the Present (2016). Only optional vivid, deep-set dreaming :: Salvaging the Future presents an attempt to conceive and apply a good degree of futurism to every aspect of its creation. From sound design, to instrumentation, to compositional production, perhaps one way to see it (or hear it) is as an illusive combination of progressive and contemporary influences that all “tap the future on the shoulder” or if nothing else, maybe exchange a hat-tip to that which is to come. Additionally, the obvious suggestion that humanity’s future may still have hope for survival and even thriving; that we may somehow redeem and persevere not by forgetting or dismissing our weight of the past, but acknowledging and accounting for life experiences as a strategy for our progress ahead. “Aside from representing phases of my life, the Salvaging series began as one idea, and ended as another,” confides De Benedictis. “The musical style of Salvaging The Future follows the suggestion of its inherent theme: a wild departure from most past and current genres, diving head first into hyper-forward approaches, perhaps in some ways “of the future.” “I would produce and perform music in harsh desert planes, steep canyons, mountainsides and summits, windswept shores and forested wilderness; I would work in abandoned buildings, housing construction, airplane flights, cafes, hotels, museums, libraries, or while staying with friends, family, or indeed at home, which was most of the time even if not by far. I tended to do a lot of re-synth types of methods, so found sounds combined with both customized sample libraries and Apple libraries were yet again the main source of instrumentation on Salvaging The Future, much like Salvaging The Present.” Also, like Salvaging The Present, there was an immense amount of processor stacking and automation, mountains of hardware, on every instrument track. “Featured on both albums was also a customized library of drum hits I created in 2014, in which each hit captures the reverb trail-from a note (or harmony) that was sung just before it. This hit library formulated a fairly unmistakable signature-sound in most of my work that followed. I still use that custom-drum-hits library to this day. However, unlike Salvaging The Present, which was completely produced on only one laptop, Salvaging The Future was composed on my first two laptops as well as my first tower. It was all old Apple gear and software, but for some reason that still sounded better to me than some of my newer gear and software, so I decided to just accept the old-system setbacks and finish the album on those devices regardless. A wild departure from most past and current genres :: “It almost broke me. I had to deal with endless system complications on every device, prompting constant work-arounds with Logic and Ableton, but the sound made it worthwhile for me.” De Benedictis continues his long, internationally recognized history of stripping ordinary objects of their normal significance to expose deep psychological truths. By tying an essential common thread between opposing genres, he has created an abstract, emotionally rich masterwork that demands to be heard for fans of avant-garde electronic exploration. Salvaging the Future was composed, performed, mixed, edited, designed and conceptualized by Dean De Benedictis between 2010 and 2025, using mostly software on laptops. His additional instruments were flute, voice, piano and guitar. Production locations were scattered throughout the US west coast but based primarily in Thousand Oaks and Santa Monica, CA. Contributing extra recorded musicians, in addition to Apple loops, include: Lara De Benedictis (vocals), D’Von Charley (vocals and native flute), Nichole Michelle Jones (vocals), Lisa Claire Mitterer (vocals), Phil Williams (electric guitar), and various ASMR artists. ASMRtists. Autonomous Sensory Meridian Response (ASMR) and Ray Kersweil’s futurist theory of the Singularity are two unrelated ideas I came across while researching this music, both have been popular but I have never before heard of them, so kudos. ASMR seems to explore some of the physical psychology of sound. The Kersweil concepts are set in the future, during the coming singularity, and all planets and celestial bodies are now shifting and morphing and changing as that same singularity. This revolutionary sonic journey begins abruptly with “My Love Is An Extinction Event” (6:10), a track whose song title invokes the concept of a rapid, widespread drop in biodiversity. Here things come together and things come apart and sometimes this happens at the same time, spinning and bouncing, falling and transferring velocity, which feels bizarre, unbelievable, dreamlike and leads into very strange restless ear-born images. The kind that will change your life. At one moment the mood goes from feeling frenetic to feeling incredibly alive and layered. This unexpected salad of situations, places, or emotional moments that seem detached from everyday reality or logic all feel pretty good, the intimate links between freeing imagination and the mind, and liberation from repressive and archaic social structures. In the beginning, deep space has no beat. Welcome to “The Outer Links”  (6:31). Coming from an intentionally beatless expanse designed to liberate the imagination, giving the listener the sensation of flying through colorful lights, and maneuvering deliberately to liberate the imagination. We are flying along at a more rapid speed now. The feeling is all about bright stars and a sense of transit. Soon everything is almost flying apart and the beat is going at a fast clip. As the album progresses, we encounter “Voca”  (3:35), where small pieces suddenly click and morph into a fast-paced, jamming run driven by a sexy bassline and seasonably hot drum tones. Perhaps the tempo is a bit fidgety but always rich in tone and interesting in context, jumping into many places to tell the story. I do not understand the punchline, but even real life itself can be strange and even uncomfortable when seeking sustenance. Music for visioning :: I think the fourth track starts in a calm memory palace illuminated with tall marble columns, with big bright halls and stairways. Soon a beat contraption comes together and the vocalists start to arrive. “They Fought To Sway” (7:18) is my personal favorite here, the vocals reach a place I have never heard before, and I like that. “Urband Glacier Fund”  (6:27) is probably holding a hidden message, leading to speculation about that extra d in Urband. Hidden portals bring delight, I think that we are in outer space coming upon some new life forms, our synthesizers are carefully subtle and fully capable. Now a new beat arrives and takes over, a new darkness has surrounded the cabin. Are there glaciers in outer space? The flute is here to take us along, with amazing high energy. Now we encounter a big cinematic sly beat and things are happening all over the place, very exciting. “ASMR Tragedy Lines” (6:44) seems to take place down in a very deep tunnel or cavern, robots are building things quietly, except for this one guy. It gets extremely quiet out here, where we are in the cavern. The perception distorts, morphs, and transforms ordinary objects and forms into strange and uncanny variations of themselves. Down there something is always sparkling. Now the whispers in the darkness take over. I keep straining to hear what the voices are planning next. The imaginary narrative shifts beautifully on “Salvaging My Story” (7:12), a track full of radiant stars, choirs, and unexpected juxtapositions that exercise the grand element of surprise. Let’s go out into the fields at night where the space ships will land, be sure to keep an eye out. There are steam powered machines running, there are crickets and I expect to find the children of the night out here. Soon there is a change. There is a shy melodic tune lingering in the caverns along with the choirs and radiant stars. Soon all of the details start coming into focus, this is a big story with plenty of flying at night. Away we are going, exercising the element of surprise, unexpected juxtapositions and non sequitur. It works. This leads right into the slow-burning sunrise of “Future Incandescence” (6:32) which unfolds like a long slow transit in deep space. Now the pace is slower and the feeling is starker, disorienting, with the hallucinatory quality of a dream. There is a language of fragments that flow together and make the whole sound. We are still on the ship, snug inside a safe metal box that is still moving, the closest star is emerging from an eclipse, there are emotions and suspense, there is tension building. The natural world takes a surreal turn on “All The Wild” (4:27), where there are strange gumblings coming from animals that I cannot see. We are all probably back in the big cave again, at night. This time with strange recordings of birds and wildlife playing in the darkness. The variety of strange sounds increases as new species come floating into our range. There are a lot of creatures heard here, such as birds or lizards cooing, insects clicking and humming. I think I hear a synth glowing, perhaps a swan, with pianos and choirs and sustained tones echoing about. Some loons explode or just fly ahead, and there are more new strange creatures. There are whales in our cave here, along with the strings and wings. “Born Of Flight” (7:09) starts in quiet secrecy before combusting into a galloping drum kit that soon clicks like a flying train, keeping the listener in a state of perpetual, blissful motion. We love our cave, it goes on forever. By the end we are clicking like a sleeping railroad carriage, always feeling motion, until we gently float into the close. The album concludes with a magnificent nine-minute epic, “Our Story Survives Collectively” (9:15), and to start we are following our guide into the well lit tunnel or hallway, there are echoes and lots of space above. There are interesting odd vocals, some with a trilling vibrato. Now for me there was suddenly a grand design to the whole program. I could see that there are complimentary combinations of elements and a thriving life force, and we are all together. Salvaging The Future by Dean De Benedictis   Dean De Benedictis is a Southern California-based artist who has always utilized his interest in a variety of styles and cultures to enrich the quality of his musical expression. He aspires to communicate a similar functionality for the experiences of his listeners. Deans’ music is the result of his will to tie an essential common thread together between opposing genres and mentalities, as well as draw from them a natural sense of emotion, expanse and mystery. Sound exposes psychological truth; stripping ordinary objects of their normal significance, to create a compelling image that is beyond ordinary formal organization, in order to evoke empathy from the listener, with a combination of the depictive, the abstract, and the psychological.Driving into the complex, shape-shifting worlds that De Benedictis creates is always a magnificent adventure. He juxtaposes those frantic, glitchy granular textures against massive, cinematic spaces, sometimes he drops a rogue flute solo or harmonica right into a heavy electronic beat. It’s the kind of music that feels less like a collection of songs and more like a living, breathing, possibly dangerous ecosystem; De Benedictis has created an abstract, emotionally rich soundscape universe that rewards the listener.“My Salvaging trilogy of albums was a sincere and perhaps far-flung attempt to tie a form of common thread between the periods of my life and the electronic music I never released during those periods. Naturally, the reoccurring concept and eventual theme of ‘salvaging time’ manifested into the project. I basically have boxes filled with music like this, built up through decades. As such, my Salvaging trilogy was only one of many projects with a similar goal – to salvage works of the past – but the Salvaging Trilogy itself might be my most qualitative among them.“There are some very clear differences in style and approach contrasting each of these three albums, but it’s really the difference between the first album and the two albums following that one where the contrast is most visible. My first Salvaging album in 2005, Salvaging The Past, was a collection of work created throughout the ‘90s in my home studio, where I was surrounded by physical synthesizers and racks of outboard gear. Sometime between that album and the next one, Salvaging The Present, I acquired my first laptop and lots of appropriate software (more laptops would soon follow).“This changed the game, and my life, in ways that I couldn’t have imagined years earlier. I was already a traveler and an outdoorsman, so suddenly having the power to virtually access an entire studio within a little portable box was very liberating, conceptually and literally. I ended up travelling far and wide with the music, albeit mostly within US borders, but still found myself creating spontaneous productions in some of America’s most extreme natural environments. Over a period of about a decade-and-a-half, I lived a separate little lifetime of fair adventure with these devices, even including some uncomfortable brushes with death.“This spanned the length of both concurrent albums after the first one, I endured to keep creating through massive amounts of life changes and personal upheaval; through each new home I found, whether on-the-road or stationary; through broken alliances and rock-and-jazz-band breakups; through family drama and harddrive thefts and accidental overdoses, and of course a pandemic. Even through it all, my personal standard of innovation-balanced-by-emotional-sincerity never faltered, which probably explains the long lapses between Salvaging albums.“My desire to musically attempt going where no man or woman had gone before, both sonically and musically, remained. Everything from my sound-design methods to my processing methods to my performing and editing methods, was all totally signature, through every twist and turn and every new resolution. I suppose that’s what’s most noticeable and even distinguishable about this last and final album of the trilogy, Salvaging The Future; it’s the one with the biggest complexities and most contrasting styles, because my desire for balance between cutting-edge method and emotional sincerity were still unwavering through even the most tumultuous period of my life.”It is only natural, after all, to keep pace with scientific and industrial progress as well as follow the lure of pure psychic automatism, to stand for transforming the alienation which many people feel in the modern period, combined with the sense of reaching more deeply into the psyche, to be made whole with one’s individuality.With the completion of this trilogy, we acknowledge our part as a remote viewer of Dean’s life over three decades. Salvaging The Future—perhaps more than the prior two albums—is a restless collage, yet it is so well mixed that it lends itself to uninterrupted full-album listening. This listener is tuning in about 2x per day at the moment. Despite the challenges these decades have wrought, the trilogy’s close with “Our Story Survives Collectively” leaves us with a sense of hope. This is music for visioning. Salvaging The Future is available on Spotted Peccary Music. [Bandcamp] Salvaging The Future by Dean De Benedictis  The post Dean De Benedictis :: Salvaging The Future (Spotted Peccary Music) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body:
Over the course of the last decade, the group أحمد [Ahmed] has carved out a distinctive approach to the jazz canon through their tireless exploration of the music of Ahmed Abdul-Malik. Mining Abdul-Malik’s compositions and his incorporation of non-Western microtonality into the jazz vocabulary, pianist Pat Thomas, alto saxophone player Seymour Wright, bassist Joel Grip, and drummer Antonin Gerbal have done more than reinterpretation. They have used the music as a foundation for both immersion and subversion of the way that the standard jazz quartet functions within post-bop structures. For last year’s Sama'a (Audition), they went into the studio for an expansive refraction of Abdul-Malik’s Jazz Sahara. During that same session, the four took a slight detour to record Play Monk, a dive into deconstructions of six pieces by Thelonious Monk, all but one of which he recorded in the late 1950s when Abdul-Malik was part of his group. أحمد [Ahmed] has incorporated Monk tunes into their live sets but this is the first time they have focused on his tunes on a recording.

While Thomas, Wright, Grip, and Gerbal have not altered their strategies in the switch of source material, there is one significant shift in the way one listens to this music. A quick search returns no other versions of Abdul-Malik’s pieces other than those recorded by the composer or أحمد [Ahmed] whereas Monk’s “Epistrophy” or “’Round Midnight” have hundreds. Even a less well-known piece like “Oska T” has dozens. Because the pieces covered are so well known, their teasing apart and restructuring of the underlying thematic kernels are more readily evident. Over two CDs, the quartet digs in, with improvisations that range between 20 and 30 minutes with the exception of a seven-minute extrapolation of “Epistrophy.” These extended explorations allow the group to excavate the forms with a focused patience, zeroing in on and elucidating microscopic details, extricating them into the fundamental elements of penetrating improvisations.

The first phrases of the opening “Bye-ya / Epistrophy” provide a glimpse of what is to come. Bass and piano circle around the theme and Gerbal’s lithe drumming circles up to drive momentum. Wright’s stabbing alto picks apart the melody and the four launch off on a circuitous inquiry, dismantling Monk’s tune into its constituent fragments and then reassembling them with constructivist abstraction. Each of the four seize on elements of the underlying piece, playing them off of each other with unwavering resolve, an approach the group continues to advance in their sweeping live sets. There is an insistent intensity as Wright’s notes pick and prod at Thomas’ skewed clusters, Grip’s free walking lines, and Gerbal’s churning free rhythms. Shards of “Epistrophy” are introduced into the mix by Grip and Thomas, slowly accruing with multifaceted erudition.

The group continues to subvert expectations with “Friday the Thirteenth” as Thomas insistently repeats the first phrase of the tune against Grip’s growling arco inversions. Wright’s keypad pops and Gerbal’s open percussion build momentum and Wright unleashes spattered honks that open into a collective four-part splintering of the theme, picking it apart and recasting it with angular exactitude, building density and intensity over the course of the sweeping 26-minute improvisation. “’Round Midnight” gets a relatively straightforward introduction with Wright intoning the theme over sinuous bass and cymbal splashes. Thomas’ spare chords enter as the quartet dynamically transposes the constituent parts of the piece with imperturbable resolution resolving with the riveting cycling hushed snare abrasions that brings the piece to a close.

A seven-minute scorching, stuttering run through “Epistrophy” serves as an interlude to an abstracted, cascading reading of “Evidence” which takes Monk’s stop-start theme and explodes it with relentless, spiraled piano phrases and the hurtling momentum of bass and drums driving Wright’s coruscating alto which prods and jabs with spiky dexterity. The 30-minute improvisation is an engulfing exemplification of unflagging invention. Monk’s “Oska T.,” structured around an obsessively cyclical riff, is a fitting conclusion to the release. The quartet slows things down to a free shuffle with bass and alto arcing over the mutable pulse of piano and drums. The four players adroitly weave their lines in and out of the collective undercurrent with indefatigable ingenuity. While others have dedicated themselves to the reinterpretation of the music of Thelonious Monk, أحمد [Ahmed]’s Play Monk is distinctive in its mastery, fully absorbing his music into the collective rigor and artistry of this singular ensemble.

items._cn_summary: 这支四人乐队长期致力于挖掘小号手阿卜杜勒-马利克鲜少被演绎的作品，他们将非西方微分音融入爵士语汇，对标准四重奏在后波普框架中的运作方式进行拆解与颠覆。本次录音聚焦六首蒙克曲目，多数原版录制于1950年代末阿卜杜勒-马利克在蒙克乐队中担任贝斯手时期。与演绎马利克原作不同，蒙克曲目拥有大量已有版本，乐评因此指出其解构与重组主题核心的方式更为可感。专辑采用双CD规格，多数即兴段落长达20至30分钟，唯独《Epistrophy》的延伸仅七分钟。乐评详细描述了开场曲中贝斯与钢琴环绕主题、鼓手轻盈推进的态势，以及萨克斯手如何以刺入式的高音将旋律拆解，四人将蒙克曲调拆为构成碎片后以构成主义式的抽象重新装配。乐评还强调各乐手紧抓乐曲元素互相角力的方式，指出沙砾般的旋律碎片如何在贝斯与钢琴手中缓慢累积，展现出多面的学识。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由德国出生、常驻肯尼亚的打击乐手 Sven Kacirek 与本土音乐人 Olith Ratengo 组成双人组 Odd Okoddo，并邀请八十三岁的传统肯尼亚 dodo 流派歌手 Ogoya Nengo 共同录制。Nengo 的演唱承载着深厚的传统根基，其声线与 Ratengo 的人声交织呼应，形成跨代际的对话。Kacirek 以 Buchla 合成器、手打击乐与套鼓构建电子律动层，多轨合成的复合节奏在听觉中逐渐显形，从生硬的并置自然过渡到有机整体。人声始终居于前景，技术手段以微妙的方式烘托而非压制传统。专辑体现了文化间的真正回应与交融，传统获得前卫质感，创新则仿佛古已有之。这种非洲传统与电子手段的跨文化协作，在全球离散语境中展现出独特的艺术张力。
