items.body: With “Realities”, Jan Dewulf does something more interesting than simply broaden Mildreda‘s sound. He removes one of the most recognisable elements of “Blue-Devilled” altogether: there is not a single sacred sample on the new album. The quasi-liturgical weight of its predecessor gives way to colder electronics, sharper industrial abrasion and passages that move considerably closer to noise. At the same time, the writing becomes more exposed, allowing tenderness, ageing, regret, loneliness and vulnerability into Mildreda without translating any of them into softness. Scheduled for release on August 28 through Dependent Records, “Realities” is an 18-track double album, also issued as a limited 2CD artbook with 48 pages designed by Henk Willems. Recurring “Reality Checks” run through its structure; Constantin “Breñal” Warter of Calva Y Nada appears on “Rückwärts”, while Suicide Commando‘s Johan Van Roy joins “Virtual Goddess”. Where “Blue-Devilled” worked explicitly with Sartre, “Realities” turns towards Camus and Sisyphus: falling, rebuilding and the uncomfortable recognition that a life does not unfold inside one stable reality, but through successive versions of it. In this conversation, that idea moves far beyond philosophy as an intellectual reference. Dewulf talks about reaching middle age and the lives no longer available to us, why the “Reality Checks” function like the seams in kintsugi, social media complicity, the strange persistence of gods after belief disappears, and why increased vulnerability pushed Mildreda towards more violent sound rather than away from it. The result is also a remarkably precise account of an artist who says he is no longer searching for Mildreda’s identity; he is now interested in finding out how far that identity can be stretched before it stops being Mildreda. Realities by Mildreda Mildreda interview Karo: Jan, when we first spoke in 2021, you told me that maturity had finally allowed you to “come home” with Mildreda. I have followed the project ever since, through “I Was Never Really There”, “Blue-Devilled”, the concerts and now “Realities”, and this record gives me almost the opposite impression: you sound secure enough in Mildreda to start dismantling parts of the language you had established. How much did making “Realities” require you to question your own idea of what Mildreda is supposed to sound like? Jan: You could argue that making music, playing in a band, writing lyrics and creating a story around it will always be a journey of exploration. But the nature of that journey has definitely changed. I’m no longer searching for Mildreda’s identity, and by now I feel I’ve figured out the DNA of the project as well. That foundation is there, and it’s solid. And precisely because of that, I can now embark on more adventurous quests: exploring the boundaries of the Mildreda sound, allowing for a broader emotional range, and seeing how far I can stretch things without losing what makes Mildreda what it is. I think that’s something you can clearly hear on “Realities”. Karo: When you sent me the album, you described it as your most emotional work and said there were “more colours in the music than ever”. Having heard it, I think the interesting thing is that those colours are certainly not all softer ones. There is industrial abrasion, noise, harsher vocals, but also enormous electronic detail, space and moments of delicacy. When you speak about colour in music, what exactly does that mean to you? Is it timbre, emotional range, dynamics, harmonic language, or the freedom to allow contradictory emotional states to exist within the same musical vocabulary? Jan: When I said it was my most emotional album, I also, and perhaps primarily, meant that on a lyrical level. I allowed myself to explore themes and emotions that are rather unusual within a genre like dark electro. I deliberately moved beyond the genre’s more traditional themes of pain, anger and darkness, making room for vulnerability and tenderness instead. That vulnerability sometimes finds its way into the music as well, in quieter, more emotional and delicate passages that are relatively new territory for Mildreda. But at the same time, I really pushed the boundaries in the opposite direction too, exploring noisier, harsher and more abrasive territory than before. So in that sense, those additional colours aren’t necessarily softer ones. It’s more about widening the entire emotional and sonic spectrum of what Mildreda can be. Karo: The distance from “Blue-Devilled” is wide. That album had an almost architectural darkness, with quasi-sacral space, ritual weight and gothic grandeur, whereas “Realities” feels more corporeal, metallic and exposed. The church-like atmosphere has largely disappeared even though the philosophical conflict has not. Did the change in subject matter make that previous sonic language inappropriate, or had you simply reached the point where you no longer needed those symbols to create darkness? Jan: Especially in Mildreda’s early days in the 1990s, that sacred element was an important part of the sound. I was heavily influenced by bands like Will, early Delerium and In Slaughter Natives, who incorporated bombastic samples of sacred chants into their dark electronic compositions. That whole wave of inspiration came back in full force while making “Blue-Devilled”, so much so that the album is packed with grandiose, sacral samples. One fan joked that if he took a shot of jenever every time he heard a monk singing on “Blue-Devilled”, he’d be completely drunk by the end of the album. He had a point: we may have overdone it a little. So with “Realities”, it was a very conscious decision not to use a single sacred sample anywhere on the album. This time, I wanted the darkness to come from a colder, more purely electronic sound. Karo: “Blue-Devilled” entered into dialogue with Sartre, particularly his idea of hell in relation to the gaze and judgement of other people. “Realities” moves towards Camus, which changes the philosophical problem considerably: from the self confronted by another consciousness towards the collision between our need for meaning and a world that does not promise to provide it. Why did Camus become relevant to you now, and was that movement philosophical first or biographical first? Jan: At its heart, “Realities” is about falling down and finding the strength to get back up again. Throughout our lives, we keep having to rediscover and rebuild ourselves after setbacks, whether they are small or life-changing. And we have to do all of that within the brief interlude we are granted in this universe: our finite lives. That is where Camus entered the picture. In many ways, “Realities” became a confrontation with the absurd. Echoing Camus and his comparison of the human condition to the fate of Sisyphus, the album revolves around that endless cycle of falling and rising, breaking and rebuilding, and forcing ourselves to create new versions of reality. We search for meaning even though the universe offers us no guarantee that there is any to be found. And yet we keep moving. That is also exactly what the title “Realities” refers to. We don’t live in one single, fixed reality, but in a succession of realities. With every setback, every decision and every new beginning, we become a slightly different version of ourselves and inhabit a slightly different world. Visually, that journey is beautifully reflected in Henk Willems’ artwork, where nature slowly reclaims what was once broken. Moss spreads across abandoned ruins, while new growth gradually softens the scars of destruction. To me, it became a powerful metaphor for the album itself: not simply a story of collapse, but of renewal. Not of defeat, but of return. Karo: Camus famously concludes “The Myth of Sisyphus” with “One must imagine Sisyphus happy”, but your Sisyphus in “End of the Line” carries something rather more specific: biography. “Forty-five, fifty-five / This is the time of your life”, followed by those “thousand lives you never led”, introduces age, memory and unrealised possibility into the cycle. Returning to the beginning at fifty cannot mean returning to the same beginning as at twenty because the person pushing the rock has accumulated knowledge, losses and consequences. Does your Sisyphus still arrive at something resembling Camus’s freedom through lucidity, or are you questioning whether accepting the absurd is enough once time itself has become part of the burden? Jan: The initial spark was actually something very personal. Not that long ago, when I turned 45, someone told me, “You’re about to enter the ten best years of your life.” Whether that’s true or not is impossible to say, of course, but there was something strangely powerful about that thought. It almost felt like an obligation to make those years count. That naturally led me back to questions that have always fascinated me: the fact that life is finite, that our time is limited, and that with age comes an increasing awareness of all the lives we could have lived but didn’t. At twenty, there still seems to be an almost infinite number of possible futures ahead of you. Later in life, some of those possibilities have inevitably disappeared. Choices have been made, things have been lost, and time itself becomes part of the weight you carry. That is where Camus and Sisyphus became particularly relevant to “End of the Line”. Sisyphus keeps pushing his boulder despite knowing that it will inevitably roll back down. To me, that endless cycle of falling, getting back up and starting again is a very powerful metaphor for life. We all have our own rock to push uphill, and somehow we keep going. So can Sisyphus still be happy while carrying that rock up the mountain again and again? I think, with Camus, that he can. Despite our mortality and the intrinsic meaninglessness of existence, we still have the freedom to create our own stories, to find joy and to give meaning to the limited time we have. Perhaps age doesn’t contradict Camus’s idea of freedom at all; it simply makes it more urgent. We’d better start pushing, living and creating meaning now, because at some point, the time really does run out. Karo: Musically, I hear more industrial language on “Realities” than on any previous Mildreda album, sometimes moving into very raw, almost noise-like territory. “Rückwärts” is particularly severe and fragmented, but that hardness runs through much of the record in the percussion, distortion, chopped structures and increasingly sharp vocal attack. What led you towards these harsher materials? Did you consciously pursue abrasion as part of the production language, and were there moments when you had to resist making a sound cleaner because its discomfort was exactly what the song required? Jan: That direction actually emerged quite naturally. But it is true that, with this album, I consciously wanted the music to be less immediately digestible than on the previous record. Musically, “Realities” has far more sharp edges, rough textures and moments of genuine abrasion. Perhaps I had been a little too cautious before, whereas this time I allowed myself to go all the way. There is a certain duality at the heart of the album in that respect: very harsh, abrasive music intertwined with vulnerability in the lyrics and themes. That contrast has always fascinated me. Nine Inch Nails taught me that industrial music can be layered with vulnerability without losing any of its power or aggression. If anything, the two can reinforce each other. Karo: At the same time, reducing “Realities” to its aggression would completely misrepresent it because this is also an extraordinarily elaborate electronic record. Across the album, sounds accumulate, separate, change depth and move around one another; dense structures can suddenly open and allow a small sample, voice or electronic detail to occupy an enormous amount of psychological space. How differently were you thinking about density, depth and layering this time, and how do you know when complexity is intensifying an emotion rather than beginning to hide it? Jan: First of all, thank you for describing our music so beautifully. I’m genuinely happy that I was able to take you along on that musical journey in that way. For me, every track is a new search for the right sound and the right balance. And I love that process. I find it incredibly rewarding to spend hours in the studio working with synths and samples, tweaking sounds and layers until they evoke exactly the feeling I’m looking for. There’s something wonderful about that moment when, after endless tweaking, the pieces of the puzzle suddenly fall into place. This time, there simply seemed to be more puzzle pieces than ever, all demanding their own space. That’s one of the reasons why “Realities” ultimately needed to become a double album. I secretly hope that listeners will surrender to that journey from beginning to end: eighteen tracks moving through very different moods, textures and sonic landscapes. For me, the complexity only works when all those layers ultimately serve that journey and the emotion behind it. Karo: The “Reality Checks” are one of the strongest compositional ideas on the album. I do not hear them as conventional interludes because they do not merely separate the larger songs or give us recovery time. They make the whole record feel interwoven, almost braided: the substantial compositions form one strand, these smaller pieces enter between them, and gradually the relationship between the two becomes part of the album’s architecture. When did you realise that “Realities” needed this structure, and what makes an idea a “Reality Check” rather than something that develops into a full Mildreda song? Jan: The idea of using interludes was there from the very beginning. I wanted something that would weave the individual songs together and make the album feel like one continuous journey rather than simply a collection of tracks. Albums like “Entities” by Project Pitchfork and “Galleries of Pain” by Placebo Effect were important references in that respect. Gradually, those interludes developed a character of their own and became the “Reality Checks”. I started to see them almost as the golden seams in kintsugi: they sit between the larger pieces, but rather than simply separating them, they bind the fractured parts into a new whole. Some echo or distort elements from the songs around them, some contain vocals, while others became little sonic adventures of their own. And perhaps that is what distinguishes a “Reality Check” from a full Mildreda song. It doesn’t need to arrive anywhere or tell a complete story. It can remain fragmentary: suggest something, disturb the balance for a moment and then disappear. Its incompleteness is part of its purpose. Karo: Their placement also gives the album something almost physiological, like a heartbeat. Pressure accumulates, then comes a caesura, a moment of recalibration, and movement resumes. Yet the “Reality Checks” are not predictable moments of relief; sometimes they open the music and allow it to breathe, while elsewhere they make the footing even less secure. In ordinary life, a reality check is exactly such a moment: the narrative we have been living inside is interrupted and we are forced to take stock of where we actually stand. Afterwards the external circumstances may be identical, but our perception of them has changed. Is that also what these pieces are doing, repeatedly altering the position from which we perceive the music around them, and perhaps offering another way of understanding the plural title “Realities”? Jan: Yes, very much so. I like your description of them as moments of recalibration, because that is exactly how I see a reality check in life as well. Something happens that briefly disrupts the story you have been telling yourself. The world may still be exactly the same afterwards, but your position within it has shifted. That connects directly to the central idea of “Realities”. We fall, we rise, we rebuild ourselves, and each time we do, we are forced into a slightly different version of reality. There is no single fixed perspective from which we experience our lives. Our perception constantly changes through loss, experience, decisions and new beginnings. “Reality Checks” translate that idea into the architecture of the album. They interrupt the flow and slightly reposition the listener before the next piece begins. And importantly, as you point out, they are not always moments of relief. Sometimes a reality check brings clarity; sometimes it only makes things more confusing. But either way, something has shifted. You continue the journey from a different position than before. And yes, in that sense they are very closely connected to the plural in “Realities”: there is never just one reality to return to. Karo: You told me that the material grew into a double album, yet for you it still tells one story. That is a difficult structural problem: eighteen pieces, radically different degrees of intensity and a very broad electronic vocabulary could easily become abundance without coherence. At what point did you understand that you were not making two albums, or an album with supplementary pieces? What makes “Realities” one work for you: narrative, emotional continuity, musical recurrence, or something that only exists through the sequence itself? Jan: There was also a very practical starting point. New albums on Dependent are nowadays released as beautiful, exclusive hardcover artbooks with two CDs. I’m a big fan of that format, but I’m not necessarily a big fan of the idea that the second disc automatically has to become a collection of bonus material. I didn’t feel like inviting a dozen remixers for this one. This had to remain my story. So in a way, I was quite happy to discover that I simply had too much to say for a single CD. There were so many musical ideas, moods and little sonic adventures that all felt integral to the same universe. Cutting them down just to fit the conventional length of an album would have felt more artificial than allowing the record to expand. And there was a reassuring precedent, of course. Nine Inch Nails showed with “The Fragile” that a double album can be an extraordinary work in its own right rather than an album plus an appendix. That record gave me confidence that abundance doesn’t necessarily have to come at the expense of coherence. For me, “Realities” is ultimately one big story. Despite the range of sounds, moods and emotions, everything belongs to the same conceptual journey: falling, rebuilding, shifting perspective and entering another reality. The “Reality Checks” help bind that journey together, but ultimately I think the coherence exists in the sequence itself. I hope the listener experiences those eighteen pieces not as separate destinations, but as chapters in one long journey through constantly changing emotional and sonic landscapes. Karo: In our first interview you described songwriting as a way of exorcising your demons. “Realities”, however, seems less protected by symbolic architecture than some of the earlier material. “Damage Done”, “Clair-Obscur” and “End of the Line” allow loneliness, emotional asymmetry, ageing, regret and exhaustion to remain recognisably human rather than disguising them completely as theology or elaborate metaphor. Has becoming more personal also changed your relationship with abstraction? At what point does transforming an experience protect the song, and at what point does it protect the writer too much? Jan: That is something that happened quite naturally and evolved over time. Initially, Your Life On Hold was the project where I allowed myself to reveal more of my soul and dig deeper into personal emotions, while Mildreda was primarily the place where I wanted to be loud, confrontational and channel aggression. But gradually, while writing new material, I found myself digging deeper with Mildreda as well. I started allowing a much broader emotional range into the project and became less dependent on abstraction or metaphor to express what I wanted to say. I think that also has a lot to do with becoming more confident as a songwriter. I no longer feel the need to hide behind anything. If there is something I want to say, I can say it openly and without disguise. And what changed with “Realities” is that I discovered I can do that within Mildreda too, without compromising what Mildreda is. Karo: You mentioned Nine Inch Nails to me while explaining the direction of this record, particularly the possibility of allowing vulnerability and emotional depth to coexist with intensity and noise. On “Realities”, vulnerability rarely means making the music gentler; quite often exposure seems to make it more violent. Did that become a compositional principle in itself, that tenderness, humiliation, rage, longing and industrial aggression do not need separate musical languages because they can actually originate from the same emotional state? Jan: What is vulnerable, fragile and delicate is also more susceptible to pain, and I think you can hear that throughout the album. There is a lot of sadness, underlying pain and unanswered longing on “Realities”. Those emotions don’t necessarily ask for gentle music. Sometimes vulnerability can be extremely violent precisely because there is so little protection around it. The best way for me to translate that duality into music was therefore sometimes to work with very dissonant, abrasive and explosive sounds. Tenderness and aggression don’t have to be opposites; they can grow out of exactly the same emotional state. That constant interplay between light and shadow runs through the entire album, I think. The fragile moments make the harsh ones more painful, and the harshness in turn makes the vulnerability feel even more exposed. Karo: The collaborators introduce another interesting contradiction. In 2023 you told me that with “Blue-Devilled” you deliberately wanted to undertake the creative process yourself, partly because after previous collaborations you needed to demonstrate that you could stand alone artistically. “Realities”, which you consider much more personal, opens the door again: Constantin Warter of Calva Y Nada enters “Rückwärts”, while Johan Van Roy of Suicide Commando appears on “Virtual Goddess”. Why did the more personal album become the right place for other voices again, and how much of their own identity do you want a guest to bring into a Mildreda song? Jan: That’s true: on “Blue-Devilled” I deliberately avoided collaborations for exactly the reason you mention. But that was an artistic decision rather than something dictated by the subject matter. I needed to prove to myself that I could carry an entire Mildreda album on my own. Once I had done that, there was no reason to keep that door closed. This time I wanted other voices on the record, and I’m incredibly happy with the people I managed to bring in. The collaboration with Calva Y Nada was actually a blessing on a very practical level as well. “Rückwärts” was one of the first songs I wrote for the album, but after living with the demo for a while, I realised I was completely stuck. I loved the track, but I simply couldn’t imagine my own voice doing it justice. Constantin has such a unique and unmistakable voice that once I started fantasising about someone else singing it, I simply couldn’t hear anyone but him. Through mutual friends we got in touch, eventually met in person, and to my delight he connected with the idea. For me, it was a genuine full-circle moment. Calva Y Nada was one of the bands that defined my teenage years, so hearing Constantin’s voice on a Mildreda record still feels both surreal and deeply meaningful. Johan Van Roy represents something very similar to me. Together with Dirk Ivens, he helped shape what dark electro sounded like in Belgium. With “Realities”, I deliberately wanted to reconnect with that cold, uncompromising Belgian industrial DNA, and “Virtual Goddess” immediately felt like the perfect track for Johan. He brought exactly the intensity and attitude I had hoped for. And I think that also answers the question of how much of themselves I want guests to bring. I don’t invite someone simply to perform a part that could just as easily have been sung by me. I want their identity to become part of the song. Constantin and Johan are unmistakably themselves on these tracks, while somehow still sounding completely at home within Mildreda. Having them both on “Realities” is a real privilege. They are far more than guest vocalists to me: they are two artists whose music helped shape my own musical identity long before Mildreda even existed. Karo: The remixes take that question of identity even further. Das Ich and Steril reconstruct “End of the Line”, while Flesh Field rework “Virtual Goddess”, and around a record called “Realities” the very act of remixing becomes conceptually appropriate: the same composition receives another body, another emphasis and another emotional temperature while remaining recognisable. Did any of those versions make you discover something in your own original that you had not consciously put there? More fundamentally, where does the identity of a song reside if rhythm, texture, atmosphere and structure can change so dramatically while we still perceive it as the same work? Jan: I have a bit of a love-hate relationship with remixes. I love them when they have a genuine reason to exist, rather than simply being part of some endless process of squeezing more material out of a release. The occasion has to feel right, and so does the remixer. That’s why I’m quite selective about both. Mildreda hasn’t actually been through the remix machine that often, so having several artists reinterpret these songs was relatively new territory for Mildreda, and quite exciting. Das Ich were genuine heroes of my youth. Their first two albums still give me goosebumps today, and remarkably, they haven’t aged at all. They were simply light-years ahead of their time. Having Bruno remix one of my songs was therefore a childhood dream coming true. And when I first heard the result, I actually did a little dance of joy. It sounds unmistakably like Das Ich, yet “End of the Line” is still clearly there. In a strange way, it feels like a true hybrid: half my song, half a Das Ich composition. Perhaps that is also an answer to your question about where the identity of a song resides. Apparently you can change an enormous amount and still preserve some kind of core that remains recognisable. I’m equally happy with the other remixes. Steril are heroes of mine as well, and they transformed “End of the Line” into a wonderfully tight club track. Flesh Field, on the other hand, happened to cross my path at exactly the right moment, so involving him was almost an act of serendipity. I loved hearing “Virtual Goddess” thrown into his wonderfully mad industrial mixture of bombast, aggression and even a touch of dubstep. What fascinates me about all three is that I can still recognise my songs, but I’m hearing them through someone else’s ears. Maybe that’s what a good remix should do: not simply decorate the original, but reveal another possible reality that was somehow already hiding inside it. The Das Ich and Steril versions of “End of the Line” were released on the June 2026 EP, while the “Virtual Goddess” release includes the Flesh Field remix. Karo: “Virtual Goddess” avoids one of the easiest traps in writing about digital culture because the narrator is implicated in the mechanism he criticises. There is a virtual goddess, but there is also a virtual god; desire becomes entangled with images, attention, views and projection, so nobody gets to occupy the comfortable position outside the system. Is complicity important here? Have we reached a point where criticising mediated reality while continuing to produce, consume and emotionally invest in it is itself one of the defining contradictions of contemporary life? Jan: This is a difficult question because there are several things tangled up in it. There is the sheer amount of our day that social media consumes, but also the way it affects how we present ourselves and how we perceive other people. Both images are inevitably distorted. At the same time, however critical I am of social media, I can’t dismiss it as purely negative. It remains, whether we like it or not, an important way of discovering music and news, staying connected and sharing your own story with the world. And occasionally you even find a good joke there. So yes, complicity is absolutely part of it. I notice the contradiction in myself all the time. I can hardly keep away from my smartphone, call it an addiction if you like, while simultaneously being deeply irritated by the whole mechanism. I’m frustrated by all those pixel-perfect façades, yet at the same time I participate in creating one myself. I criticise the game while continuing to play it. And artificial intelligence is adding yet another layer of complexity to all of this. The boundaries between what is real, constructed, enhanced or entirely artificial are becoming increasingly difficult to define. We seem to be living inside a fascinating and slightly disturbing science-fiction film, except that none of us gets to sit outside it and simply watch. Karo: “Götterfall” almost feels like an older Mildreda argument surviving inside an entirely different philosophical environment. We have discussed your atheism before, and the quasi-sacral architecture of “Blue-Devilled” has largely vanished, yet somebody is still firing at gods who remain silent, mocking and apparently impossible to kill. If those gods are no longer theological, what has taken their place? Are there ideas, institutions, authorities, memories or even people we consciously stop believing in while continuing to grant them enormous psychological power? Jan: The ancient Greek historian Herodotus tells us that the Getae would shoot arrows into the sky during thunderstorms, threatening their god. I’ve always found that an incredibly powerful image, and I had actually used it before in a Your Life On Hold song. But it was simply too strong not to bring into the Mildreda universe as well: man, confronted with a reality he cannot accept, firing his arrows at the heavens. I also knew I wanted a song in German on the album, which allowed me to reshape the idea into something new. The arrows became bullets, and German inevitably gives the whole thing a very different weight and character. But the central idea remained the same: we are powerless and insignificant, raging against forces that are infinitely larger than ourselves. Karo: “Reality” widens the scope dramatically at the end: headlines, war, mediated violence, environmental destruction, the repeated consumption of catastrophe through screens. Much of the album has dealt with extremely intimate realities such as desire, damage, loneliness, ageing and unrealised possibilities, and then the individual is placed inside this enormous informational environment. Is the movement outward suggesting that there is ultimately no purely private reality, because even our most intimate emotional lives are continuously penetrated and reorganised by images, narratives and catastrophes arriving from outside? Jan: Despite what the title might suggest, this closing track is something of an outsider on the album in terms of content indeed. Where the rest of the album navigates my inner landscape, this song shifts its gaze to the world around me, our planet, and it isn’t doing well. Long-time fans who were with us back in the cassette days may recognise this piece. I wrote the first demo thirty years ago. I had always intended to give it a definitive version someday, and this album finally made that possible: new lyrics, new sound and a long-awaited rebirth. Karo: Finally, you already have concerts around the new-album period, including NCN in Deutzen on September 6 and Fourscher Festival in Erfurt in November. What happens after those dates? Are further Mildreda concerts already being discussed, and is the ambition eventually to take “Realities” on a more extensive tour of its own? Jan: I definitely hope to play a lot of shows with Mildreda in 2027. A few things have already been confirmed, but there’s still a lot up in the air. If the stars align, it could turn into quite an adventurous year! About Mildreda Mildreda is the Belgian dark-electro project led by producer, vocalist and songwriter Jan Dewulf. Its roots go back to the mid-1990s, when Dewulf, still in his teens and strongly affected by the cold Belgian electronics of acts such as The Klinik, began working with synthesizers and home-recording equipment. His self-released cassette “II Castrato” appeared in 1995, followed by “De Laffe Denker” in 1996. The latter circulated widely through the electro underground, and Mildreda subsequently shared stages with acts including Plastic Noise Experience, Terminal Choice, Covenant and VNV Nation. Dewulf later put Mildreda on hold and concentrated on Diskonnekted, while also completing a degree in philosophy. He returned to Mildreda with the digitally released “Coward Philosophy” in 2016. After signing with Dependent Records, the project released “I Was Never Really There” in 2021, bringing the early Belgian dark-electro foundations into a substantially more detailed contemporary production environment. Guests on that record included Dirk Ivens, Cyan of The Eternal Afflict and Numb’s Don Gordon, while Claus Larsen of Leaether Strip handled mastering. The concept album “Blue-Devilled” followed in December 2023. Built partly around Jean-Paul Sartre’s treatment of hell and the judgement of others, it expanded Mildreda’s melodic and atmospheric vocabulary while retaining its Belgian and Canadian dark-electro foundations. “Realities”, released on August 28, 2026 through Dependent, contains 18 tracks across two discs and is available as a limited 48-page hardcover artbook designed by Henk Willems. The album features Constantin “Breñal” Warter of Calva Y Nada on “Rückwärts” and Johan Van Roy of Suicide Commando on “Virtual Goddess”. Its conceptual grounding shifts from Sartre towards Camus, while recurring “Reality Checks” connect the individual compositions into one continuous album structure. Mildreda’s official biography describes the project as led by Dewulf; the live incarnation consists of Jan Dewulf and Christophe “Salva” Salvatore. The single “Silk Skin” preceded the album in August 2026. Interview by Karo Kratochwil.
items._cn_summary: Mildreda 全新专辑《Realities》摒弃了前作标志性的圣歌采样，转向更冷峻的电子音墙与尖锐的工业噪音，并融入接近噪声音乐的段落。18首作品以双CD形式发行，伴随48页艺术画册。专辑结构中穿插的"Reality Checks"如同金缮中的接缝，串联起存在主义主题——从萨特的引用转向加缪与西西弗斯，探讨坠落、重建以及现实的多重版本。客串阵容包括Calva Y Nada的Breñal与Suicide Commando的Johan Van Roy。访谈中，Jan Dewulf谈及中年危机、社交媒体共谋、神性的残留以及脆弱性如何反向催生更暴烈的声响。整张专辑展现了创作者在确立身份DNA后，有意拆解既有语言、向更极端方向延伸的创作意图。

items.body:
Old pals Christina Vantzou and Félicia Atkinson reflect on coastal living on their first collaborative album, blending environmental echoes from Rome, Normandy and Hydra with mellow synth, piano, Rhodes, vibraphone, lap steel, gongs and spoken word, pulling us into the sublime.

The third chapter in RVNG's ongoing "Reflections" series, 'Water Poems' crystallises a creative relationship that began way back in 2009. Vantzou and Atkinson have performed together before, most notably in 2019 at Philharmonie de Paris, but this is the first time the duo have made a record together. Both artists live by the sea, Atkinson in Normandy on the French coast, and Vantzou in Greece, using that shared experience to power a series of hazy dream sequences filled with subtle gestures. "The sea was not taken as a monolithic postcard," Atkinson explains. "But more of a person; an energy, a mystery, a complex character we face everyday, as human beings living by the sea."

Indeed, the esoteric energy of the sea - its tides, force, majesty and hypnotic, mystical pull, is captured by the duo's eddy of electroacoustic treatments and bespoke natural soundscapes. They recorded the material in a factory on the island of Hydra in Greece, at Villa Medici in Rome and at home in their respective studios, adding expressive environmental recordings from Delphi and the Eftalou Hot Springs. The record plays like a single, hazed thought, ebbing and flowing through the same shallow waters. Words emerge and disappear into carefully processed sounds at first, before forming sentences and whole thoughts on the second side. "How can a body swim," Atkinson mouthes. "How can a person dream?"

Gorgeously, quietly seductive gear from two of the very best at this sort of thing, one to file next to Meitei's sublime 'Sen'nyū (泉涌)' from last year - recline and drift into it.
items._genre: ambient / electroacoustic / modern composition / spoken word
items._cn_summary: Christina Vantzou与Félicia Atkinson的首张合作专辑是RVNG厂牌"Reflections"系列的第三篇章。两人均临海而居，分别驻于法国诺曼底和希腊海德拉岛，创作灵感源自共同的海岸生活体验。录制跨越希腊海德拉岛工厂、罗马美第奇别墅及各自的私人工作室，并融入德尔斐与埃夫塔卢温泉的环境录音。音乐采用柔和的合成器、钢琴、Rhodes电钢琴、颤音琴、膝上钢吉他与锣等乐器，配合电声处理与定制自然声景，营造出朦胧的梦境序列。文本元素起初以经处理的声音碎片浮现，至第二面逐渐形成完整的语句与思想。整张专辑如同一段流动的意识，在浅层水域中潮汐般呼吸与回荡，将海的神秘能量转化为沉浸式的声学冥想。

items.body:
Still influential three decades after its release, Rachel's' debut album is a low-key genre classic, welding the cinematic orchestrations of Carter Burwell to nascent post-rock structures and influencing bands like A Silver Mt. Zion and Clogs in the process.

Originally deployed on Touch And Go's sister label Quaterstick in 1995, 'Handwriting' was a complete anomaly at the time. There was a feeling that the album had only appeared on the label because it'd been the home of Rodan, the popular post-hardcore outfit that Rachel's founder Jason Noble had been a member of. But as time ticked on, Rachel's forward-thinking fusion of post-rock and chamber music began to appear more prescient. The band was originally conceived by Noble and viola player Christian Frederickson in the late '80s, but when Rodan blew up, Noble was too preoccupied to follow up their experiments. Time, of course, ticked on and Rodan imploded, so Noble and Frederickson picked up the pieces, inviting pianist Rachel Grimes to contribute. And the band's debut is a real one-off; they'd follow it with the brilliant Nyman-esque 'Music for Egon Schiele', but by that time their post-hardcore/post-rock echoes had all but disappeared. As it is, 'Handwriting' is at the root of a sound that almost immediately blossomed further north in Montréal. 

Linking the tangled riffs of Slint and of course Rodan with the scenic ambience of Labradford and, most importantly, Michael Nyman's minimal compositions, Noble, Grimes and Frederickson pre-empted something that's permeated throughout the scene at large over the three decades that followed. Even 'M. Daguerre', one of the album's early highlights and its jazziest track, that hews closer to The Necks' early material than anything else, provides a tangible blueprint. But it's the cooler, quieter moments that keep us coming back to 'Handwriting', like the emotive 'Seratonin' or the absolute milestone 'Full on Night', a stripped-to-the-bone Southern gothic post-rock jam that dissolves into a mass of radio static, film samples and chugging steam trains. If Godspeed hadn't heard this one before they recorded 'F♯ A♯ ∞', we'd be very surprised.
items._genre: post-rock / chamber music / minimalism / experimental / contemporary classical
items._cn_summary: 这张首作将后摇滚结构与室内乐编制结合，以弦乐、钢琴和电影化的管弦乐编排构建独特声响。它把缠绕的吉他段落、氛围音乐的景观感与尼曼式简约主义融为一体，在1995年显得异常前卫。部分曲目带有爵士倾向，接近即兴室内乐组合的早期风格；另一些作品则从南方哥特式后摇滚段落滑入无线电静噪、电影采样与蒸汽火车声，形成强烈的画面感。专辑预示了蒙特利尔后摇滚场景的方向，对后来的乐队产生深远影响。

items.body:
Probably the biggest curveball in rap since Lil’ Bs ‘Rain In England’, Cities Aviv lands on Black Truffle with a set of psilocybin-infused dream sequences influenced by Jandek. Strange but true!​

Sticking out like a sore thumb next to Black Truffle’s usual lineup of avant, jazz, minimalist and electroacoustic pioneers and mavericks, Cities Aviv is the work of Wilbert Gavin Mays, who also records as African-American Sound Recordings, squeezing hip-hop conventions thru a chopped and screwed haze of “hermetic décollage”packed with fuzzy ambient interludes, loopy clouded reflections and stream-of-consciousness bars. 

Gavin Mays has always been on the perimeter of many scenes, happy enough to draw his own landscape while everyone else churned up the same old mud. That's truer than ever on his recent run, culminating in this brilliantly unexpected Black Truffle co-sign. Operating on his lonesome, Mays creates music that can't be pigeonholed - it's barely even rap. He spits on the two-part title track, but his words dilate awkwardly over noisy, new age synths and blown-out, pitch-screwed rhythms. They might not even be strictly on the beat at all, a mood that he prolongs throughout 'Even Colder Spring’, an album that in places sounds more like Seefeel than it does MF DOOM.

While Mays’ work can sometimes read claustrophobically bleak, the production here is surprisingly approachable; the instrumental ‘Martine Drift’ could almost be a snatch of Cluster’s Zuckerzeit caught through dial-up internet, and the distant drums of ‘L_area’ cross with lo-fi IDM, while closer ‘Final Heaven’ dissolves a cloud of loops thru almost seven minutes of ecstatic, rippling distortion. And as the label point out, the cover art is inspired by Jandek’s Corwood Industries label, which gives you some idea of where it's at.

items.body:
I can feel the waves is Frances Chang's debut on RVNG Intl.

"A boundary-pushing musician and multi-media artist from Brooklyn, New York, Frances Chang disrupts accepted reality through her unique and enchanting compositions. Chang’s songs are an exercise in communication, probing the tension between idiosyncratic personal experience and the drive to understand, and be understood, through a collective language.

For “I can feel the waves,” a piano-centric melody is ornamented with primitive electronics and poetic vocals. The track boldly demonstrates Chang’s strength for unconventional yet contagious songwriting, and pioneers a genre the artist refers to as “slacker prog”: roomy and playful, offbeat and occasionally jarring, brimming with spiritual and emotional resonance.

The b-side, “Marry,” is a rollicking yet laid-back composition, with undaunted wobbly kicks bubbling under pianistic textures until a dialogue, acted out between Chang and Sylvia Gorelick, takes the foreground in the final moments of the track. As the instrumental carries its freewheeling pulse forward, the conversation, inspired by films like Kenneth Lonergan’s Margaret and Catherine Breillat’s Fat Girl!, along with Broken Social Scene’s “Anthems for a Seventeen-Year Old Girl,” turns toward the relationship between internal subjectivity and the external necessity of “staying small.”

Where is Frances headed from here? A piano is at the center, synths and strings swelling around its shoulders. A little less tension, a lot more production. Some shadows will be encountered, some forgotten skeletons unearthed. Music excavated from the subtler, deeper layers of cerebral and shared experiences. Music that is truly its own."
items._genre: experimental pop / art song / contemporary composition
items._cn_summary: 这张首张专辑以钢琴为核心框架，叠加原始质感的电子音色与诗性人声。评论提出"slacker prog"这一自创概念来概括其美学——松散、俏皮、偶尔突兀，在精神性与情感共鸣之间游走。作品展现出对非常规旋律的偏好，旋律具有传染性却拒绝落入流行套式。B面收录了一首以对话结尾的作品，灵感来自肯尼斯·洛纳根与凯瑟琳·布雷亚特的电影文本，探讨内在主观性与外部"保持渺小"之间的关系。整体制作指向更深层的挖掘，钢琴居中，合成器与弦乐环绕其肩，意图在减少张力的同时增加制作层次。

items.body:
One of electronic music's most influential recordings, back in circulation.

Most readers of these pages will know the story, but to indulge you with a recap, Gottsching was part of electronic krautrock heroes Ash Ra Tempel and in 1981, off the back of a Klaus Schulze tour, sat down one evening and dropped a continuous piece of music which would uncannily imagine the arc of dance music for a quarter of a century.

Early adopters in the Chicago and Detroit warehouses and mediterranean pleasure palaces must have thrilled to the balanced and continuous surging flow of the hour long piece - even over two sides the mix is perfect for building a club atmosphere and suggesting avenues for mixing, whilst using merely two chords throughout. the minimalism offsets the percussive splendour perfectly - several years later the tune was rediscovered and co-opted into the huge italo house smash Sueno Latino, which cemented its foundation in the burgeoning balearic scene of the time and proceeded through several spells of rapturous revival throughout the nineties, not least when figures like Carl Craig and Basic Channel issued their own radically different reshapes and remakes of the piece.

Very satisfying then to have this Gottsching sanctioned edition, where the game might truly be said to have begun in earnest. As they say on the august walls of the Hardwax emporium - buy or die.
items._cn_summary: 这张1981年的录音由德国电子音乐先驱Manuel Göttsching录制，是一张长达一小时的连续电子音乐作品，仅用两个和弦构建，却以极简手法呈现出层次丰富的律动与氛围。它预言了未来二十五年舞曲音乐的发展走向，被芝加哥和底特律的仓库派对率先采用，后被融入意大利浩室经典Sueno Latino，并经Carl Craig和Basic Channel等先锋人物重新演绎。极简主义与打击乐的辉煌在此完美平衡，作品既适合俱乐部混音使用，也具备独立聆听的冥想特质。此次再版经艺术家本人授权，确保了原始意图的忠实传达。

items.body:
Dreader than dread dub vapors from Ghost Dubs, in a lineage stretching from Dadawah to Burial Mix, Vainqueur to Resilent, Pole to Rod Modelll...​

Toiling in Berlin’s deep seam of abstract dub practice that scrolls back to Rhythm & Sound’s earliest via Pole’s dusty convections and Chain Reaction's fritzed mutations; Ghost Dubs embodies the art of dub as method with a strong haul of dematerialised, sludgy tramplers operating close to the scuzzy heart of Kevin Martin, aka The Bug. Uncompromisingly in-the-zone and dank as a bong, the dozen cuts get right under the skin, up-the-pharynx, with an intoxicatingly sedated and hallucinatory quality that impresses murky, vaporous patterns on the back of blunted eyelids and may possibly raise knees to its slompy skank and imaginary physics. 

Of course, the sound is rooted in the innovative, half century-old traditions of Jamaican dub, as established by King Tubby and Lee “Scratch” Perry, and developed by the likes of Scientist or Mad Professor. But Ghost Dubs picks it up at the point where it diffused into techno and noise during the ‘90s, taking that sound as a jump-off into his microcosm of granular, atomised atmospheric disintegration that nevertheless holds to a steady ballast of scoop-worrying sub-bass tremors. No doubt anyone who’s followed the devolution of this sound outside Jamaica, from NYC illbient to Berlin dub techno, will recognise his hands-on-desk tekkerz ushering the sound into oblique new spaces with a canny sense of proprioception that locates it somewhere in fissure between classic and contemporary soundspheres.

From the caustic attrition of ‘Chemical’, thru the inverted mulch of ‘Dub Lobotomy’, to the sensuous but elephantine trample of ‘Hot Wired’ and tumescent swell of ‘Circles Lines’ ,Ghost Dubs leaves his clammy fingerprint on every cut. Some are primed to bend your Clarks, as with the bilgy step of ‘The Regulator’, and airborne skank of ‘Thin Line’, and the harness-tugging pressure of ‘Dub Battle’, but they’re all held in check with a overarching slowness that gels the 12 tracks as a proper end-to-end listen in the manner of Pole’s early albums with a deeply reliable robustness and temper that stakes it out as arguably canonic tackle.
items._genre: dub techno / experimental dub / dark ambient electronic
items._cn_summary: Ghost Dubs延续了从牙买加King Tubby和Lee Perry的dub传统出发、经柏林dub techno脉络发展的暗潮电子路线，将dub作为一种方法论进行解构。整张专辑十二首曲目呈现去物质化的黏稠质感，低频次低音如地震般缓慢推进，颗粒感十足的声音在空气中瓦解又重组，营造出令人眩晕的催眠氛围。制作上强调手动操控的即兴感，将dub的混音空间美学与90年代纽约illbient、柏林techno的噪点处理相融合。每首曲目虽各有侧重点——从灼蚀般的频率侵蚀到膨胀的声波涌动——但被统一的迟缓节奏粘合为完整的端到端聆听体验，沉稳而厚重，堪称为这一脉络中具有典范意义的作品。

items.body:
Tyondai Braxton’s new album, his first full-length release since the recording of his 2022 symphonic work, Telekinesis, reveals itself as unlike what came before and marks the beginning of a new chapter with UK label Erased Tapes. First off, there’s a lot more music here, 70+ minutes of pure electronics and sound design. Plus, it’s divided in a way that’s out-of-step with the longer forms the 47 year-old composer/producer has previously imagined into being. Of the album’s 15 tracks, more than two-thirds are sub-five minutes.

"The album brings together mostly newer works alongside pieces composed across the past decade, some of which appeared previously as standalone releases. To fully represent the scope of this period, Braxton incorporates the Dia / Phonolydian (2022) and Multiplay (2023) singles into Splayed Werks, foregrounding the project’s long-form compositional arc. Along with “Salt Point” and previously unreleased commissioned works such as “4 Zones” (2018) and “K Space” (2021), these pieces were always part of a broader, evolving body of material. Here, they are re-edited as newer versions and remastered by the excellent Matt Colton at Metropolis Studios in London and woven into a continuous narrative. The result is not so much a compilation, but a record that traces its own lineage in real time: a body of work composed across years, now fully realized as a single, cohesive statement.

What the circumstantial facts can’t reveal is the social, in-real-life context of Splayed Werks, an expansive episodic work that plants a musical flag on a turbulent period, and on which darkness and ambiance, rhythm and light, instinct and precision, organic textures and messy playfulness all share space. These Werks take stock of a constantly evolving world, as well as the evolutions experienced by their creator.

It may be a perfect album for 2026, a time when the sonic landscape continues to fervently embrace increasingly radical hybrids, at once club soundsystem-ready, art-installation-leaning, and music-school-mediated. But also, importantly, intuitive and hand-crafted. It’s no stretch to say that Tyondai had a hand in building this world. His two decades-plus-long career has seen him co-found electronic prog-punk heroes Battles (which he’s described as “a laboratory that masqueraded as a band”); performing as a duo with Philip Glass; write numerous electro-acoustic and chamber commissions for celebrated American new-music ensembles such as Bang on a Can All-Stars, Alarm Will Sound, Third Coast Percussion, Brooklyn Rider, and Yarn/Wire; having his “part installation, part band” HIVE project appear at The Guggenheim Museum, Sydney Opera House, and a 3-night residency at Big Ears Festival; and deliver a series of technologically ambitious, at times orchestral works for lauded labels of electronic, experimental and future-music, Warp and Nonesuch Records.

Meanwhile, the world outside has also radicalized. Mechanisms behind the creation, promotion, distribution and broadcast of new experimental music have been violently disrupted, even as audiences for it have grown. In the post-COVID streaming age, juxtapositions like “popular” vs “underground,” and “album” vs “collection” vs “project” have been more in-flux than ever before. The volume and acceptance of previously neglected ambient and contemporary classical sounds has been tempered by a lack of critical context, seeded with algorithmic buffoonery and AI fabrication. Such tensions enlighten not just the make-up of Splayed Werks, full of music recorded between 2018-2025, but its relatively simple sonic-collage forms.

The Splayed shapes and structures have also been influenced by the transformations in Braxton’s personal life. That Tyondai is now a father may not come as a surprise, but the fact that the man who rebelled against his formal music-school education in the late-‘90s, has, in 2022 become a professor of music composition at Princeton University, does. This lifestyle change—a full-time academic gig, escaping the careerist hamster-wheel beholden to commissions and collaborations, a home studio as his own workshop and testing ground, with the desire to finish things and the perspective to not be precious about it—is also key to the album’s sound. Braxton’s time is his own, and his idea of what it means to be an artist in our time has evolved as much as the surroundings. This too is what Splayed Werks is about. It may be a cliché to call each ensuing album by a veteran artist their “most personal,” but it’s no stretch to say this one best reflects who Braxton is in 2026.

As a portfolio, Splayed Werks hews to the menu of a dance music meets minimalist electronic composition, a throughline that stretches from IDM absurdists like Aphex Twin and Autechre, to contemporary immersives like Mica Levi and Laurel Halo. (And, to a lesser degree, to Braxton’s comrades and occasional collaborators, Kieran “Four Tet” Hebden, Jeffrey Cantu-Ledesma and Ben Vida.) It’s a world in which the multitude of dirty rhythms strays far outside club-land’s big rooms—though one can imagine expert mixing hands and a world-class soundsystem transforming the dubwise lo-fi linearity of “Oslo” into a psychedelic wonder, while the interplay between the bass-synth and the constantly deviating shuffle on “UnFS” may qualify as a leftfield banger. And its composed beatless spaces have little to do with current ambient proclivities—the at-once aggressive and ecstatic, panning miniature, “Realistic Water” sounds like power Laraaji.

The spectrum of Braxton’s ideas and directions reveals a voracious mind at play, changing up without overcomplicating the proceedings. Two different pieces called (fittingly) “Multiplay” layer and connect skittering textures in beatwise whimsy, before giving way to a droning dread and organised noise; yet each is adorned with birdcalls to balance the synthetic with the pastoral. “Nimble FX” is also built on hyper-jittery stop-start rhythm lines, and great big cinematic synths. All this music feels fluid, seemingly ready to change in the moment rather than having been dependent on some grand design. Meanwhile, longer, older, more spacious compositions like “4 Zones,’ whose short parts assemble into a narrative-free sound design, and the closing “K Space,” whose chaotic ambiance gives way to what sound like Moog hits, are more grounded, their inclusion shaping Splayed Werks into a multidimensional space, instinctive in how it all fits together."

“Every record I’ve ever finished, I’ve been shocked with what it is. I’ve never known it was finished until it was. Then you get to learn about it retroactively. If I’ve done it right, the finished thing will feel like its own personality, its own being, its own vibe. [Splayed Werks] included.” - Tyondai Braxton

items._cn_summary: Tyondai Braxton的新专辑《Splayed Werks》是他在Erased Tapes厂牌发行的首张全长作品，收录了70余分钟纯电子与声音设计作品，将过去十年间创作的曲目重新编辑、重新混音，串联成一条连贯的叙事线。专辑包含15首曲目，多为五分钟以内的短篇，与此前以长篇为主的创作路径形成反差。Braxton早年联合创立电子前卫乐队Battles，曾与Philip Glass合作二重奏，为Bang on a Can All-Stars等知名新音乐合奏团撰写委约作品，并在古根海姆美术馆、悉尼歌剧院等场馆呈现跨界项目。这张专辑既非简单合辑，也非全新创作，而是一段跨越十年的创作脉络的完整呈现，涵盖黑暗氛围与节奏光感、有机质感与即兴玩味的多重张力，映射出创作者在动荡时代中持续演进的内省轨迹。

items.excerpt: Joining the 4AD roster, NYC avant-rock four piece YHWH Nailgun unload an 11-minute clip of pure math-punk artillery, all demon-possessed vocals, screaming organs, angular riffs and byzantine rhythms. Think U.S. Maple, Battles, Captain Beefheart, Pere Ubu and Still House Plants blended with 'Scum'-era Napalm Death and you'll have some idea. Deployed only moments after Drake dropped not one but three bloated sets of playlist-ready mall pop, 'Magazine' arrives like a cool breeze during a heatwave.
items.body:
Joining the 4AD roster, NYC avant-rock four piece YHWH Nailgun unload an 11-minute clip of pure math-punk artillery, all demon-possessed vocals, screaming organs, angular riffs and byzantine rhythms. Think U.S. Maple, Battles, Captain Beefheart, Pere Ubu and Still House Plants blended with 'Scum'-era Napalm Death and you'll have some idea.

Deployed only moments after Drake dropped not one but three bloated sets of playlist-ready mall pop, 'Magazine' arrives like a cool breeze during a heatwave. See, it's common sense in the AI era to feed the algorithms more, not less, increasing your chances to snag that illusive viral hit by relying on pure volume. Not hampered by the limitations of the format (remember, the "classic album" was only 40-odd minutes because vinyl demanded it), artists and labels have been hedging their bets, packing records with collaborations, remixes and undeveloped ideas in the hope that one of them might end up getting even half the traction of AFX's seemingly throwaway 'QKThr'. YHWH Nailgun laugh in the face of this logic, not just challenging 2026's idea of what an album should be, but 1966's, too. If you thought '45 Pounds' was lean, 'Magazine' trims even more aesthetic fat, cooking down the meat of jazz fusion, prog, noise rock, post-punk and grindcore like it's Wagyu, searing it off and providing just an umami-rich shaving to taste.

The whole process is surprising because so many of YHWH Nailgun's references were already bloated. The prog rock era was when the double album became almost commonplace; 'Magazine' meanwhile could quite easily be crammed onto a 7" at 45RPM. And yet, they've only increased in power since last year. Opener 'Ghost of Love' does more in a minute-and-a-half than most tracks do in three or four times the duration, spinning Jack Tobias' carnivalesque, Farfisa-like synths around Sam Pickard's pliant drums like matted spiderwebs, but leaving just enough room for Zack Borzone's no-wave shouts and Saguiv Rosenstock's hacking fragments of melody. 'Stillness Blues' is shorter still and somehow packs even more in, assembling screamo brickwork over industrial strength bass rasps using Pickard's clattery start-stop patterns as the mortar. It's hard to say this stuff's exhausting - it's over before you've even really come to grips with it - but YHWH Nailgun have a way of drawing you back in, again and again, just to try and catch a whiff of what's actually going on. 

There's the Radiohead-like moan of 'Innocent Sigh', the Eli Keszler-does-Pere Ubu intensity of the minute-long 'Ballerina' and the title track, 35 seconds of breakneck beats, bleeps and shouted phrases that rudely cuts off before it's even had the chance to fully extend its claws. It's a shocker, an eccentric, hyper skillful, deeply original blur of influences and innovation that really does remind us just how punchy rock music can be.
items._cn_summary: 纽约四人乐队YHWH Nailgun签约4AD厂牌，发行了这张时长仅11分钟的专辑，以极端精简的篇幅承载密集的实验元素。乐评将其与U.S. Maple、Battles、Pere Ubu、Napalm Death等跨时代乐队并置，凸显其融合爵士融合、前卫摇滚、噪音摇滚、post-punk与grindcore的杂糅美学。每首曲目短至数十秒，却在远藤ミチロウ式的嘶喊、Farfisa合成器的诡异盘旋与断裂式鼓点中塞满层次。乐评着重指出该作对当下'以量取胜'算法逻辑的反抗——在Drake发行三张冗长流行专辑的语境下，以'和牛薄片'式的浓缩手法呈现饱满风味。评论将其比作一张可压缩至7寸唱片的45RPM曲目群，却在强度上远超去年的《45 Pounds》，是一份紧凑、高技能且极具原创性的摇滚宣言。

items.body:
Swedish jazz icon Christer Bothén returns to Black Truffle backed by Ghosted's Oren Ambarchi, Johan Berthling and Andreas Werliin, playing bass clarinet and donso n’goni over the trio's signature kraut-jazz grooves. Hypnotic, trance-inducing biz FFO Natural Information Society, Don Cherry's 'Organic Music Society', Jon Hassell, The Necks.

If you're up on your Swedish jazz, there's no way you won't have stumbled across multi-instrumentalist Bothén. He's still best known for palling around with Don Cherry when the jazz great moved to Scandinavia, even teaching him how to play the donso n'goni, a sacred "hunter's harp" from the Wassoulou region in West Africa that Bothén had picked up when he was in Mali. And he's continued to perform with various local artists and outfits, conspicuously appearing on Ghosted's 2022 debut album just mere moments before Ambarchi's Black Truffle imprint re-issued his lost Afro-fusion classic album 'Trancedance'. Last year, Bothén finally issued his first solo n'goni album and now he's back on Black Truffle with this fleshed-out collaboration with the Ghosted crew, leading Ambarchi's Leslie-cab guitar drones, Berthling's bass and Werliin's drums.

Berthling and Werliin take the lead at first on the title track, hammering out a rotating groove before Bothén lets rip on bass clarinet. And playing a side role, Ambarchi might have the most important presence, using his signature phased, organ-like tones to provide anchoring drones for Bothén's spirited improvisations. He's even more pivotal on 'Antigorite', playing cascading staccato notes over those Leslie moans and creating an rhythmelodic foil for the other three players' more traditional interplay. But it's when Bothén plays the n'ghoni that the album really hits its stride; on 'Lizardite', those buzzing tones offset Ambarchi's crystalline twangs, filling in for Werliin's imposing basslines. It's the moment where everything else just drops into place, creating a structural crescendo before the album careers into darkness on the brilliantly moody closer 'Chrysotile'.
items._cn_summary: 瑞典多乐器演奏家 Christer Bothén 携低音单簧管与西非猎人之琴 donso n'goni，与 Ambarchi 的 Leslie 吉他长音、Berthling 的贝斯和 Werliin 的鼓组展开对话。乐评指出作品的真正亮点在 n'goni 段落，低鸣的弦乐质感与吉他清亮泛音交织，在结构上形成渐进高潮后转入阴沉结尾。整体以催眠式循环律动为核心，将 Don Cherry 式的有机爵士语汇与 Krautrock 推进感融合，氛围层次丰富，文本质量详实。

items.body:
Our Darkness descends upon Dark Entries with a reissue of Anne Clark’s epochal proto-house masterpiece from 1984.

"As a young poet, Clark found herself drawn to London’s emerging punk scene. She became acquainted with Psychic TV affiliate David Harrow, with whom she would collaborate on 1983’s Changing Places and 1984’s Joined Up Writing. “Our Darkness,” off the latter album, was released as a single on Ink Records that same year, and became an underground club hit. It’s a singular piece of music: Clark’s lyrics, delivered with equal parts muscular confidence and unease, speak of urban alienation and heartbreak, while Harrow’s production pummels the listener with hydraulic beats and gloom-laced arpeggios. The song’s spirit would prove influential on both the early Chicago house and Detroit techno scenes, where mechanistic funk and existential despair could catalyse dancefloor mayhem.

This reissue offers three versions of “Our Darkness”: the original 12” remix, the Razormaid mix, and a previously unreleased dub version uncovered by David Harrow. Also included is the extended mix of “Sleeper in Metropolis,” another dancefloor hit of Clark’s, as well as the elegiac “Poem for a Nuclear Romance.”

“Our Darkness” channels timeless longing and contemporary dismay, a classic overdue for a little light shed upon it."
items._cn_summary: 这张1984年发行的单曲合辑由Dark Entries厂牌再版，收录了Anne Clark与David Harrow合作的经典之作。Clark以兼具力量与不安的诗歌朗诵为核心，歌词触及都市疏离与心碎主题；Harrow的制作则使用液压般的强劲节拍与阴郁的琶音铺陈氛围。这种融合在当时的地下俱乐部场景中产生了深远影响，被视为芝加哥浩室与底特律技术的精神先驱。再版包含原版12寸混音、Razormaid混音以及Harrow本人发现的未发行dub版本，另附《Sleeper in Metropolis》扩展混音与《Poem for a Nuclear Romance》。整体呈现出文学性与机械感并重的美学，冷峻的合成器肌理下涌动着存在主义的绝望情绪，是早期电子舞曲与暗潮交汇的关键文献。

items.body:
Michael J. Blood lends two rugged, tumping takes to Intertoto’s rudely groggy beatdown house

‘If I Take You Home’ is the first cut from London’s Intertoto since his well received album ‘Thermal Shadow’ (2023) and continues down a midnight path of mid-tempo, strutting beatdown roughly guided by likes of NWAQ and Kassel Mosse.

MJB steps it up a gear or two in a ‘Walk of Shame Mix’ built from woodcut kicks and gritty sampler revs plus additional vox like Martin Rev just walked in the room and did a Travolta “huh?”, plus a banging ‘Morning After Mix’ cloaked in muffled party noise and prompting jelly legs back to the ‘floor.
items._cn_summary: 这张EP是Intertoto在《Thermal Shadow》后的首支作品，延续其中速、午夜氛围的beatdown house路线。Michael J. Blood为其制作了两个混音版本：'Walk of Shame Mix'以木击鼓和粗粝的采样器推进，并加入类似Martin Rev即兴人声的插段；'Morning After Mix'则包裹在闷响的派对噪音中，营造出双腿发软回到舞池的律动感。整体呈现粗粝、昏沉而带有街头气息的俱乐部声响，在常规house框架中注入了实验性的采样处理和声音质感。

items.body:
Deep club modernist Sa Pa mints his own new label, Dub Techno For Life, with four top drawer cuts of textured, strident pressure tipped FFO classic Chain Reaction x Short Span.

Since 2015 Sa Pa has carved a heads-down path between techno, proper, and its conceptual adjuncts in ambient and sound designer atmospheres, most recently on Short Span and Astral Industries. Now taking matters into his own hands, the ‘Girls on Tour EP’ squares up his most robust club material alongside more experimental urges for a definitive self-portrait displaying a fine spectrum of strengths. 

The four tunes clearly speak to his diversity within a theme, checking for a firm touchstone in Andreas Tilliander aka Mokira with the 10 mins of rolling, claggy heft to ‘Mokira Ultra Dub’, unshelving his 2016 rework for deep ’26 ‘floors, alongside the puckered elegance of ‘Waiting For You’, harking to roots in Teutonic house minimalism, whereas the B-side attends to grubbier urges in the bittersweet, sludgy budge of ‘Modular System’, and lusher, abstract feels on the Actress or Rezzett-esque whorl of ‘World Saving Banger’.
items._genre: deep techno / dub techno / ambient / experimental
items._cn_summary: 这张EP是Sa Pa自创厂牌Dub Techno For Life的首发作品，收录四首曲目，在俱乐部律动与实验声响之间取得平衡。A面以绵长厚重的滚动节拍向Andreas Tilliander致敬，同时保留Teutonic house的极简优雅；B面则转向更粗粝的质感与抽象氛围，融入类似Actress或Rezzett式的螺旋结构。整体上，作品既延续了Chain Reaction与Short Span的经典脉络，也展现出艺术家在声音设计与环境音乐领域的积累，将深沉的低频、细密的纹理和富有张力的节奏组织成统一的个人肖像。对于关注当代电子音乐中实验性与功能性交汇的听众，这张EP提供了值得深入聆听的细节层次。

items.body:
Harking back to the vertiginous ambient sound of 2007's 'Language Barrier', Jeff McIlwain references Steve Reich and Susumu Yokota on his tenth album - his most cinematic, emotional project yet.

It makes sense somehow that after penning the poppy 'Long Light', McIlwain needed to walk in the opposite direction. Because the Lusine project has never just been one thing; since its beginnings in the late '90s, McIlwain has used the name to release choppy IDM, sturdy trip-hop, reductionist techno and placid ambient biz. Like 'Language Barrier', 'Melting Days' developed from film score work, and you can almost see the visuals on opener 'Sightline'. McIlwain uses the word "ambient" carefully; sure, the music is pegged to its washing, slow-motion pad sounds and submerged, brassy drones, but it's not entirely beatless. Here, McIlwain lets a molasses slow, almost inaudible kick do most of the heavy lifting, while a double-time click stands in for the hi-hat. On 'Bird's Eye', meanwhile, metallic hits flutter around the eroded central rhythm while McIlwain muffles his pads in the deep background.

He builds momentum on 'Pendulum' by waking up his deep, dubby soundscape with womping subs and wintery hits and on 'Intruder' curves the remnants of a voice around a skeletal, glitchy beat. McIlwain's idea of ambient music is open and all encompassing - it still belongs in the back room, but it's not just wallpaper.
items._cn_summary: Lusine的第十张专辑《Melting Days》回归2007年《Language Barrier》的眩晕环境声响，并援引Steve Reich与Susumu Yokota的影响，从电影配乐工作延伸而来。开场曲《Sightline》以流动的慢速pad与沉没的铜管drone铺陈，几乎不可闻的低音kick与双倍速click替代常规hi-hat，在无拍与微节奏间游移。《Bird's Eye》用金属质感的敲击环绕被侵蚀的中心律动，而《Pendulum》通过厚重的dub声景与womping低音推进能量，《Intruder》则将人声残片嵌入骨架化的glitch节拍。McIlwain对ambient的理解开放而包容，音乐既适合置于背景，又具有值得专注聆听的细节层次，在氛围铺底与节拍驱动之间保持了精巧的平衡，呈现出其最具电影感与情绪张力的创作面向。

items.body:
Club Romantico salute an unsung pioneer of modern club movements, Daniel Pineda ov Nguzunguzu - a producer of early Kelela and the short-lived Future Brown with Fatima Al-Qadiri - with a handful of lush yet venomous originals plus a Kelman Duran link-up 

You can’t talk about the 2010’s club sound without acknowledging Daniel Pineda’s influential, border-smudging productions as half of Nguzunguzu, with Asthma Maroof. Along with the likes of Total Freedom, Pineda’s work ushered the freshest wave of syncopated club music from the US at a time when Night Slugs (and Numbers.) and its American division, Fade To Mind, were hybridising UKF with Latin house, Jersey and B-More club and a groundswell of virulent Global South rhythms that began to percolate Westwards via blogs (this was the salient stuff when talking about blog-era, not the fidget-house pish) by the end of the ‘00s. 

Pineda’s ‘Landlocked’ firmly marks his return to a scene he sowed nearly decades ago, swerving from the heart-in-mouth pads and Dutch Bubblers-type groove to ‘De La Mama’, a a slower variant of that tresillo formula in ‘Gritos’, via the full-bore 145BPM intensity of ‘Fuerte’, a video clash-meets-Ballroom romp ‘Heavy Fact’, and the pneumatic subs and drill clack of a ‘Quema’ primed for carnival season. Another crucial bridge of Global South and Western club music, Kelman Duran tags in on the EP’s slowest, heaviest, ‘Loko 4 Eva’, strapped with below-belt quake and hardest drum cadence bound to get crowds slapping the walls.
items._cn_summary: Daniel Pineda 作为 Nguzunguzu 核心成员，曾深刻影响 2010 年代俱乐部音乐场景。这张 EP 标志着他回归，收录了从高速 145BPM 的强硬节拍、拉丁 tresillo 变体，到 ballroom 与视频对抗风格混种的多首曲目，并与 Kelman Duran 合作带来一首低频沉重、鼓组凌厉的慢速作品。制作上融合拉丁律动、Jersey 与 B-More 俱乐部元素，兼具甜美旋律与尖锐质感，延续了他打破地域边界的声音实验。该作由独立厂牌发行，展现地下俱乐部音乐的前沿面貌。

items.body:
Ezra Feinberg’s third album Soft Power sees the composer-guitarist enlist an impressive array of fellow musicians including Mary Lattimore, David Moore (Bing & Ruth), Jefre Cantu-Ledesma, and Robbie Lee.

"Defined by its abundance of melodies, repeating figures and ecstatic improvisations, Soft Power exudes an enlightened and transformative spirit to empower the listener. The compassionate, tender-hearted opener ‘Future Sand’ deftly interweaves flutes and steady arpeggios. The Reichian pulse beneath the soaring melody is played not on the customary analogue sequencer, but on finger-picked acoustic guitar, one of the lodestars of Feinberg’s compositional approach. ‘Soft Power’, the buoyant and mesmeric title track that follows builds over a rich bed of guitars and a reverb-y Rhodes melody reminiscent of a Strata East LP, its narrative arc bountiful in energy, optimism and future dreaming, a perfect accompaniment to long days of summertide.

‘Pose Beams’ blends the chamber-jazz approach of Penguin Café Orchestra with a balletic kosmische, climaxing with a galvanising crescendo and “free improv” section performed by fellow New Yorkers - Robbie Lee (piano) and Jefre Cantu-Ledesma, whose granular and modular synths sprinkle particle dust over the expressive drumming of John Thayer. ‘Flutter Intensity’ evokes in part the music of Cluster as played on acoustic guitars, which ping-pong across the stereo field, providing the canvas for a plaintive vibraphone line reminiscent of TNT-era Tortoise. Instruments move in tandem, but also drift and glide allowing them the space to hang in the air, the variegated rhythms, textures, and tones all laced into the fabric of the album.

At the centrefold of the albums 7-tracks is ‘The Big Clock’, a tryptic piece that evolves from pairs of stretched varying tones, creating fields of technicolour over an unabashed motorik beat, serving to offset the pastoral and ambient registers heard elsewhere. It features the first of two appearances from David Moore (Bing & Ruth) who plays lilting piano lines on the come-down. ‘There Was Somebody There’ returns to the album’s earlier wistfulness, a hard stereo-panned soundworld with lightly strummed, interlocking acoustic guitars combining to pigment a washy, painterly scene. David Moore and Jefre Cantu-Ledesma provide reviving synths, the underlying pulse that seems to simulate a life cycle; another day on Earth. The album closes with the reflective ‘Get Some Rest’ featuring Mary Lattimore, whose harp pluckings set a dreamlike tone against bare organic acoustics and flourishing flutes to create a sense of realignment and restoration.

Feinberg artfully transcends the listener to an enriched place, his compositions distinguished by the deep humanity that lies at their core, plugging the listener into a state of wide eyed being, open and alive. Soft Power then is Ezra’s own mantra but also one of power giving - a colourful catharsis translated into music. Feinberg’s music always speaks to the listener, but Soft Power, in whispering, speaks loudest."
items._genre: ambient / kosmische / chamber jazz / experimental / acoustic
items._cn_summary: Ezra Feinberg在第三张专辑中邀请Mary Lattimore、David Moore等乐手，以原声吉他指弹为核心，构建出兼具极简主义脉冲与自由即兴的声响世界。开篇曲以长笛与稳定琶音交织，标题曲在混响电钢琴与吉他层次中铺陈出乐观的夏日叙事；后续曲目融合室内爵士、kosmische与实验氛围，钢琴、模块合成器与鼓组在自由段落中碰撞出细腻的粒子质感。专辑中部以三乐章结构的《The Big Clock》呈现motorik节拍与彩色音场，而结尾曲在竖琴与长笛中归于宁静。整体上，作品在重复音型与即兴漂移之间取得平衡，不同乐器既协同又各自悬浮，形成一种充满人性温度与疗愈感的听感体验。

Swiss saxophonist Co Streiff and American trumpeter Russ Johnson join forces once again on Oracle , a six-track date where both bring their imaginative, open compositions to the fore. 15 years after In Circles , the pair—backed by the cooperative rhythm team of bassist Christian Weber and seasoned drummer Gerry Hemingway (replacing Julius Sartorius)—
items.body: Label: Sunnyside Records, 2026 Personnel - Co Streiff: alto saxophone; Russ Johnson: trumpet; Christian Weber: double bass; Gerry Hemingway: drums. Swiss saxophonist Co Streiff and American trumpeter Russ Johnson join forces once again on Oracle , a six-track date where both bring their imaginative, open compositions to the fore. 15 years after In Circles , the pair—backed by the cooperative rhythm team of bassist Christian Weber and seasoned drummer Gerry Hemingway (replacing Julius Sartorius)—is back in action. Despite the recording hiatus, the band got together in 2019, developing further ties that culminated in a 2023 tour. Johnson’s “ Horizontal Heartburn ”, initially a vehicle for Hemingway’s balance of dry and wet toms and syncopated hi-hat pulsation, follows with dramatic shifts in urgency, tension, and release. A staccato-driven section pumped up with unison horn lines soon morphs into a lyrically conscious theme contoured by tone-center shifts. Johnson’s noble way of articulating phrases is substantiated over sturdy bass plucks, and the piece soon engages in marching steps, leading to a frantic final dance. Streiff’s “ Smithy Street ” invites us to a funk-rock groove, perfectly suitable for measured avant-garde considerations. The saxophonist also contributes “ Remember Little Feather ”, a free-bop swing ride where she adds clever motifs, taking us to Ornette Coleman and Don Cherry. The tempo rises to double time for Johnson’s adrenaline-infused statement, with Hemingway stealing the spotlight at the end as he embarks on climactic rhythmic tapestries overflowing with interesting ideas. While the final track, “ Oracle ”, offers a creatively bluesy atmosphere, Johnson’s “ Sanguache ” comes shrouded in a cool vibe enhanced by nonchalant parallel melodies and a strong, hi-hat-accentuated backbeat. This tune preserves its lyrical side even when the band makes a somewhat unexpected turn into rock. One of the strongest pieces consists of a combination of Streiff’s “ In Circles ”, first recorded on the previous album, and Johnson’s “ Yellow Crane ”. Warm bluesy colors, a breezy tone, and an uncluttered rhythmic texture emerge with a 3/4 feel. Weber’s excellent skills and attention to detail make the transition to the chamber-jazz painterliness of the second tune, which enters in reflection mode with foundational bowed bass maneuvers. Oracle provides an effective sonic canvas, showcasing the distinctive chemistry between these two leaders and the depth of what they can create together. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Horizontal Heartburn ► 03 - In Circles / Yellow Crane ► 05 - Remember Little Feather
items._genre: avant-garde jazz / free jazz / post-bop / chamber jazz
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是萨克斯手Co Streiff与Trumpeter Russ Johnson时隔十五年后的再度合作，共收录六首作品，由贝斯手Christian Weber和鼓手Gerry Hemingway组成四重奏。音乐在开放作曲与即兴之间展开，涵盖自由波普、前卫爵士到室内爵士的多种面貌。曲目如《Horizontal Heartburn》展现力度与张力的戏剧变化，带有多变节奏和齐奏段落；《Smithy Street》融入放克摇滚律动；《Remember Little Feather》则呈现自由波普的摇摆感，并呼应Ornette Coleman和Don Cherry的传统。最后一组将旧作《In Circles》与《Yellow Crane》结合，以3/4拍的温暖蓝调色彩过渡到室内爵士的弓弦贝斯氛围。整体上，专辑强调两位领奏者的默契与作曲深度，节奏组提供细腻支撑，展现了既具结构意识又充满即兴活力的声音图景。

items._cn_summary: KILTER的新专辑以单个水分子为主角，用十个乐章描绘其形成、蒸发、降雨、深海与分解的循环。作曲方式本身构成叙事核心：三位成员各自以每分钟50拍的速度写下50小节草稿，再组合成整体，将自然过程转化为结构性的音乐对话。爵士金属的编制与实验性的作曲手法结合，使作品兼具即兴张力与精确控制。该专辑由ALTER-NATIV发行，延续了前卫音乐场景中对跨媒介叙事的探索。
