items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — The Zzebra gang is benefitting from the boon that came in the form of keyboardist/composer Tommy Eyre, whose previous band, Riff Raff, had recently disintegrated. As the instrumental songs are being realized, Tommy convinces the band to bring aboard former band-mate Alan Marshall for some vocals. 1. "Panic" (4:34). a take-no-prisoners opener for the album, it speeds along at breakneck speed using a fairly simple template for its basic structure but then employing loud horns and a kind of choir-vocals approach over/within the peloton. It's good but it could have used something . . . more. (8.875/10)2. "You've Lost That Lovin' Feeling" (6:10) slowing it down to create a smooth jazzy cover of the iconic song first made famous by The Righteous Brothers. Nice warm electric piano from Tommy Eyre, nice presentation of the main melodies of the verses from the horns (Dave Quincy's soprano sax is key), and then guitar-led ramp-up for the chorus before giving way to Steve Byrd's acoustic guitar for the solo over the second verse giving way to sax and horns for the climb back to the second electric guitar-led chorus. At this time, the four-minute mark, the music kind of empties out, slowly, carefully replaced by a Eumir Deodato/Richard Wright-like passage over which a synthy-pan flute sound takes the lead in a very Jazz-oriented section. Mellotron and reverberating electric piano usher the pan flute to its finish as well as to the song's close. (8.875/10)3. "Karrola" (3:59) a repeating rapid-fire bass and guitar line opens this one, over which the horns and rest of the band present the rest of the layers of the song with Dave Quincy's alto sax taking the first solo over some power Jazz coming from John McCoy and Liam Genockey's driving rhythm section. Tommy's electrric piano and then horns and Loughty Amao's African vocal chitter-chatter fill the treble end of the next minute before the whole band converges to take us out with the main theme. Reminds me of both NUCLEUS and post-Third THE SOFT MACHINE. (9/10)4. "Liamo" (5:54) this Jazz-Rock Fusion tune feels as if the master tape of the previous song were taken down to half speed--which makes the legato lines of each of the instruments in the overall weave seem so slow and deliberate. Horns are very clear and deliberate while electric guitar and electric piano seem to dominate the fills and flourishes occurring over the top. In the fourth minute a chorus of vocalists seem to chant/sing an African-like line ("Liamo") while Steve, Dave, Liam, and Tommy continue to add their responses between the chant lines (in their breath pauses). The problem is that the vocal lines being slowed down as much as the rest of the plodding instruments, it feels as if the band is playing one of those exaggeratedly depressing New Orleans funereal processionals--only I keep waiting to hear the sudden shift (as the movies show it) into high-spirited music of celebration and elation. But, it never happens. The musicians more than prove themselves but the overall energy and feeling the listener is left with is more akin to big animal stomping. (8.75/10)5. "Death By Drowning" (2:58) Tommy Eyre is given some time to show off some of the applications his discoveries on his new electronic keyboards have revealed. In the third minute Dave Quincy joins him with some plaintive soprano sax play. Very Zawinul-esque. (4.375/5) 6. "Tree" (6:01) It turns out that the previous song was an intro to this one as Tommy's pensive pan-oscillating electric piano chord play opens this one before vocals and "distant" semi-muted soprano sax join in to sing about something metaphorical. Nice. At 2:18 there is a rather sudden and delightfully-welcomed shift into higher gear as bassist John McCoy takes off with some very animated racing funk play daring everyone else to try to catch him. Tommy is the most successful as his multiple keys are right there at the front of the pack but Liam and Loughty don't seem able as their sounds are left in the distance. Eventually, Dave's soprano sax convinces everybody to slow back down, which brings the team back to the opening motif for a vocal-led finish. Nice. Easily my favorite song on the album (despite its flaws). (9.5/10) 7. "Put A Light On Me" (4:59) clavinet! funky synths! Alan Marshall gets a truly lead vocal role in/over this one as John and Liam lay down an equally-funky rhythm track to match that of Tommy's keys. Alan is great though the band/producer still, obviously, don't trust him enough to give his vocal track appropriate front-and-center spotlighting. (How ironic that the lyric he's singing is about "put the light on me" as he finds himself not wanting to live in the dark! "I'd rather be on my own," he sings.) A catchy, memorable earworm of a song. Another top three. (9/10)8. "La Si Si - La So So" (5:12) opening with another great high-speed rabbit run from John McCoy to lead the way, everybody else is very quick to get in line, even Liam's drums, but more importantly, the horn section's accent blasts and, of course, Tommy Eyre's electric piano. (He's such a consummate professional!) The first true solo isn't launched until the very end of the second minute: it's Steve Byrd's searing John Tropea-like electric guitar, followed by Dave's tenor sax. They're both excellent and the rhythm section below maintains an awesome display of energy and togetherness. (Big shout out to percussionist Loughty Amao!) Great NUCLEUS-like finish to the album. A true Jazz-Rock Fusion classic! My other top three song. (9.75/10) Total time 39:47I have to admit to having higher hopes and expectations for this album--especially after just finishing the week of getting to know the output of the band RIFF RAFF--where Tommy Eyre and Alan Marshall previously spent some time. A-/five stars; a minor masterpiece of Nucleus-like Jazz-Rock Fusion led by some very skilled bass, sax, and keyboard players. Though there are some low points of inconsistency, the highs are respectably high. Recommended to all Jazz-Rock Fusion lovers.

items.body: Left: P+D 02 01 02 (2024); Right: M P Landis & Michael Sarin, May 18, 2024 at L/A Arts, Lewiston, ME Adjacent to a drumkit, two large boards hang above a stage clad in drop cloth. A third lies flat on a small table surrounded by paint bottles and upturned pot lids that will become ad hoc palettes. Each board is covered in paper and divided into grids by white painter's tape: the small board into nine squares and the larger two into twelve. It's the end of June 2026 at the Apohadion Theater in Portland, Maine. Just ahead, the fifth meeting of painter M P Landis and drummer Michael Sarin in a collaboration they've come to call, concisely, Paint & Drums. Fans of creative music may recognize Landis's paintings from the album covers of artists like Flow Trio , [ism] , and Sabir Mateen . His work is part of an estuary somewhere far downstream of the Abstract Expressionists: gestures that range from child-like markings to purposive strokes that convey the whole body's movement; textured clots and layers of color; obscure figures and shapes that could be letters or symbols but offer a mute refusal. But Landis will say he feels less affinity with other visual artists than he does with musicians. Indeed, what stands out about Landis's work is how deeply committed his methods are to the same reactive, exuberant ethos that drives the free improvisers. Music—especially jazz and improvised music—has long been part of Landis's work, both in the studio and in a live setting. In a 2006 conversation with the writer Fred Schmalz, he described arriving at a point in the 1990s where he began using music "as a jumping off point to get beyond my ideas and find a way of working that transcends technique and becomes more emotional and dance-like." Joe Maneri/Mat Maneri/Randy Peterson #1 - #4 (2001). Created live at the 2001 Vision Festival, NYC His career in the decades since validates Mike Heffley's musing in Northern Sun, Southern Moon. "If one were a painter," Heffley wrote, free improvisation "is music that might be the most fruitful aid and stimulus to the process. It encourages one to get physical with one's tools and media, to delight in them as ends in themselves, whatever means they might develop into therefrom." Talking with Schmalz, Landis describes exactly that: "I feel almost like the music uses me or, I guess I use the music to use me. There is a certain surrendering to what I am listening to which helps me jump right into physically moving; making marks, grabbing paint, etc. It overcomes the endless problems of decision and throws me right into the act of creating." Some of Landis's paintings bear titles that pay tribute to the music he was listening to as he painted. But music's influence is more deeply seated. Top: David S. Ware: Onecept triptych (mp13.01, mp13.02, mp13.03) (2013) Bottom Left: PIANO SKY (JOE MANERI) (2003); Bottom Right: lp13.06 (derek bailey) (2013) Landis moved from painting on street corners and in the audience at concerts to frequently painting on stage in collaboration with musicians, dancers, and other visual artists in the vibrant Brooklyn arts scene. He remains a prolific collaborator. The live performances of that period culminated in a tour with the Jump Arts American Road Project in 2002, Landis taking the stage with poet Steve Dalachinsky, dancers, and musicians like Tom Abbs, Daniel Carter, Steve Swell, and Okkyung Lee. Cisco Bradley's recounting of the tour in The Williamsburg Avant-Garde touches on Landis's intense engagement with his materials and an approach to live painting that's still present in Paint & Drums: "[Landis] would paint through the entire evening of performances, with two wooden panels covered in paper on which to work. One panel was covered by one large piece of paper, while the other panel had multiple smaller pieces stapled to it. Landis described his process: 'I painted the whole board, not thinking about where one piece of paper stopped or started. I liked how it gave the work a sense of being midstream, like capturing a sound in time.' He added, 'The intensity of the music made the painting intense. It felt like I was doing months' worth of painting within a few hours.'" Left: american road project 1L (2002); Right: j.a.a.r.p. [#12.] (2002) It was during his time in NYC that Landis met Sarin, then drumming in the storied Thomas Chapin Trio (just one facet of his deep and continued embeddedness in the New York avant-garde). Nearly two decades later, Sarin lamented that he never had a chance to see Landis paint in a live setting and asked if he'd be willing to collaborate. Two performances were arranged in May 2024, and the duo have now met three more times in 2026. A Visual Musician There's an enticing trap, or at least a long stroll to a dead end, in approaching the relationship between Landis's paintings and free jazz. It is to interpret them as somehow "representing" the music. Landis is clear on this: "I don’t mean for [the music] to define the work because I’m not interested in making visual representations of music, or anything for that matter. These paintings and drawings are artifacts of a creative process; a recording of my reactions to not just music, but to life and my living it." Establishing that the relationship is indirect, two smaller traps await, both common responses to abstract music and painting. Treading carefully between them, I'm likely to get a foot caught in each. The first comes from the dismissive "Even I Could Have Done That" school of art criticism; the other adopts a transcendental tone that inflates the abstract nature of these artforms until they're lofted into the clouds. Something like "overwhelming directness" versus "overweening mystery," to borrow from Stanley Cavell. Left to Right: MONK 3. THINK OF ONE (2005); MONK 4. HACKENSACK (2005); MONK 5. 'ROUND MIDNIGHT (2005) The first response is an almost defensive tensing in the face of such directness. A move to immediately let the air out before the overweeners get too jazzed up. "I get it. Your painting is like free jazz: random and improvised and spontaneous." Nothing enigmatic here. You don't really have to know anything, you just have to do. Splatter the paint, whack the drum, toot the horn. This attitude tends to badly underestimate the skill that's required to achieve the allegedly facile result, but there's something perceived here, a focus on the plain fact of bodies in action, that can't be entirely dismissed. The process, the doing, is integral—it's what's insisted by these artforms, what we can always sense even when we try (willfully or otherwise) to bracket it out. In viewing pieces like the "Monk Work" paintings, those initial impressions of sheer spontaneity belie the fact that, just as in lots of jazz and improvised music, accumulated experience and an incredible depth of consideration are channeled into an application of skill, shaping an ongoing process that didn't have a specific end in mind when things got underway. What get overlooked are all the particularities: the whorl of circumstance, body, and action that actually birthed that painting or moment of music. Landis's painting isn't merely like free jazz because both can be loud and break rules. Many of his pieces represent a series of events and decisions through time—sometimes over weeks and months—that are fervently attuned to intention and accident and their intertwining. Left : 16.35T (2016); Right : 19.155 (2019) We often fall back on visual metaphors when trying to talk about music, but the counterintuitive thing about Landis's paintings is that their material likeness to music is not visual, but temporal: they are "impossible" images that inscribe action-through-time in the same way that music does as it plays out. This sense of movement-across-time leaps from their surfaces. Looking at a piece like 16.35T , I really do find myself reaching for musical concepts: there's a staccato rhythm to the marks, which have a lively motion in their stacks of contrapuntal bands. There's dissonance in the dabs of glowing green, which seem to punctuate moments in the painting's development. The paintings have no telos, just as improvised music isn't about getting to the end of playing. They aren't planned and realized ends or even a representation of an instant or "the now" but rather they are a holding-open, a paradoxical attempt to spatialize temporality, or express it all at once. The time-taking is the work in the way music is the running of the clock. This temporal nature is never more apparent than during live performance. There, we see the changing cadences of painting, the transformation of color and form as new strokes merge with old, the accumulation of layers that continually supplant the painting's character, even as glimpses of its previous features remain. Brice Marden once said of Jackson Pollock, "He doesn't apply the image; he lets the image evolve out of the activity." Landis: "I like to push what I make ‘til it feels right, in some inner logic kind of way, even when that leads me to something that might look off or clumsy, but in a way that attracts me." All of these evolved and evolving particularities are exactly why just anyone couldn't create that painting or improvise those sounds. Those unrepeatable elements in concert with the artist's grappling are what constitute the work. If such painting or music could be said to have "content," this is all it could possibly be, and encrypted. You may be physically capable of executing the work, but you could never be existentially capable—you have no access to its means of creation. Top, Left to Right: wd3060 (2006); wd2034 (2004); wd5625 (2013) Middle, Left to Right: wd5921 (2014); wd6016 (2014); wd6058 (2014) Bottom, Left to Right: wd6831 (2016); wd7972 (2019); wd6562 (2016) This idea of paintings as ledgers or accretions of activity is hyper-concentrated in the wd series ("warehouse drawings"). Landis produced 10,000 wd pieces in the nearly thirty years between October 1996 and March 2025. Nearly all began as a folded piece of paper that Landis would carry with him throughout the day, often marked with notes, reminders, shopping lists. "Later in the studio, I chronologically staple them to boards, usually working on 20 at a time, drawing and painting on them, often in multiple layers over many days, weeks and sometimes months in response to whatever is happening in my world at each session." Like a recording of an improvised performance, the wd paintings are the record of happenings that can't ever be restaged, a ledger of events that could never be repeated exactly so. Their accumulation of texture, their creases and sometimes ragged edges, are evidence of their travel through the real world, are the grounding reminders that, however abstract the visuals, they are the products of a creative drive that is selfsame with Landis, moving through life. Though Landis has retired the wd series, hints of their methodology have emerged in a new FP series created on small pieces of folded hand-made paper. Left to Right: FP26.78 (2026); FP26.103 (2026); FP26.174 (2026) Paintings from the wd series often made their way back to music, and the influence began running in the opposite direction. Several have been used as album art, and over the years musicians would ask Landis if they could use a painting as inspiration for music. Most notably, Loren Connors and Suzanne Langille took a number of wd pieces and projected them in the studio while recording, which was subsequently released as I Wish I Didn't Dream . During the pandemic, Landis began a series of smaller, heavily contingent paintings called "Notes." Each month, he starts dozens, which he lays around the house or beneath paintings in the studio, allowing them to gather stains and marks of daily life. "Notes" can be shuffled and combined into larger pieces called "Compositions," forming the basis of graphic scores. In 2024, the Cannery in Penobscot, Maine staged a series of concerts in which "Compositions" were performed by musicians like E. Jason Gibbs, Phillip Greenlief, Leslie Ross, Steve Norton, Laura Cromwell, and others. Top, Left to Right: Note 138 (2020); Note 126 (2020); Note 154 (2020); Note 1131 (2026) Bottom, Left to Right: Note 964 (2025); Note 1121 (2026); Note 1 (2020); Note 702 (2023) Accepting that there's something more than brute, unskilled doing behind such vast and varied artistic output, the "overweening" approach—a propensity I admit I must actively temper—starts from trying to articulate the interesting whatness of all those coalesced particularities . But it can be quick to flight and risks overstating its case. In seeking some ultimate source for often dumbfounding glimpses into a pure creative stream, it also risks leaving the artist behind entirely. Firebrand critic Robert Hughes famously had little patience for this. He once wrote that all of the "verbose obeisances to the Ineffable" in discussions of Mark Rothko's work tended "to be coercive, because of a deep uncertainty about the nature of his art." (I'm not sure what Hughes would make of something like Paint & Drums, though I can imagine him satisfied, standing before the large paintings at the end of the show, still gleaming and dripping.) Hughes's warning is not unfounded, but it's also dismissive of the role uncertainty and small-i ineffability play in the experience of art like Landis's (or Rothko's, for that matter). We find the ineffable creeping up not because this sort of art is a direct mainline to the transcendent Godhead or a manifestation of universal Truth, but because it carries the possibility of ringing within us some deeply sympathetic tone, a personal and close-feeling resonance that never quite carries through into words. This isn't absolute or guaranteed. In truth, it is fleeting and infrequent. But we each know our own private tone and we hope in our encounters to feel that vibration. Returning to Cavell, in "Music Discomposed" he says these kinds of art are " known by feeling , or in feeling," and this underlies our anxiety and difficulty in communicating this knowledge: "I want to tell you something I've seen, or heard, or realized, or come to understand, for the reasons for which such things are communicated (because it is news, about a world we share, or could). Only I find that I can't tell you; and that makes it all the more urgent to tell you. I want to tell you because the knowledge, unshared, is a burden . . . It matters, there is a burden, because unless I can tell you what I know, there is a suggestion (and to myself as well) that I do not know." This uncertainty is not a defect. It is an essential component of the improvised musical set, and of Landis's practice as he steps into his studio each day and faces dozens of paintings in various stages. And, Hughes's self-certainty aside, I think it is also the essential, brightly dark core of our aesthetic experience of these works. It's the same doubt the skeptic amplifies until it distorts into nothingness, easy to dismiss. Uncertainty—not-quite-knowing—is the grip that pulls the artist into the stream, and it's also the grip that gets us by the collar and stops us, to look or to listen. Picking up a paint brush or a saxophone are also attempts to convey news about a world we share, or could. Left: 15.14 (2015); Right: 20.03 (2020) "Somehow Precise, Intense, and Vague All at Once" The heading is Michael Gallope's description of what he calls music's "affective inconsistency," but it also beautifully captures Landis's paintings and the particular energy of his live collaboration with Sarin. One of the more charming aspects of Landis's and Sarin's partnership is that they still aren't quite sure of it. Each time, they gently ease into a start and there's always some hesitation about whether they've finished. This thread of uncertainty runs through the whole performance, is what fuels the excitement, but it also feels more palpable than during a musical improvisation. Left: M P Landis and Michael Sarin, May 15, 2024 at the Apohadion Theater, Portland, ME Top Right: P+D 04 01 03 (2026); Bottom Right: P+D 03 02 02 (2026) In the audience, witnessing the real-time change in the paintings draws out tensions between arising aesthetic judgments and a curiosity about what continuing will yield. As elements emerge in the paintings, there are times when things "feel" finished, or where particular sections or forms satisfy some personal preference. I find myself becoming protective, secretly wishing that further actions will spare a notable swirl of black or a blaze of orange that still burns though layer after layer. I wasn't alone. At several of the performances, others talked about fearing a painting was "ruined" at points during the show, feeling satisfied with a certain stage of the process and forgetting that the process must continue, that the painting in the moment they esteemed it also arose by that process. After the April 2026 performance, one enthusiastic young audience member bantered with Landis about the range of emotions he felt during the show: "At one point, I actually felt angry with you, man! I thought you fucked it up!" Imagining how you think someone should be behaving toward certain sounds or stimuli also leads to subverted expectations. I wonder if the way Landis is moving should be more . . . what? Theatrical? Synchronized? Wouldn't that be inauthentic? How do I suppose live painting and drumming should look, and where'd those ideas even come from? It feels like the risks of improvising are magnified. And are they greater for M P? Notes melt away, but marks on canvas remain. Left: P+D 01 02 04 (2024); Center: P+D 01 01 03 (2024); Right: P+D 02 02 08 (2024) It's all quite different from watching two musicians improvising. At times they seem at odds, or moving just past one another. Sarin whips himself into a storm, a deluge of creative energy that—in my mind—is an arc of electricity shooting across the stage to directly animate M P's limbs. But Landis is opening a paint bottle or looking for a brush. All that, just dissipated! But has it? I presume bolts of lightning, but am likely missing the charged potential in the air. In some ways, it becomes easier to sense these shifting emotions when there's a visual element, a continuing remnant. In music alone, things often move so quickly that only the most egregious "missteps" or a complete failure to gel create notable feelings of resistance in the witness. Here, things move as fast, but your eyes are drawn to the canvas, which holds on to the movement of the performance like streaks of light in a long exposure. Through all these contours, there's an unmistakable resonance between what Landis and Sarin are doing, if not an equivalence. I feel an immense mental force that wants to draw their activities into a neat consonance, but it's like pushing repelling magnets together. As Landis has always maintained, the painting doesn't "represent" the sounds any more than the reverse. Instead, there's a joyous, if ambiguous, exchange of energy. You can see that it's mutually reinforcing. Sarin is palpably exhilarated. The propulsion of his drumming spurs Landis into action, and the emerging images become mutable graphic scores, giant ever-changing "notes" urging Sarin further. The exact how just evades a tight grasp. Together or separately, the painting and drumming are abstract art that many would accuse of being untethered. But there's something stubbornly literal in their doing. The paintings are just that: caked and layered paint, ink, and pastel, thick and viscous or water-thinned and dripping. The drums: driving, rhythmic, sometimes crashing, deafening, sometimes the faintest texture of hand's skin on drumskin. It is all, plainly, what it is, a frustrating tautology because there is yet, as Sarin said at the end of the most recent performance, an alchemy. "Whole" and "Divided" Painting from Paint & Drums 4, May 9, 2026 at the Loove Annex, Brooklyn, NY Fever Bed To quote another M-P, Maurice Merleau-Ponty wrote in "Cézanne's Doubt" that "before expression, there is nothing but a vague fever, and only the work itself, completed and understood, will prove that there was something rather than nothing to be found there." I'd gently propose shifting the sense of the word "work": M-P wrote l'œuvre , a finished piece of art, an "artifact" of the creative act. I'd like to read it as the doing, le faire, le travail —the undertaking of creating. I often sense that vague fever while listening to improvised music, like the back of my hand against a warm forehead, and admittedly less often when facing a painting. I vicariously feel it in the dim light, watching Landis and Sarin on stage. Still, I sense in myself an inhibiting self-consciousness, like I'd never be able to start, even as I also discover expectations and opinions welling up and fading away as the performance plays out. Once in motion, there's an odd sort of courage in continuing to mark the canvas, to pound the drum, but I wonder if the central task of the improvising artist is to continually overcome that uneasy inertia and just begin . An unstopping at imagination's edge that risks mistake and awkwardness and dissatisfaction to possibly reach something that at best can only be hazily made out, and not at all while sitting in caution and doubt. Unsure if you can know you've reached it. Something about the feeling of reaching. Left: FEVER BED (MAT MANERI TRIO) (2003); Right: manifestation (before fire music) (2001) See much, much more of M P Landis's work, including video clips and other pieces from the Paint & Drums performances, on his Instagram or Facebook pages. You can see what Michael Sarin is up to on his Instagram page. All photos of paintings used with the artist's permission. All performance photos by Dan Sorrells. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body:
“The thing about playing the tuba in an orchestra is that you don’t have to play that much,” admitted composer Matthew Wright, who grew up playing the tuba in orchestras and funk bands, “but it’s the best seat in the house. You hear music back to front. The percussion and the brass are loud, so you hear all their detail, and the strings are this kind of ethereal thing that’s off in the distance.”

For the Kent-based Wright, who also improvises using turntables, samplers, and processers – most impactfully with Trance Map, his partnership with Evan Parker – this early realization nurtured a sensibility leading to the creation of immersive works that mix composition, improvisation, and technology. Cracked Glaze (False Walls) is a case in point, as it utilizes notated material – “dot music” is his good-humored term – improvisation, and Wright’s real-time sampling and processing immediately fed into surround sound, all of which he remixed for the CD.

Wright’s collaborators on Cracked Glaze represent various facets of his work. Ensemble Klang, an ensemble of mostly Dutch new music virtuosi, was an early champion of Wright’s compositions. Spheric Totemic is a Wright-instigated, flexibly configured improvising group with, on this occasion, Mandhira de Saram, Alexander Hawkins, Neil Charles and Stephen Davis. Sofia Jernberg, whose Musho with Hawkins was one of the brighter lights of 2024, is new to Wright’s constellation.

Historically, the conventional wisdom among exponents of freely improvised music is that the larger the group, the more apt the music will be muddied. It is a yardstick that is also prevalent among practitioners of contemporary composition. Individuality – of the improviser, of the composer – is more difficult to assert in or through a crowd. Although there are more than a dozen musicians heard on Cracked Glaze, there is no nebulous sprawl or complexity for complexity’s sake. Abstraction is tethered to figuration, the spine of the piece being a descending line that repeatedly submerges and reemerges, giving the interactions of voices clear relationships.

“In a lot of my written work for ensembles there is a central concern that tends to last a long period of time, an idea that will give the piece structure. I’m really interested in music being a kind of terrain that you can hear through and around, so that when you are listening, you are experiencing a kind of ‘visual’ situation. I guess this goes back to my work with vinyl records, because records make music a physical surface, where you can place the needle anywhere in the terrain of the music.

“In the improvised work, I don’t want to be the guy that says to improvisers, ‘this is how it goes.’ Improvisation, in a free context, is about distributed leadership. It’s about this beautiful situation of people saying, ‘the music could go here’ or ‘I hear the future of this music in what you’re playing,’ and the kind of listening that leads to those sorts of situations.

“Having the opportunity to work with a group that is mainly readers – Ensemble Klang – and a group that is mainly improvisers – Spheric Totemic – and Sofia Jernberg, gave me the opportunity to do something I haven’t done much of in my music, to have a spine that is unfurling but is always there. It doesn’t necessarily always have to be the main focus of the piece, but it will always be there. It will structure time in a certain way; improvisers can do whatever they want to do, and the music will be as much about them as it is the spine. I was really interested in having a sort of ‘object’ in the space of the improvisation. It’s almost like in the visual art world, where you have people moving around in a gallery but there’s a sculpture there. It’s in the room with you.”

Another virtue of Cracked Glaze is that it is the type of work that initially seems to come out of nowhere. It smacks of singularity. However, Wright’s backstory reveals that he did not come out of nowhere, as he has a pedigree linking him to England’s most consequential institutional incubator of experimental music, as well as its most venerable, living exponent of improvised music. Both associations largely account for how Wright’s disparate interests – several of which were common among Gen Xers in their formative years but were delayed in being assimilated into experimental music – were shaped into a mature aesthetic, and yielded in Cracked Glaze an arguably definitive statement.

“My experience, first of all, was writing music and playing in brass bands and funk bands and small improvising groups with friends,” Wright recently explained. “But I also liked writing chamber music for people who would take it away and play it somewhere else. I might not even be there for the performance. This background took me to study at the University of Huddersfield with the Professor who set up the Huddersfield Contemporary Music Festival, Richard Steinitz. I was very lucky. It was kind of random. He was my composition teacher. So, I was very lucky to have experiences like knocking on the door for a composition lesson and Richard Steinitz saying, ‘Ah, Matt, I can’t possibly teach you right now, but meet Karlheinz,’ and the door opens and there’s this world-famous composer from another generation that I had read about, but never dreamed I would meet.

“Contemporary classical music was a big part of my education, but I DJed as a kid. I was really interested at that point in the ‘80s and ‘90s when software, sampling, and DJ technology, was becoming affordable. It started showing up in people’s homes. Contemporary classical music and DJ culture were colliding in my mind when I was a kid. The only kind of formal education I could get was a classical education, along with some jazz theory, but it was largely based on dot music, written music. Then there was this other (non-written) side, like DJ culture and all of the great heritage of Black music that DJ culture is part of, and that was a kind of informal education I studied for myself.

“When I was a real little kid – like 12 or 13 – I made a lot of bedroom productions with a basic computer and turntable setup, really focused on instrumental hip-hop. I started to scratch around then, just watching how it was done on TV. My main inspirations were DJ Premier of Gangstarr, Terminator X of Public Enemy, and Maseo of De La Soul. When I was around 18 or 19, as a student, I DJed for a few parties, playing mainly funk, hip hop, and drum ‘n' bass. Around the same time – 1996-98 – I was in a few pop/funk bands that needed a DJ, so I did a few things with beat juggling and matching the pitch of the horns with turntable scratches, etc.

“In 1999 I DJed for a social event at the Huddersfield Contemporary Music Festival and I decided to just play fragments of music that I loved at the time: The Jazz Warriors, Louis Andriessen, Loose Tubes, Squarepusher, Björk. On the basis of that weird mix, I got the call to DJ at Abbey Road for the launch of a music charity, the PRS Foundation, in 2000. That was both a social event and included some (not entirely successful!) experimental scratching. When I moved to Holland to study with composer Louis Andriessen in 2002, I joined a trio with laptop artist Tom Tlalim and saxophonist Keir Neuringer – now of Irreversible Entanglements – and we played a few house parties and small gigs with our own mix of free improv and beat-based electronica. That same year the Huddersfield Festival commissioned ‘Presents from an Edited Then’ which was a 70-minute piece for The Apollo Saxophone Quartet and me DJing, designed for a club venue, again a mix of ‘social’ and ‘experimental’. That’s when I got interested in the worlds of contemporary classical music and DJ culture colliding.”

One of the first projects Wright embarked on was to compose for turntables and to teach classically-trained percussionists how to use them, integrating John Cage’s early work for percussion with the innovations of Christian Marclay and Otomo Yoshihide. “In a piece called Contact Theatre I had literally written out all of the material for notation-reading percussionists”, Wright said of the work. “If you look at a musical stave with the four spaces between the lines, I used those spaces to represent the four spaces on a vinyl record. The space that would be a F in the treble stave, that’s the space on the outer edge of the record, before any musical material appears on the vinyl record. All of the musical material on the record is included in the second space, and then the space at the center of the record was the third space, and then the label itself in the fourth space. You can prepare those spaces, put stickers on them. I would literally write percussion rhythms and they could produce those rhythms by dropping the needle on the record and get a ricochet effect or specify a section of the record I want to be played, say a saxophone solo three minutes into the record. I developed these ‘half-contact’ techniques where the needle sticks like a locked groove, and I taught the basics of hip hop scratching to percussionists, even though the music didn’t sound anything like hip hop.”

Wright then began to assess the proportions of and the relationships between the elements of his aesthetic and how to integrate them in his work. “Cracked Glaze is a collision of all of the above. I have been doing ensemble work and turntable work and installation work, but a lot of my focus is on the work with Evan in mixing and even post-production of the Trance Map material. Post-production is really part of the process, and Evan is very interested in exploring all that. Although Cracked Glaze doesn’t involve Evan, it brings to equal terms all of the sources I work with. There’s some notation written for Ensemble Klang with holes in that notation, space for the improvisation group of Spheric Totemic and Sofia Jernberg. They have start and stop times for the improvising, and they also sometimes have cues for some notation. I’m also mixing them live on stage, taking samples and remixing them and using the turntable as well. Then I take all that material and work on it a little in the studio, not to radically change the piece but to bring out some of the elements that you would hear live but not in a stereo recording. The piece brings together notation, improvisation, and technology, but not as separate forms. They all intersect. That’s where they all join on the map.”

In a roundabout way, the title of the piece speaks to the processes of its creation. It refers to the glazes used in high-fire ceramics that are formulated to crack on temperature; even though they are applied in an even manner, the cracking results in a surface that can be likened to a mosaic assembled with random tiles, with dark, hair-thin spaces between them. Though the results are subject to a unique firing, the experienced artist knows how to promote cracking that is pleasing and avoid cracking that ruins the piece.

“It may be interesting to talk about how jazz standards have worked in the past,” Wright responded to the idea of controlled cracking, and chuckling at the notion that he controlled the gas valve. “An excellent standard is one that can be played in its entirety and feel integrated and beautiful, but it is also a catalyst. It offers itself up to be cracked, to be turned into something new. In some ways, the use of notation to suggest a response is fascinating to me. On a technical level, there are definitely moments where I say to the improvisers, ‘at a certain point you will hear a line and at that point, that pitch, that’s your moment; if you’re improvising, the natural ebb and flow of the group will go to you’. But I don’t say ‘you should crack it’ to them; I say ‘it’s yours’.

“And there’s a third element there, the equivalent of the heat – the processing and the spatialization. I’m taking the feed of everybody, the notated music and the improvised music is coming to my setup, and I’m able to remix it and sample it. I’m an agent in the cracking, too. Whether it is notated or not is not the point, because it’s all going through the same system and being splintered into surround sound. That’s the third element, the sound design is a catalytic element.”

Wright pointed to a poster in his studio of a still influential Japanese textile exhibition he attended in his early 20s. “What I loved about that,” he said, “was that the dynamic shapes of these textiles are very rigid, spatially, but the textiles themselves have all sorts of holes in them. They are almost like fishing nets. I tried to create something similar by creating a structure that’s flexible but has holes in it. If we play this piece again, the melody line and the structure is going to be exactly the same every time and the improvising and the specialization will be different every time. That’s a long-winded way of saying I tried not to over notate.”

Wright acknowledged that post-production, particularly when the work was created in a surround sound environment and is remixed for stereo, creates a distinct experience of the work, and perhaps represents a new iteration of the pursuit of perfection in the studio, exemplified by Glenn Gould. “My pieces are concepts that have a sort of quantum existence,” Wright maintained. “What I mean is that if we are going to present the piece live, then there are circumstances that will be dynamic for the audience in the live space that may not be so dynamic when hearing it at home. In the live space, I’m dealing with surround sound. There are a whole lot of options to try to present that sort of experience in the stereo format. When it comes to making a CD or something online that people will listen to, I consider the domestic setting. I also consider that many people listen to music on the go, with headphones or their phone. You may be walking down the Avenue of the Americas and everything around you is changing, but there’s one consistent thread in the music.

“You have to consider the multiple ways that people listen now. I do hope that people will sit at home to listen to it. In that situation, it’s much closer to reading a book because it’s a solitary experience. You’re sitting with it for 40 or 50 minutes. Wearing headphones creates an interior experience. I really treasure those kinds of listeners and it’s a real privilege when someone spends that time with something that I’ve made with my musical friends.

“In the history of improvised music there have been many vehement statements about the relationship between free improvised music and recording. I totally get that, but I suppose that the question we now have to consider is what happens when you improvise with a recording. We don’t want the karaoke thing! How does the recording come back into the improvised music experience in as fluid a way you would have with another musician with an instrument? An instrument is obviously a technology of its own and the recording is the result of the technology. We need to make sure the technology is as flexible as any other instrument. The other thing I’m really fascinated by in the history of free creative music is the evolution of incorporating electronics. It’s really interesting for me when an electro-acoustic improvised situation might suggest that the music is not happening in the present tense, but in the past or the future.

“The thing I’m really interested in is those previously separated camps of notation, improvisation, and technology becoming one and the same, where there is an equaling out of the three. You’re not relying on one form of expression. And this seems to be causing a real revitalization of the scene, where people are mastering their separate disciplines and are also negotiating with each other. I think there’s more opportunity for creative music because of the dialogue between notation, improvisation, and technology. Looking for the connections between them is the main creative impetus. It’s not paper; it’s not technology; it’s not adherence to one way of making music. It’s about thinking about the connections between the people you’re working with. Saying ‘all of the above’ may be too easy an answer, but it does ascribe equal value to notation, improvisation and technology. These are all zones on the map and they all overlap each other, so the paths between those zones are what I’m interested in.”

***

Wright’s projects frequently overlap, the post production of one coinciding with the development of another. With summer approaching, Wright was mixing a duo session with Pat Thomas that has the flavor of This is Trickster; a Spheric Totemic album, and a Trance Map + recording on which Parker and him are joined by harpist Milana Zaric and Richard Barrett.

The presence of Barrett is particularly intriguing, as he pioneered improvised electronic music beginning in the 1990s – largely through FURT, his partnership with Paul Obermayer – laying groundwork for Wright and others. Additionally, Barrett’s compositions are renowned for testing – and often surpassing – the presumed physical limits of instrumentalists.

Barrett and Wright are part of a trajectory of composers foregrounding technology in their work. An earlier dot on the line, one that is essential but not obvious, is Conlon Nancarrow. The expatriate composer is the inspiration for Wright’s next major work, “Passing Nancarrow.” Wright’s latest project with the Belgian ensemble BL!NDMAN (the exclamation point is intentional) also has Hawkins in a key role. The piece debuts next year, marking 30 years since Nancarrow died.

“The idea of the piece is based around Nancarrow being obsessed with Art Tatum’s playing,” Wright explained. “He sampled Tatum in the form of piano rolls, using technology from a hundred years ago. What we will do is, while Alex improvises in real time, his notes are captured and this will trigger all sorts of reactions from the group. In a way, we turn Alex’s music into a piano roll.”

Wright was partly inspired by the writer and documentary film director Helen Borton’s comment that jazz and blues collide like a “hurricane” in Nancarrow’s music. Replace “hurricane” with “Nancarrow” and you get the gist of Wright’s conceptualization for the recording he is currently mixing – “four hurricanes of all kinds of crazy sounds.” Wright also considered the music of Squarepusher, Aphex Twin, and other exponents of electronic dance music, that influenced him when Nancarrow died in 1997, leading him to include “strange, intelligent dance music in the piece.”

However, the nexus of Nancarrow, Barrett, and Wright, is the consideration of the limits of music humans can create in real time, and how to get to the edge of those limits, if not extend them.

“Nancarrow reached for impossible, post-human music. But in my current work, I don’t have an artistic interest in post-human AI. I’ve heard a lot of AI-generated music and read a lot of AI research, and the thing I’m already bored by is that AI can do almost anything. Like a musician that can play everything and just won’t stop playing to give space for others, AI doing anything and everything is boring to me when you don’t hear inspired choices and you don’t hear the human labor or the human need for considered space in the music. But, I’m open minded. I just haven’t heard anything that inspires me yet. Back to the human level, in Alex’s piano playing, there is that reaching beyond what is supposedly humanly possible, to reach a new vista for what is possible.

“You can say that, for his times, Nancarrow was making a post-human kind of music, but we should remember that he sat there, punching holes. So, I don’t hear a sort of pre-AI in his music, a piano that can do anything, but the blood and the hours of Nancarrow sitting maybe six months to create an explosive two minutes. I want to know how humans feel when they hear music and when they make music. If that is aided by technology, the idea is that the technology helps musical thinking like an instrument helps musical thinking. My interest in technology is the same as Alex’s interest in the piano, there’s a tradition of human tool use there that in a sense heightens the human listening experience if done successfully.

“Another thing I like about Nancarrow was that he was true to his beliefs, which is why he left the US for Mexico City, which resulted in him working in relative isolation. He just got on with it. A few people had experimented with the player piano before, but he made it his own. I appreciate that you can hear the edges in music and you’re OK with not being able to know everything beyond that edge. I guess the difference between the scene we have now and Nancarrow’s situation is that we can go to the edge together in a collaborative spirit.”
