items.body: Escape With Romeo‘s return stopped being interesting simply as a comeback with 2024’s “Suspicious Bliss”. That album established that Thomas Elbern was not interested in reopening the band’s history merely to revisit it; there was new material to write and, increasingly, a present worth responding to. “Night After Night”, released on August 7, 2026 through Zeitklang, continues that trajectory with a harder, more immediate record built around guitars, electronics and a growing unease with the systems shaping contemporary life. The circumstances behind it were different too. After forty years working as a music journalist for national radio, Elbern suddenly found himself with considerably more time, and sketches already sitting on his hard drive began turning into songs. At the same time, the world entering those songs had become increasingly difficult to separate into “online” and “real”: surveillance, AI, algorithmic behaviour, political extremism, digital dependence and the erosion of privacy all appear across the album. What interests Elbern, however, is less dystopia as spectacle than the moment when something previously intolerable becomes ordinary enough to be accepted as the “new normal.” That tension also reaches the language of the record. Titles such as “Edit Me Out” and “Cancel Anytime” take expressions associated with platforms and subscriptions and apply them to people, while “New World Order” looks at the vulnerability created when increasingly large parts of everyday existence are handed over to digital systems. Musically, Escape With Romeo remain recognisably themselves, but the references continue to expand: “Wrong Side of Town Pt. 2”, for example, emerged after Elbern encountered Skeler and began imagining what EWR doing hardwave might sound like. I spoke with Thomas Elbern about “Night After Night”, AI and what he calls “hijacked emotion”, why individuality can coexist with extreme predictability, independence after more than three decades, the practical realities of touring as a trio, and why Escape With Romeo still have reasons to move forward rather than simply preserve what they have already built. Night after Night by Escape with Romeo Escape With Romeo interview Karo: When I reviewed “Suspicious Bliss” for ReGen, the record seemed to exist in a productive contradiction: the music had become more physical and guitar-driven just as the lyrics were becoming increasingly preoccupied with technological intrusion, isolation and a reality that could no longer quite be trusted. “Night After Night” is harder, more emotional and more direct. Did “Suspicious Bliss” already contain the beginning of this record, or did something change in the two years between them that demanded a different degree of force? Thomas: I would say that “Night After Night” follows the same path that “Suspicious Bliss” already craved. My personal situation was also different: my career as a music journalist working for national radio finally ended after 40 years. Suddenly, I had a lot of time, and all those sketches that were already on my hard drive began to form into songs. The surroundings played a role as well. Watching catastrophic news and seeing more and more worst-case scenarios developing in the world encouraged me to make an album like this. Karo: “Night After Night” is an interesting title because it suggests duration rather than catastrophe. Not one decisive collapse, but waking repeatedly into the same anxieties, systems and headlines until the exceptional becomes ordinary. Is that accumulation important to the album? Is the record concerned less with disaster itself than with what happens psychologically when people become accustomed to living inside conditions that would once have seemed intolerable? Thomas: That’s a very good point. Yes, it is exactly the accumulation that is described here. It’s the thing people call “the new normal.” What was intolerable in the past can become the new reality, and there seems to be no collective outcry. Instead, we see growing racism, homophobia, income disparity, hate speech and leaders who make everything worse. Karo: “Edit Me Out”, “Cancel Anytime” and “Something That Lasts” almost form their own vocabulary of contemporary relationships. Words that belong to software, subscriptions and digital services have slipped very easily into the language of intimacy. Has that linguistic shift become interesting to you as a songwriter: the idea that people can now be edited, muted, cancelled, replaced or simply unsubscribed from? Thomas: A lot of the titles on the album are “internet speech”: “Edit Me Out”, “Cancel Anytime”, or the song “What They Don’t Tell You”, which is not on the album. They all circle around things you read very often in blogs and publications. It’s the idea that the intimacy you mentioned has stopped being genuinely private. It’s also the idea of masses becoming extremely predictable while still believing themselves to be individuals. I got this idea while reading a lot of travel blogs. People travel through Bali or Laos and think they are doing something individual. People think that they are using a product, but instead they are the product. And yes, in that sense, they are all extremely replaceable. Karo: Artificial intelligence was already present on “Suspicious Bliss”, while in our 2024 conversation you spoke about computer-generated voices and described the DAW itself as an instrument. The question feels different now. AI is no longer merely something an artist can use or write about; it increasingly influences distribution, visibility, recommendation and even judgments about value. Has the real concern shifted from what machines are capable of creating to the decisions we are gradually allowing them to make on our behalf? Thomas: Again, a very good point. The DAW nowadays, or certainly in the foreseeable future, can create almost anything. Even the artist who was once needed to programme it and provide the input it needs can now be reduced to somebody writing a prompt while the computer does the rest. To quote our famous song “Somebody”, with a wink, this is the “hijacked emotion.” On the other hand, in combination with a great artistic vision and real skill, this technology could lead to something completely new. But most of what I currently hear and see online is AI-generated shit that feels like cosmic debris, or a bad idea of chart music, while consuming far too many resources. Karo: “New World Order” enters territory where dystopian language has almost become exhausted through overuse. War, AI, surveillance, extremism and environmental collapse are no longer speculative vocabulary; they are part of everyday information flow. How do you stop a song about the present from merely reproducing that background noise? At what point does a general anxiety become specific enough to turn into music? Thomas: With “New World Order”, everything started with the trance arpeggio you hear at the beginning. Lyrically, it could be seen as a protest song about the possibilities of digital surveillance combined with greedy corporations that will enslave you and take over your digital existence. “Your beautiful saviour will shoot you in the back” is a metaphor for how two-faced everything is in “New World Order”. It’s similar to the idea in the dark comedy film “Brazil”, where a simple typing error, changing the name Tuttle to Buttle, can ruin somebody’s entire life. In 2026, it can be the deadly phishing email, a vicious Trojan on your computer or your social media account that turns your life upside down. The idea of “New World Order” is essentially: stop for a moment and think about what actually surrounds you in 2026. Karo: “Wrong Side of Town Pt. 2” returns to “After the Future”, an album you have spoken about with considerable ambivalence, and which became connected, indirectly, to the period when you decided Escape With Romeo had reached an ending. Why reopen that particular door now? Is “Pt. 2” continuing the narrative of the original song, or are you also revisiting your own relationship with a period of the band you once wanted to leave behind? Thomas: It’s actually neither of those things. I always loved the atmosphere of the original, particularly the cinematic quality of the sounds involved. Then I went to a gig by Australian DJ and producer Skeler in Cologne the night before, listening to and enjoying all that wave, hardwave and phonk-related material being played there. I went back to my DAW the next day and tried to recreate what I had heard through a follow-up to “Wrong Side of Town”, using new lyrics, guitars and beats. It’s my idea of EWR doing hardwave. Karo: “You Need the Drugs” is an unusual cover because the original already sits between musical worlds: WestBam and Klaus Jankuhn’s electronic language meeting Richard Butler’s unmistakable Psychedelic Furs presence. Escape With Romeo has occupied that border between electronics and guitars for most of its life. Did the song feel strangely familiar for that reason? And at what point in the rearrangement did it stop feeling like someone else’s material? Thomas: The idea of doing “You Need the Drugs” was born and realised even before the album itself took form. I heard the original at a New Year’s party and immediately heard the EWR version in my head. It was clear that our version would become very much Escape With Romeo. Guitars, guitars, guitars were the key. Karo: Frenzy Erl’s role here goes far beyond drumming: the two of you recorded, mixed and produced the album together, and he also mastered it. Does having a drummer involved at every stage alter the hierarchy of a recording? When the person responsible for pulse is simultaneously making decisions about density, space and final sound, can rhythm begin to determine the architecture rather than simply inhabit it? Thomas: When I make a demo or even a final production, I also programme the drums that I hear in my head. Frenzy usually plays the drums when the song has reached its genuinely finished version. During the final phase of production, we decide together where the aural journey should go. What is important is that we normally mix and master everything in Frenzy’s studio in Munich, where there are no distractions and we can finish the album together. Karo: Stella Tonon’s contribution to “Suspicious Bliss” was already more interesting than straightforward backing vocals; you said in 2024 that she immediately understood where her voice belonged inside the material. On “Night After Night”, does the presence of another voice ever change the point of view of a song itself? Can a voice entering from outside destabilise the narrator and make you hear your own lyrics differently? Thomas: Talking about the opening track, “Edit Me Out”, the female voice there is actually a sample. That is nothing new for me; my way of working has always been very hip-hop in that respect. If I find a great legal sample that I want to work with, I go for it. So that female voice is a major part of “Edit Me Out”, but many of the other female voices and improvisations on the record are very much Stella. She always brings her own particular idea into the music of EWR. She fully understands and feels both the sadness and the rough elements in the music, and she can respond to them with her unique voice. Karo: You once described the audience as the place where a song is finally tested: only onstage do you discover whether its internal logic actually survives contact with people. Escape With Romeo is now taking these songs out as a trio, despite studio arrangements that can contain almost unlimited layers. Has that smaller configuration forced you to identify what is genuinely indispensable in a song? What remains once production is stripped away and three people have to make the idea physically convincing? Thomas: Interesting point! We are studio nerds and take full advantage of every sound source we can get hold of. But if you want to survive financially as a touring band, you have to make decisions that nearly every band makes nowadays. That is called backing tracks. You have to decide which parts of the sound are the most important. Those are played live. The rest becomes like a parallel universe coming through the speakers. Making that distinction is always crucial. But I also think that, as a trio, we cannot strip things down much further than we already do. Drums, guitar, bass and the main vocal always have to be live. Karo: Escape With Romeo built a genuinely independent structure remarkably early, with label, studio and management gradually becoming part of the same ecosystem. But independence in 2026 is a peculiar condition: an artist may own the masters and finance the record while still relying on platforms, distributors and opaque recommendation systems to become visible. Has independence become less about escaping gatekeepers and more about choosing which gatekeepers one is prepared to depend on? Thomas: Having been independent for more than three decades, I can say that the game is always changing. The role of record companies has largely vanished for us; now everything is about live gigs and promoters. Yes, it’s also about numbers and streaming, but it is still, as it always was, about luck. If your music gets used in a famous series or film, you automatically reach another level. And today’s gatekeepers are tomorrow’s open doors. It’s a complicated music world and nobody is particularly happy about it. But in the end, connecting directly with your fans will always remain one of the main points. Karo: There is something counterintuitive about making a record more direct after nearly four decades of accumulated technique, experience and musical memory. Young bands are often direct because they have relatively little to discard; an established artist has to decide what no longer deserves to remain. Is directness for you now partly an act of subtraction? And after 13 albums, is making something immediate actually harder than making something elaborate? Thomas: I found working on the previous albums quite liberating. From a production point of view, it is always a pain in the ass, because it’s the final 15 percent that creates most of the work. But it is liberating in the sense that we don’t have to prove anything to anyone. We can evolve and do whatever we think is right for EWR. Making an album is both elaborate and, in this case, immediate, so “Night After Night” feels like a natural step in our history. Karo: And finally, where can people actually catch Escape With Romeo on the road in the coming months? Which dates or places are you particularly looking forward to, and is there any show on this run that matters most to you? Thomas: We are touring mainly in Germany in 2026, and we plan to play more abroad in 2027, if the world is still standing. That includes Europe and South America. Karo: Thank you very much for your time, Thomas. Thomas: Thank you, Karo! “Night After Night” is out now through Zeitklang. Escape With Romeo’s confirmed 2026 tour begins in Munich on 19 September and continues through Cologne, Essen, Karlsruhe, Bielefeld, Nuremberg, Rüsselsheim, Hamburg and Berlin, before crossing into Poland for the Shadow Dance Party at Pod Minoga in Poznań on 31 October. A December date in Rhede is also confirmed, while the band says further dates for 2027 are being developed. About Escape With Romeo Escape With Romeo were founded in Cologne in 1989 by singer, guitarist and songwriter Thomas Elbern. Before starting the project, Elbern had fronted the new-wave band Seltsame Zustände and had been a guitarist and songwriter with Pink Turns Blue. The first Escape With Romeo album appeared in 1989, and the early track “Somebody” became one of the songs most closely associated with the band, helping establish an audience beyond Germany. The band’s own historical account describes the project as growing from Elbern’s initial setup of Atari computers, drum machines, four-track recording, turntables, guitar and bass into a full live band after “Somebody” began circulating in clubs. From the beginning, Escape With Romeo combined guitars with electronic production rather than treating rock and electronics as separate phases of the band. Their long-used description, “Post Punk meets modern Electronica,” remains a useful shorthand, although the catalogue itself has moved through considerably more territory: new wave, darkwave, alternative rock, electronic pop, acoustic work and, increasingly in the current period, elements of trip-hop, post-rock and contemporary electronic production. The early album sequence included “Escape With Romeo,” “Autumn on Venus,” “Next Stop Eternally,” “Blast of Silence” and “How Far Can You Go?” Later records included “Come Here White Light,” “Love Alchemy,” “Psalms of Survival,” “Emotional Iceage,” “Samsara” and “After the Future.” From 2001 onward, releases were issued through Zeitklang Records, the label established and run by Elbern. In 2017, Elbern announced that Escape With Romeo would come to an end. A farewell period followed, including the band’s final tour in 2018 and festival appearances in 2019. What was intended as an ending did not remain one. During the pandemic years Elbern began reconsidering the project, and Escape With Romeo returned in 2022, initially through newly arranged versions of older material and the double compilation “Based on a True Story – Best of Escape With Romeo.” The official notes to the 2022 versions of “Refuge” and “White Room” explicitly described those recordings as the beginning of the band’s return. The more consequential step came with “Suspicious Bliss” in November 2024. Rather than continuing primarily through retrospective material, Escape With Romeo released an entirely new album. Its harder guitar sound, electronics and dystopian lyrical concerns established the direction that now continues into “Night After Night”. The band themselves described “Suspicious Bliss” as a fresh start following their 2022 reorganisation. Released on 7 August 2026, “Night After Night” is Escape With Romeo’s 13th studio album. It contains fourteen tracks and was produced by Thomas Elbern and Frenzy Erl, with Erl also handling the mastering. “You Need the Drugs” is the album’s one outside composition, written by Klaus Jankuhn, Maximilian Lenz/WestBam and Richard Butler; the remaining songs are credited to Elbern. The record was preceded by 2026 singles including “Fear’s a Ghost” and “Sound and the Fury”. Escape With Romeo currently perform live as a trio: Thomas Elbern on vocals and guitar, Tobias Schwartz on bass and vocals, and Frenzy Erl on drums. Stella Tonon remains part of the wider recording world around the band and contributed vocals to recent material, including the “Suspicious Bliss” period and subsequent recordings, but she is not part of the touring trio. The current configuration is deliberately compact. Elbern describes guitar, bass, drums and lead vocals as the elements that must remain genuinely live, while additional studio layers are carried through backing tracks. That division is less an attempt to reproduce the recordings literally than a practical decision about which components constitute the physical core of Escape With Romeo onstage. The band begin the “Night After Night Tour 2026” in Munich on 19 September, followed by Cologne, two Essen shows, Karlsruhe, Bielefeld, Nuremberg, Rüsselsheim, Hamburg and Berlin. On 31 October they cross into Poland for the Shadow Dance Party: Halloween Edition at Pod Minoga in Poznań, followed by a December show in Rhede. The official band site says further dates are being developed for 2027, while Elbern tells Side-Line that the plan is to return to broader international touring, including Europe and South America. Interview by Karo Kratochwil.

items.body: Chilean producer and composer Santiago Nicolás released “Atrición” on 18 August 2026, the first release under the solo alias he took from his own name, Santiago Nicolás González Lihn. The five-track EP is self-released, digital, and runs a little over 21 minutes. He composed, produced and mixed all of it. The tracklist runs “Todo Archivo Tiene una Grieta” (5:08), “Lo Primero Es la Contracción” (4:27), “Ensayo Continuo de Precisión” featuring Kimin Kim of the Korean band PCR (3:43), “No Todo lo que Arde Tiene que Morir” (5:15) and “Un Canto para el Herido” (2:48). Downloads are offered in MP3, FLAC and 24-bit/96 kHz at a name-your-price minimum of nine dollars. Two of those tracks appeared first as singles. “Ensayo Continuo de Precisión” went out on 28 May 2026 and “Lo Primero Es la Contracción” on 4 June 2026, both mastered by the producer at Estudios 6AM in Santiago. Atrición by Santiago Nicolás Where the Santiago Nicolás lyrics on ‘Atrición’ come from The words did not start as lyrics. They come from a series of poems written in the waiting room of an oncology centre, and the record sets that material against political violence, borders, archives and inherited trauma. The EP mixes hard, exact drum programming with the forward motion of contemporary techno, and the mix keeps every impact audible rather than smoothing it into texture. A physical edition is planned through the label Anything That Makes Light, collecting the poems alongside unreleased visual material, photographs and notes. It has not yet gone on sale, and no date has been given. About Santiago Nicolás Santiago Nicolás is the solo alias of Santiago Nicolás González Lihn, a producer, composer and artist based in Santiago, Chile. He has spent over a decade across electronic music, noise, experimental composition and post-punk, and opened the alias in May 2026. He records and has recorded under several other names. As Access Device he released a run of albums on Bandcamp between 2021 and 2023, among them “Detrás del Paisaje”, “Nueve Variables”, “Ceremonias” and “Ori. Gen” in 2021, “Luminiscencia” in 2022 and “Eón Codex” in 2023, working from Mexico City for part of that period. With filmmaker Pedro Roca he forms the Chilean duo Ángel de la Guarda, whose “Sentencia” appeared in June 2022, followed by “Crimen” the same year and “Alfanumérico” in 2023. His most recent band credit is The Deadly Affair, whose album “Visions Through The Sense of Silence” came out on 16 May 2025 through Anything That Makes Light. González Lihn wrote and composed every song on it and co-produced with Atom™, who also mixed and mastered the record; Diego Lorca played drums and Louise Schmidt Aguayo played bass and sang backing vocals. The Santiago Nicolás alias began releasing in May 2026 with the two singles that now sit inside “Atrición”. The EP is his first full release under the name.
items._cn_summary: 智利制作人Santiago Nicolás以本名开启个人solo项目，发行首张五曲EP《Atrición》，全长约21分钟，由其本人独立完成作曲、制作与混音。作品将硬朗精确的鼓机编程与当代techno的前进感相结合，混音中每一个冲击都清晰可辨，未被柔化为背景纹理。歌词文本源自作者在肿瘤中心候诊室写下的一系列诗作，内容涉及政治暴力、边境、档案与代际创伤。EP包含与韩国乐队PCR成员Kimin Kim的合作曲目。下载提供MP3、FLAC及24-bit/96kHz格式，自定价九美元起。此外计划通过厂牌Anything That Makes Light发行实体版本，收录诗作与未公开的视觉材料、照片与笔记。艺术家此前以Access Device等名义活跃，并参与智利二人组Ángel de la Guarda及乐队The Deadly Affair，横跨电子、噪音、实验作曲与后朋克领域逾十年。

items.body: Duisburg post-punk duo Mottek87 released “Kleinkunst” on 14 August 2026 as a self-released digital EP. It runs three tracks and just over nine minutes: the title track at 2:46, “Oszillation” at 3:16 and “Widerstand” at 3:00. Downloads are offered in MP3, FLAC and 24-bit/44.1 kHz at a name-your-price minimum of one euro, and no physical edition has been issued. Zbigniew F. and Jürgen W. record as Mottek87 in a downtown Duisburg apartment with the shutters closed. The two mix post-punk guitars, cold synths and programmed drums, with Jürgen W. singing in German. Their own release copy describes them as “two long-time friends from Duisburg telling stories from a region in transition”. Kleinkunst by Mottek87 What Mottek87 mean by ‘Kleinkunst’ The German title carries a double meaning: cabaret or variety performance on one reading, small art on the other. The duo set out what they wanted the word to do here: “Kleinkunst is about realizing that change is not automatically freedom.” They added a second line on the same point: “Sometimes something gets better, and you still need time to stop being angry about it.” Their Bandcamp page places that reading in a region undergoing structural change, which is the setting the duo have used since their first upload in January 2025. About Mottek87 Mottek87 are a post-punk duo from Duisburg in Germany’s Ruhr area, formed in 2024 by Zbigniew F. and Jürgen W., two long-time friends of Polish descent who decided to make a record after an evening of drinking beer and listening to records. Jürgen W. sings; the pair build their tracks from guitars, bass, programmed drums and sparse synthesizers, with lyrics in German. The project’s first upload was the track “Grausamkeit” on 6 January 2025, followed a month later by the album “Wir kaufen und verkaufen alles” on 7 February 2025. The single “YOGTZE” arrived on 3 August 2025, the album “Zadamy Chleba” on 28 November 2025, and “Duisburger Schule” on 10 April 2026. Every Mottek87 release has been self-released and digital-only, sold directly through Bandcamp at name-your-price. The duo have not signed to a label and have not announced live dates. “Kleinkunst” is their sixth release in nineteen months and their first since “Duisburger Schule” in April.
items._cn_summary: 德国杜伊斯堡双人组Mottek87以自发行数字EP《Kleinkunst》延续其后朋克路线，三首作品总长仅九分钟，紧凑而直接。乐队以冷峻合成器、后朋克吉他与编程鼓构建声响，德语演唱贯穿始终。标题“Kleinkunst”带有双重含义，既指卡巴莱式的小型表演，也指“微小的艺术”，核心主题围绕“变化并不自动等于自由”展开，并涉及鲁尔区结构性转型背景下人们的复杂情绪。作品在狭窄的公寓中录制，呈现封闭而内省的气质。作为乐队十九个月内的第六张发行，这张EP延续了他们自2025年以来的高产节奏，依旧保持独立、数字-only的发布方式，未签约厂牌也无现场计划，整体风格统一，歌词立意带有地域与时代观察的维度。

items.body: Band: Hesse Kassel | Album: Morir Saltando | Genre: Post-rock | Year: 2026 From: Santiago, Chile | Label: Amuleto For fans of: black midi, Swans, Kayo Dot Bandcamp Chilean post-rock sextet Hesse Kassel are back with their second full-length release. Last year’s La Brea had a ton of really solid music on it, but on repeated listens, its biggest hindrance is its crushing length. Eight songs with an average runtime of nearly ten minutes can make for an exhausting experience, even in the hands of very skilled songwriters and musicians. The songs on Morir Saltando (Eng.: To Die Jumping) retain all the strengths of those on their debut, but they are more focused, giving them more impact. The album opens with its longest song, the 14-minute “Pornomiseria”. The words are half-spoken, half-sung, and often shouted. Right from the get-go, this song is bristling and anxious. Strains of post-punk and krautrock are evident in the instrumental backing, featuring jittery and angular guitars over a hypnotic rhythm. When the band launches into instrumental sections, I love the weightiness of the piano. That, in turn, allows the bass to take on something more of a leading role, getting a few brief show-offy passages. Lighter jazzy moments are interspersed among heavier passages, with the two sides of Hesse Kassel’s music complementing and playing off one another. I need to compliment the mastering and mixing on this album. On a record so full of chaos and dynamic contrasts, every element of the music is crisp and clear. It never comes off as sterile, but it also avoids muddiness. There’s still a ton of grit and edge, but the complex arrangements shine through. “No Me Puedo Relajar” (“I Can’t Relax”) is a furious, tangled mess of post-punk riffage played with heavy-metal fury. Guitars buzz and twist around each other like a noisier version of 1980s-and-onward King Crimson. Relatively mellow jazz tones open up “El Reflejo” (“The Reflection”). It’s a nice bit of breathing room after the preceding song. The flute, in particular, helps this song float. There’s still a sense of unsettled tension, even with the milder timbres. As the song progresses, the band gradually ups the intensity. Guitars squeal and crash, and the vocals become more desperate. The final minute or so of this song is a noisy cavalcade of guitars and piano that ties it all up beautifully. “Maripsoa” (“Butterfly”) features jittery and speedy guitar licks, along with multi-parted vocal arrangements. This song features some of the strongest ties to the Windmill Scene on this album, with half-mad ranting over wonky, wobbly riffs. “Sancho Plagio”, the shortest song on the album, kicks off with fuzzy, throbbing bass and features a frenetic marching rhythm. The madcap call-and-response vocals add to the oppressive, martial feel. Smooth synths provide a calming counterweight. It ends with the most-metallic guitar lines on the album, providing an incredible amount of diversity in under four minutes. Morir Saltando concludes with “Tulpa”, where jazz once more takes center stage. It doesn’t take long for Hesse Kassel to plunge back into their high-intensity insanity. They skillfully shift between airy jazz and slashing walls of atypical guitar chords, with plenty of technical flashiness along the way. Hesse Kassel’s Sophomore album shows a marked improvement in focus and songcraft. The six compositions on Morir Saltando demonstrate not just the bandmembers’ impressive technical chops but also their unique compositional tendencies. Score: 88/100
items._cn_summary: 智利六人组 Hesse Kassel 的第二张全长专辑聚焦于后摇滚与后朋克的交汇地带，同时融入大量爵士段落与实验性结构编排。相比处女作冗长的叙事，新作将篇幅压缩至更具张力的篇幅，开篇十四分钟的曲目以半说半喊的人声在焦虑不安的氛围中铺陈，棱角分明的吉他与催眠节奏交织，钢琴的厚重感为器乐段落奠定重量级基底。制作层面在混沌与清晰之间取得平衡，复杂编排中的每个元素都保持了可辨度。后续曲目在暴躁后朋克与温和爵士段落之间交替推进，长笛的轻盈漂浮为情绪留出呼吸空间，而末段噪音的吉他与钢琴则将张力推向高潮。智利独立厂牌的出身为这张专辑增添了非主流地区的视角价值，与用户关注的前卫实验、暗潮后朋克、爵士即兴口味高度契合。

items.body:
Recorded in 1991, 'Rise' sweeps up all known recorded material from A.R. Kane's Rudy Tambala and Cranes vocalist Alison Shaw, aka inrain, compiling a classic 7” for Rough Trade with additional, previously unreleased tracks. It’ll no doubt provide many with a first introduction to a prescient project by two scene legends, delving into shoegaze, dub, electro and trip-hop refractions of the highest order. It's the most essential Music From Memory release in a hot minute, crucial listening for all A.R Kane obsessives (that should be all of you) or anyone into Seefeel, Locust, Zurich.

For someone for whom Cranes' ‘Tomorrow's Tears’ and A.R Kane’s ‘Lolita’ are two absolute foundational texts, this reissue is basically something like a holy grail. Back in 1991, inrain appeared on Rough Trade's Singles Club series with a brief but brilliant 7" that sounded as if it'd been beamed in from another planet. A.R. Kane had already broken the mold, but these three tracks juxtaposed Shaw's dreamy vocals with dubby, spacious electronics and shimmering guitars in a way that wouldn't really rise to prominence until years later. Music From Memory do the heavy lifting here, remastering that original 7" from the original DAT tapes and adding the extra track 'Biology' and an alternate version of 'Sleep' to bump up the package. 

It's those original tracks that have us by the throat - we really can't believe they've been so slept on over the years. '...And Julie Rose' sounds like it should have been picked up for a Duophonic release a decade later, while 'Sleep' completely pre-empts Seefeel's 'More Like Space EP' that wouldn't appear for another couple of years. 

Prophetic, brilliant stuff.
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了1991年A.R. Kane成员Rudy Tambala与Cranes主唱Alison Shaw以inrain名义发表的全部录音素材，包括当初在Rough Trade Singles Club发行的7寸单曲及其未发行曲目。评论指出，这三首原始作品将Shaw空灵的嗓音与dub质感、空间感强烈的电子音色以及闪烁的吉他层叠融合，制作手法在当时极为超前，预见了数年后才流行的Seefeel等乐队风格。Music From Memory厂牌从原始DAT磁带完成重制，并附加一首'Biology'与'Sleep'的替代版本以扩充内容。评论将其形容为'预言式'的创作，强调其在shoegaze与dub、电子交叉领域的开创性意义，对于研究A.R. Kane或早期英国地下场景具有档案价值。

items.body:
A Colourful Storm's Fleetway Tapes series follows classic entries from Time Is Away, Vladimir Ivkovic, Felix K, Young Sparks and others with a heart-stopping selection put together by Berlin-based film journo Florence Scott-Anderton, a fathoms-deep, laser-focused mix that doesn't come around often, engulfing high-art/low-culture TV samples with a series of cues excavated from film - think of it as a sort of Blockbuster Video nostalgia-tinted answer to Time Is Away's flawless thematic mixes.

Florence knows her shit. Not only does she provide words and sounds for MUBI's international film mag Notebook, where she's covered Tōru Takemitsu and crafted an ode to Derek Jarman, but she's a resident on NTS's ace Sounds on Screen. Nose through her archive and you'll find a deep dive into the sonics of lesbian cinema, an exploration of Aussie icon Nicole Kidman's filmography, a mix dedicated to Japanese vanguard Satoshi Kon, a history of the sounds of Iranian cinema and loads more (really, there's so much). And it's this same anti-hierarchal level of expertise and passion she brings to 'A Requiem for Prime Time', a very personal journey thru her memory banks that collages dialog samples, TV ambiance, art oddities and various soundtrack selections that eschew the usual narrative. We'll be honest, we've gotten pretty fatigued with the OST industrial complex and its parallel stream of repetitive, hyper-referential shovelcore outings from genre dorks whose interest in music peaked with 'Stranger Things'. Thankfully, Florence opts to sail down a completely different channel, not avoiding the mythologised synth wave completely (Simon Boswell's killer 'Hardware' cue 'It's Horrible... I Love It... What Is It?' shows up as a bonus like a peanut in caramel) but concentrating on dislocated, provocative and often completely overlooked sounds that drift far from the established "score bro" cult canon.

"It's not like you want to be an accountant," a muffled Australian voice narrates over ketamized SFX on the opening side. "You, like me, want something that is creative, that is out there a little bit." A clip from Peter Mullan's 2002 drama 'The Magdalene Sisters' appears, pulling us right back to that moment when trip-hop aesthetics bled into Hollywood's mainstream, and before long we’re riding a different train of thought, stitching cavernous twee rock with pastoral post-Glass minimalism and scratchy, evocative environmental recordings. Canned sax solos and airy guitar plucks fade into cuts from Mike Figgis's notorious experimental film 'Timecode', and somehow Woijciech Kilar's end credits from Francis Ford Copolla's 'Bram Stoker's Dracula' show up for some thematic relief. On the flip, Florence opens the side with waved, Eno-style psychedelic ambient that's ruptured by a beat isolated from Joe Delia's sordid score for Abel Ferarra's famously abhorred erotic thriller 'The Blackout'. From here, we're catapulted across Christophe Beck's 'Bring It On' soundscapes, a cloudy, sub-heavy ambient marvel from Brooklyn artist Alex Bienstock and even Joe Jackson's aborted theme for 'Mike's Murder', a 1984 Debra Winger vehicle that had its entire soundtrack replaced with a more palatable one from John Barry.

Really, we can't say enough about this one. If you've been following Scott-Anderton's mixes (if you want just one, we recommend her Krzysztof Kieślowski selection), you'll already know how vital her point of view is, but she takes us to a completely new zone with this one. It's a head-scratcher that'll have you wondering what it is yr actually listening to - a way to contemplate the Y2K era as it completely vanishes into popular mythology.
items._genre: ambient / experimental / soundtrack collage / hauntology / electronic
items._cn_summary: 这张混音作品由柏林影评人Florence Scott-Anderton操刀，是A Colourful Storm旗下Fleetway Tapes系列的延续。她从个人影像记忆中取材，将电视剧对白、环境录音、电影配乐片段与氛围音乐并置拼贴，跨越trip-hop、twee摇滚、后极简主义、迷幻氛围与实验电子等多种风格。作品刻意回避近年来泛滥的OST怀旧潮流，转向被忽视的、断裂的、不入正典的声音素材——从Abel Ferrara的实验惊悚到Mike Figgis的先锋影像，呈现出一种反等级制的策展视角。整体不是线性叙事，而是一段跨越电视、电影与个人记忆的声音漫游，强调采样本身的文化考古价值。

items.body:
The Sultans of Sludge slang a definitive label debut for Sub Pop, bringing their singular sound to roost on a legendary label local to their origins in the US north west, whose rugged landscapes fed directly into the LP’s formidably primal concentration of dualistic energies

Hailing some 30 years since Sunn O)))’s formation, their eponymous 10th studio album reckons with forces of nature - time and space, dark and light - for 80 minutes of air-shuddering pressure limning epic, craggy vistas from a thick haar of distortion. Subtly enlivened with field recordings made in forests near Bear Creek Studios, Woodinville, Washington, where O’Malley says they would “go hiking and be out in the woods, spend time outdoors”, the resulting six-part sequence sees the duo drill down to fundamentals with an absorbing sense of purpose and telepathically-attuned intuition. A notable dearth of other contributors also means it’s one of their truest statements as a duo; just Stephen O’Malley & Greg Anderson howling into the wilds on all instrumentation, from trusted axes to keys and electro-acoustic sorcery. 

At this point, not to labour the arboreal metaphors, but it may take a certified guide to see the wood for the trees in Sunn O))) lands, such is the uniquely coherent sprawl of their sound at 30 years up to the hilt in atonal rock doom. Our hair’s not long enough to lay claim as spirit guides, but after 23 years of bearing witness to them live, and ingesting most of their LPs, we can say this side is wholly emblematic of their radical steez. Between the two 18 minute totems of a ‘XXANN’ laced with location recording of running water at tender points, and a ‘Mindrolling’ monstered with claw-handed riffs, they take it to typically stare-down levels of intensity with the sustained threat of ‘Does Anyone Hear Like Venom?’, and billowing sheets of subharmonic distortion harnessed in ‘Everett Moses’. Closer ‘Glory Black’ is, however, a sort of sore thumb with a relatively conventional riff progression and rising banks of silvery wheeze that collapse into keys and field recordings, hearkening most closely to the duo’s precedents and NW peers in the Sub Pop roster, Earth, or even another touchstone, Black Sabbath, at their most strung out. 

Heavy as your life.
items._genre: drone metal / doom / experimental / field recording
items._cn_summary: 这是Sunn O)))成立三十年来第十张录音室专辑的同名作，也是他们签约Sub Pop厂牌后的首张作品。专辑以六首曲目构建长达八十分钟的声音压迫，核心由Stephen O'Malley与Greg Anderson二人独立完成所有乐器演奏，从吉他到键盘再到原声电声实验，罕见地没有其他客座乐手参与，使整张作品成为组合最纯粹的二人表述。制作层面大量融入华盛顿州伍丁维尔Bear Creek Studios附近森林的实地录音，包括流水声与户外环境声，与失真音墙形成有机融合。'XXANN'与'Mindrolling'各以十八分钟体量构成全专骨架，前者穿插流水声采样，后者以重型riff贯穿。'Does Anyone Hear Like Venom?'呈现持续威胁感，'Everett Moses'运用次谐波失真形成低音震动，结尾曲'Glory Black'则回归相对传统的riff结构，散入键盘与田野录音。整体延续了乐队对黑暗、原始、缓慢膨胀之声的三十年探索，与Earth、Black Sabbath一脉相承却又不断推进边界。

items.body:
More slick sophisti-pop from the CPH scene via GB aka Gustav Berntsen, kinda heavily reminds us of a Japanoise/ jazz fusion take on Sam Prekop’s self-titled alltimer with bits of Red House Painters, Steely Dan and Prefab Sprout in there too.

Berntsen was stationed in London when he was writing 'Herzprung' and began to collect copies of the infamous free rag Metro, that he cut to shreds to fix up the lyrical portion of the songs. Once he had this in check, the Danish singer-songwriter called up his most trusted collaborators and booked a week at a studio "in the Swedish wilderness", where he dubbed the songs live to 24-track tape, encouraging improvisation and collaboration. And there's certainly a knottiness to this material that's unique to Bernsten; like many contemporary Copenhagen-based operatives, he's clearly well versed in classic rock and pop, from Fleetwood Mac and Steely Dan to Chick Corea and Haruomi Hosono, but he doesn't stop at pastiche, instead bringing his own absurdities to the table. "The Simpson's Season Six," he calls out harmoniously on opener 'Adrenaline', interrupting a stop-start drum fill and riffs that wouldn't sound out of place on a Gastr del Sol record. 

It would be hard to label 'Herzprung' post-rock, but there's a sense that Berntsen has at least learned from the genre's Chicago-era excesses. He seems to be driven by a holistic understanding of pop; at their heart, his songs are impeccably written, yet he's also not interested in taking the clearest path. On 'Belly', his cool-headed harmonies and almost tropicalia-strength choruses are complicated by winding instrumental sections and a phenomenally atmospheric dip into tape-fuckt cosmic ambience, while the lengthy 'Shit River' is a slowcore anthem that Berntsen expands with a full choir and an arsenal of synths.
items._genre: sophisti-pop / art pop / jazz fusion / experimental pop
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由哥本哈根音乐人Gustav Berntsen创作，在瑞典荒野的录音室中以24轨磁带现场同期录制，鼓励即兴与合作。他将伦敦地铁免费报纸剪碎拼贴作为歌词素材，在精致旋律的骨架上缠绕了复杂的器乐段落与磁带实验声响。专辑以Steely Dan、Prefab Sprout的优雅流行传统为出发点，融入了Chick Corea与细野晴臣的爵士融合语汇，并在Gastr del Sol式的碎裂节奏中寻找出口。从冷酷的和声到热带感的副歌，从慢核圣歌到磁带宇宙氛围的深潜，歌曲始终拒绝走最直白的路径，在流行结构内部植入独特的怪异性与实验性。

items.body:
Barnt’s mnml 2012 kosmische waltzer for Matias Aguayo’s Cómeme is repackaged with a new master and Jens-Uwe Beyer + Crato revisions.

The kinky schaeffel is in effect on ‘gaffe’, which takes on a 2nd wind in its brighter, robust remaster, while Jens Uwe-Beyer evens out its irregularities for a disco-ready remix, and best of all, a ‘Magazine Hallucination’ mix that initially jettisons the beat and opens upwards, outward into majestic ambient zones, before its pulled back in a screwed echo of the original waltz groove.

items._cn_summary: Barnt在2012年为Matias Aguayo旗下厂牌Cómeme发行的一张minimal kosmische电子作品以重新母带处理与全新混音版本形式再版发行。原文母带呈现更为明亮饱满的质感，而Jens-Uwe Beyer的混音版本将原作的棱角磨平，趋向disco友好方向。最出色的'Magazine Hallucination'混音首先剥离节拍，向上向外展开，进入宏大的氛围空间，随后被打回的扭曲回响将原华尔兹律动以变形的方式重现。此再版展现出原始版本与多种解构重塑之间的张力，将舞池功能性与实验性氛围探索并置，体现出Cómeme厂牌一贯的实验电子美学。

items.body:
Carrier winds the rhythmic tension to breaking point on his 4th self-released 12”, flexing fine-tuned muscle memory and inch-tight production in acres of negative space across a trio of soundsystem phantoms that dance in the long shadow of D&B and broken beat science. Huge tip FFO Autechre, Burial, Photek, T++.

Now three years into a generational run of inspirational plates - including an AOTY ’25 with ‘Rhythm Immortal’ for Modern Love - Carrier’s core sense of discipline and restraint continues to yield peerless reward on ‘Thresholds’. A lifetime’s love of, and immersion in, fwd UK dance musics has prompted him to chase a particular dragon of syncopated swerve and cavernous psychoacoustics to logical, next-level depths diffusing that dread pressure with an adroit, tendon-twitching precision and tactility.

Carrier has been instrumental in reminding ravers what was lost when D&B went stadium and pop-chart scale over the past decades, daring to run against the grain, trust his instincts, to return a sense of mystery and bold experimentalism to what was once a thrilling paradigm. This new trio of cuts eke exquisite nuance from tweaked fundamentals, swivelling 2-step off the bone into smoky hall-of-mirrors reflections of ‘Cure’, and specialising in a razor’s edge, toes-off-the-ground sorcery in a recursive, wraithlike zinger, ‘Scout’ that dips to the sexiest, tongue-tip breakdown, beside the tantric, anticipatory chicanery of ‘Black Channels’ which finishes us off with an all-tension-no-release weapon for the ages.
items._genre: drum and bass / broken beat / experimental electronic / IDM
items._cn_summary: Carrier 在其第四张自发行黑胶中，将节奏张力推向临界点，在大量负空间中展现精密的制作工艺与肌肉记忆般的律动掌控。三首作品围绕声音系统美学展开，深植于英国舞池音乐传统，融合碎拍科学、2-step 切分与回响幽灵般的声学空间。评论提及与 Autechre、Burial、Photek、T++ 等人的风格关联。专辑强调纪律与克制，从基础元素中榨取微妙差异，营造紧张而不释放的悬停感。Carrier 致力于将神秘感与大胆实验性带回曾令人兴奋的鼓打贝斯范式，对抗该类型走向体育场与流行榜的商业化趋势。三首曲目分别展现不同的氛围变体：从骨架上旋转的 2-step 迷雾、性感而递归的幽灵段落，到全程张力无释放的终结武器。

items.body:
Influential Brum punks/post-punks Swell Maps captured in their snotty pomp, 1979, for the legendary John Peel Sessions - just a year before disbanding, and prompting everyone from Sonic Youth to Nirvana in their wake.

“Noisy, chaotic, and defiantly experimental, Swell Maps may not have found commercial success in their time, but their impact on music is undeniable. An inspiration to bands such as R.E.M., Sonic Youth, Dinosaur Jr., Pavement and Nirvana, with Kurt Cobain famously being a fan and often seen sporting a Swell Maps T-Shirt. A democracy within the confines of punk’s anything is possible, members Biggles Books, Jowe Head and brothers Nikki Sudden and Epic Soundtracks—helped shape the landscape of post-punk and DIY music. Now, for the first time in over 40 years, The John Peel Sessions brings together all three of their recordings for John Peel, a figure instrumental in championing their sound.

Formed in the early ’70s and fully realised by 1976, Swell Maps embodied the DIY ethos, launching their own label and self-releasing the jagged, frenetic debut single ‘Read About Seymour’ in 1978. Peel was an early supporter, playing their record as soon as it landed on his desk—a moment the band described as one of disbelief and elation. His regular airplay of their music helped solidify their cult status, and these sessions capture the raw energy, off-kilter melodies, and boundary-pushing creativity that defined them."
items._genre: post-punk / experimental punk / DIY / lo-fi / noise rock
items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了英国伯明翰乐队 Swell Maps 于1979年为 BBC 著名 DJ John Peel 录制的全部三场电台现场录音，乐队在解散前一年留下了这些原始的现场档案。Swell Maps 是早期 DIY 精神的代表，成员自己创办厂牌、自行发行唱片，将朋克的自由气质推向更粗糙、更具实验性的方向。录音中保留了嘈杂的吉他噪音、失谐的旋律、随性的节奏切换和粗糙的声场处理，没有任何后期修饰，呈现出朋克场景中罕见的即兴与解构意识。这些作品后来深刻影响了 Sonic Youth、Nirvana、Dinosaur Jr.、R.E.M. 等乐队，Kurt Cobain 曾多次身穿乐队 T 恤亮相。合辑让听众第一次完整听到这些电台录音原貌，是了解后朋克与地下实验音乐谱系的重要史料。

items.body:
One of the UK’s most distinctive filmmakers returns to the sea, replete with his original synth score - as on ‘Bait’ and ‘Enys Men’ - but notably damper, deeply blue; surely evoking fellow Cornish native AFX’s ‘SAW II’, BoC interludes, Mordant Music, classic folk horror OSTs.

Centred around the tale of a trawler that returns, sans crew, to a Cornish harbour years after it was thought lost, ‘The Rose Of Nevada’ typically draws on what Mark Jenkin knows best - the people, places and metaphysics of the Atlantic peninsula - whilst ideally emphasising the atmosphere with his special ingredient score. His palette of tape-smudged analog synths feels especially washed out and suggestive of his subject in its briny tone and oceanic scale, which evidently works a treat as a discrete work in its own right, severed from imagery. 

There’s possibly a Kernewek word for “hiraeth”, or “sehnsucht” - a sense of longing, nostalgia - that we’re not aware of, but may perfectly fit the feeling of Jenkin’s music here. Sea-legged loops and sustained drones colour the air with a palpable melancholy in passage from the bittersweet tang of ‘Kneebone Barton’, as used on the trailer, and throughout the album’s patches of decaying wheeze, staining the surface like rust or efflorescence on weathered coves. 

And in the day-dreamiest sense it all fades in/out of consciousness with a perfectly ghostly wow and flutter, as leaching from ‘Through The Gaps’ parts into the slurred whorl of ‘What’s Your Name,’ ephemeral concrète of ‘Look At It’, and final folksy shuffle off into the horizon with ‘Rose of Nevada.’ Here’s looking forward to the film.
items._genre: ambient / analog synth / drone / experimental folk horror OST
items._cn_summary: Mark Jenkin 为电影《The Rose Of Nevada》创作的原创配乐专辑，以磁带质感模拟合成器为主体音色，呈现出潮湿、深蓝的海洋氛围。音乐围绕康沃尔郡一艘失踪多年的拖网渔船空船归港的故事展开，合成器音色被刻意处理得褪色模糊，带有盐渍般的粗粝感与海洋尺度。专辑中持续的低音嗡鸣与循环乐段在空气中铺展可感知的忧郁气质，从预告片使用的苦涩曲调到贯穿全辑的衰败气息，层层叠染如锈迹或风化崖壁上的盐霜。各曲目之间以完美的幽灵式抖动与失真相互渗透，具体音乐元素与最终民谣式散拍交替出现，使整张作品即便脱离影像也能独立成立，具备极强的氛围感与冥想特质。

items.body: Review by greenpete — Closer to psych than what we know as prog, The Piper at the Gates of Dawn was released August 5, 1967. It is a surreal, slightly ominous title for a rock album. Surprisingly, leader Syd Barrett didn't conceive it. He borrowed it from his favorite chapter in his favorite book, Kenneth Grahame's fantasy classic The Wind in the Willows. But the title expertly sums up the mixture of science fiction and children's fantasy that inform the words and music on the record.Within these grooves we share English tea with all varieties of the phantasmagoric. Hallucinating gnomes. Existential scarecrows. Sinister, mind-reading cats. Outer (inner?) space denizens. "The doll's house, darkness, old perfume?"Ok, I hear you snicker. "This is the kind of airy-fairy stuff that gave hippies a bad name." You may be right. A lot of this stuff was done by hack musicians/writers eager to hitch a ride on the magic bus. But . . . Long before the Summer of Love became an innocuous clich� and marketing tool, there existed a few imaginative, English art students bent on taking music, words, and art to undiscovered areas. The blueprint for the new music was created by the band Pink Floyd, helmed by the youngest member, Roger Keith (Syd) Barrett of Cambridge, who named his band after two of his beloved cats (who were named after two obscure American bluesmen).According to his sister, Barrett had a rare condition called "synesthesia." Most of us only hear sounds and see colours. But some "synesthetes" can evidently see sounds, and hear colours. Barrett, a talented painter as well as musician, apparently exhibited this condition as a child and budding artist, years before he ever touched a hallucinogen.In early 1967, Barrett penned two eye-opening singles that titillated the London youth underground: "Arnold Layne," a true story about a Cambridge transvestite who stole women's underwear from washing lines; and "See Emily Play," a slice of English whimsy that teeters on insanity.Based on these singles, EMI Columbia financed Pink Floyd's first full-length LP. It was recorded in Abbey Road Studios, right when the Beatles were putting the finishing touches on Sgt. Pepper. Legend has it that the Floyd members occasionally peeked in on Lennon and McCartney to absorb the brilliance. I propose it was the other way around.If so, what might John and Paul have heard? There are two faces to this record: an unsettling and ragged trip into space (I'll call it the Gates of Dawn) and a pleasant and pastoral trip back to childhood (The Piper, and this would be all Syd). I'll save The Piper songs for later."Astronomy Domine" "Pow R. Toc H.," and "Interstellar Overdrive" come close to the later Floyd sound and were staples of the band's blinding, liquid-light-fantastic live shows. All soar into space on the static-y strings of Barrett's guitar. "Astronomy" is bolstered by Nick Mason's tribal drumming, and the 10-minute "Interstellar" by Richard (Rick) Wright's cosmic organ. "Pow R. Toc H.," one of the album's lesser songs, is an instrumental crammed with vocal and instrumental sound effects, but it has a characteristic spacey Floydian closeout.Let me interject that Barrett on guitar was no Eric Clapton. But he made up for technical inadequacy by bravely exploring the instrument's electric and aural capabilities (using a silver Telecaster adorned with 15 circular mirrors). He pioneered a technique of channeling bottleneck slide through an echo device, and it gave the Floyd a distinctive eerie sound.Back to the songs: "Take Up thy Stethoscope and Walk" is Roger Waters' very first composition. Nothing notable here except the paranoid vocals by Barrett."Lucifer Sam" is a sleek nugget about a third feline owned by Barrett, a mysterious Siamese named Sam. The descending chords and twangy guitar lines have been described as "psychedelic Duane Eddy," and recall the Sloan-Barri hit sung by Johnny Rivers, "Secret Agent Man." Sean Connery always pops into my head. It's the closest song to a "hit" single on the album, IMO.Now for The Piper part of the record: these songs were written exclusively by Barrett. "The Gnome" and "The Scarecrow" might as well be solo Barrett. I'm not sure if anyone else even plays on them, except perhaps Mason offering soft percussion help. Both are pastoral evocations that capture children's fascination with the unreal possibly being real. "The Scarecrow," also, has a rolling melody that may have made Paul McCartney blush while eavesdropping on the proceedings."Chapter 24" is a collection of observations lifted from the I Ching and set to music: "Change returns success/Going and coming without error/Action brings good fortune/Sunset, sunrise." This song may have been inspired by Barrett's interest in Eastern philosophies. Like other young people seeking new ways of thinking, he'd attempted to join a Sant Mat sect, but was rejected for being too young.The oddest song here is probably "Bike:" "I've got a bike/You can ride it if you like/It's got a basket/A bell that rings/And things to make it look good/I'd give it to you if I could/But I borrowed it." Note the rhyming, alliteration, and syncopation. Also, the little lyric twist at the end. On surface, the lyrics seem like nonsense. But Barrett was a skilled writer, and like all great writers, he understood the power of letters and words.Now for the pi�ce de r�sistance, the two songs that may be the cream of all English psychedelia. Musically and lyrically, they're a joy to listen to: "Matilda Mother" and "Flaming.""Matilda Mother" is a bittersweet memory of Barrett's about fairy stories read by his mother, with lyrics partly inspired by Anglo-French writer Hilaire Belloc, especially his 1907 parody Cautionary Tales for Children. The best psychedelic music was less about hallucinating through drugs than about transcending the mundane, and in "Matilda Mother," Barrett yearns to throw off the rigidness of adulthood and return to the comforting calm of his mother, and the "scribbly black" lines she recited, where the phantasmagoric was tangible, colours pulsate with life, and "everything shines." Rick Wright, the low-key, underrated keyboardist in Floyd, who later also wrote several evocative songs about childhood, sings the verse, while Barrett sings the slightly bitter chorus ("Oh, oh mother/Tell me more?")."Flaming" is my favorite song on the album. Originally entitled "Snowing," it's a tune that requires little effort to listen to, just opened ears, an open mind, and a willingness to float on "eiderdown" through fields of buttercups and dandelions. Listen to this with a good set of headphones and let Wright's deep organ fills wash over you, and Barrett's stirring multi-tracked vocals warm your insides. You may giggle at the sudden entrance of a cuckoo. But then, you're supposed to. On surface, this song is about playing hide-and-seek. We were all children, once, so who cannot relate to that? But, as Lewis Carroll, Kenneth Grahame, and Syd Barrett all knew, words have different meanings. This song is just as much about the exhilaration of being invisible, floating like a fetus, gazing at the hustle and bustle of a world gone cuckoo."Flaming" clocks in at a mere two minutes and forty-two seconds, but it's more imaginative than all four sides of The Wall. And it has one of the most beautiful musical closeouts ever devised. John and Paul certainly walked away shaking their heads in astonishment. It's obvious where they got the final notes for "She's Leaving Home."Many have tried over the years, but nobody writes songs like this anymore. Very few back then could, either.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是平克·弗洛伊德的首张录音室专辑，由西德·巴雷特主导，融合科幻与儿童幻想的意象，呈现出既诡谲又天真的双重气质。音乐上以迷幻摇滚为基础，加入太空摇滚的声响实验，如《Astronomy Domine》中部落式鼓击与失真吉他的宇宙漫游，《Interstellar Overdrive》长达十分钟的管风琴与即兴段落，展现出早期前卫摇滚的雏形。巴雷特独特的联觉感知赋予作品鲜明的色彩感与声音想象力，歌词涉及幻觉中的侏儒、存在主义稻草人、读心猫等超现实形象，区别于当时商业化的嬉皮士产物。专辑在艾比路录音室录制，与披头士的《佩珀军士》同期制作，但更显粗粝与不可预测，为后来的太空摇滚和实验音乐提供了重要参照。

items.body:
Since everyone else has written something about the centennials of Miles Davis and John Coltrane, why not join the parade? It is a good opportunity to look at the timeline of bassists the legendary trumpeter and saxophonist used. Born just under four months apart, the pair worked together under the elder Davis’ name periodically between Fall 1955 and Spring 1957 before a more steady affiliation in 1958-1960.

It is in that latter period that this analysis will begin, as it gives a convenient bit of serendipity: the fact that two of the their most famed albums were made in that period, Davis’ Kind Blue (March 2nd and April 22nd, 1959 for Columbia) and Coltrane’s Giant Steps (May 4th–5th and December 2nd, 1959). And the analysis will end with Coltrane’s death in 1967, which came during the tenure of Davis’ “second great quintet” and before his groups swelled and electrified during his fusion period.

As such, we begin with the same man, the bassist on both those albums: Paul Chambers. He had taken up the bass a decade earlier in his adopted home of Detroit (where he was a student at the seminal Cass Technical High School ... more on that later). He arrived in New York in 1954 at 19. By the time of Kind of Blue and Giant Steps, he had been on over 100 sessions from dozens of leaders, with multiple dates under Davis (with whom he had started working in late 1955) and Coltrane (who had used him for several albums in 1957-58 as well as both fellow sideman for many others and Chambers also hiring Coltrane for his own sessions). In addition to the five albums he led, Chambers played on sessions for Benny Golson, Curtis Fuller, J.J. Johnson, Lee Morgan, Red Garland, Sonny Clark, and Sonny Rollins.

The collaboration between Davis and Chambers was remarkably fruitful before and after Kind of Blue and solidified a part of Davis’ music that had previously seen widely differing players like Tommy Potter, Oscar Pettiford, Al McKibbon, and Percy Heath. The rest of 1959 saw multiple engagements around the country and closed with recordings that would be part of another monumental record, Sketches of Spain, that paired Davis’ group with the Gil Evans Orchestra. 1960 continued that momentum with more Sketches of Spain recording and almost non-stop touring, including two stretches in Europe, from Spring onward. 1961 and 1962 had more of the same activity, the documents being Someday My Prince Will Come and Quiet Nights. Then, quite suddenly, Chambers left Davis’ group in early February 1963.

It should be stated that Chambers did not restrict his activities solely to Davis, recording over four dozen albums during the period with, among many others, Jackie McLean, Wynton Kelly, Benny Golson, Hank Mobley, and Curtis Fuller. And after leaving Davis, he worked steadily with an array of leaders through the end of 1968, sadly passing away from tuberculosis caused and/or aggravated by drug abuse at only 33.

Stepping right into the Davis group was another Cass Technical High School alumnus: Ron Carter. Nearly 26, Carter was already prophesying his prolific career, participating in over three dozen albums since 1960, with the likes of Charli Persip, Yusef Lateef, Eric Dolphy, Don Ellis, Coleman Hawkins, Cecil Payne, Jaki Byard, Wes Montgomery, Bobby Timmons, Tadd Dameron, Dizzy Reece, Ken McIntyre, Milt Jackson, Benny Golson and others, plus waxing his leader debut, Where?, for Prestige subsidiary New Jazz in 1961.

It was Carter’s arrival that heralded Davis’ soon-to-be seminal band, though it took until Fall 1964 for its personnel to solidify. With Carter, Davis recorded Seven Steps To Heaven and played the Antibes festival in 1963. What is interesting though is while the “second great quintet” is thought of as a monolith, the bass chair had some upheaval/fluidity, depending on how you look at it. Gary Peacock – already a veteran and likely the only person to work for both Bud Shank and Albert Ayler – took the chair for nearly six weeks in the spring of 1964, Carter returning thereafter through the end of the year. 1965 began auspiciously with the January recording of E.S.P. but then things derailed with a convalescing Davis unable to play. And when he could, in November and December, Carter, a hot commodity, was absent, spelled by Peacock once more, then Reggie Workman, who had come up around the same time as Carter and had already come and gone in the groups of Coltrane. In 1966, Carter would return to the group but only partially, participating in East Coast performances, shows elsewhere having either Richard Davis, Carter’s only real equal in terms of fecundity, or in the Peacock mold of eclecticism, Eddie Gomez, returning permanently in October, just before the album Miles Smiles. 1967 was similar: Carter was on board when not busy elsewhere, Gomez on call, then Albert Stinson for one show (a little over two years before his passing – see Bass Tragedies column in Issue 94) and then another veteran, Buster Williams, for a tour (and playing on one track of the 1981-released compilation album Directions). Carter would fill a fixed point for all of 1967, including the albums Sorcerer and Nefertiti and would continue with Davis through the middle of 1968.

Like Chambers or perhaps even more so, Carter was also on the greater jazz scene during his tenure with Davis. He recorded on sessions led by his fellow Davis bandmates but also by everyone from Bobby Timmons, Charles Lloyd, Donald Byrd and Bobby Hutcherson to Jimmy Smith, Shirley Scott, Eddie Harris, and Stanley Turrentine, to name only a handful. He has, of course, gone on to be likely the most recorded bassist in jazz history.

Paul Chambers’ time under Coltrane was shorter and more intermittent. After Giant Steps he was part of, along with the rest of Davis’ period band, November 1959 recordings that would partly comprise Coltrane Jazz and be brought back 18 months later as one of three individual bassists taking part in the Africa/Brass recordings (though his contribution was only heard on the 1995 complete sessions version).

Also in 1959 was a Birdland engagement for Coltrane where either Ahmed Abdul-Malik or George Tucker, both established and close in age to Coltrane, were on bass.

In 1960 Coltrane hired the slightly younger Steve Davis in what seems to be his first professional engagement. Davis stayed in the band through the end of the year for all its live dates and played on music recorded in October and released piecemeal on My Favorite Things, Coltrane Jazz, Coltrane Plays the Blues, and Coltrane’s Sound. Though Davis lived until 1987, his credits after Coltrane were slight: the Mangione Brothers, Dave Burns, McCoy Tyner, Kenny Dorham, James Moody, Freddie McCoy, and Eddie Jefferson, all made in the ‘60s. One deviation in the year came via Coltrane’s shared date with Don Cherry, The Avant-Garde, where bass was handled by either Charlie Haden or Percy Heath.

1961 was a year in flux, bassist-wise, for Coltrane. He introduced a concept to which he would return later in the decade by using two bassists for an engagement at Chicago’s Sutherland Lounge in March: Raphael Don Garrett and Workman, the former, about six years younger, working with Roland Kirk, Paul Serrano, and Eddie Harris, the latter 11 years younger, sideman for Gigi Gryce, Donald Byrd, Duke Jordan, Richard Williams, and Dave Pike.

Workman would be part of the aforementioned Africa/Brass, as would, separately, another bassist, Art Davis, already with credits under Max Roach, Lee Morgan, Booker Little, Hal Mooney, Ernestine Anderson, Dizzy Gillespie, Leo Wright, Clifford Jordan/Sonny Red, Abbey Lincoln, and Booker Little. But in May they were together for Ole Coltrane and nearly a month at the Village Vanguard in August. Workman would become the fixed bassist for Coltrane through the end of the year for concerts, including a European tour, and a small portion of the Ballads album from the end of the year. An exception was Workman either alternating or alongside Jimmy Garrison for a November stint at the Village Vanguard.

If not for a family health crisis forcing Workman to leave the group at the end of 1961 and return to his native Philadelphia, he likely would have stayed with the band and jazz history been quite different. It should be said that Workman hardly is a footnote, becoming one of the most revered players of his generation. But it was Garrison who became the anchor. Born between Garrett and Workman, prior to joining Coltrane he had worked with Philly Joe Jones, Curtis Fuller, Kenny Dorham, Jackie McLean, JR Montrose, Walter Bishop, Jr., Ornette Coleman, Bill Barron, and Ted Curson.

Unlike Carter and Davis, once Garrison was on board, he stayed there. That was mostly to do with Coltrane’s packed schedule of touring and albums and that, unlike Davis, he was healthy and non-combustible. From 1962-1964, Garrison was omnipresent, including the bulk of Ballads, Duke Ellington & John Coltrane (where he split duties with Ellington’s period bassist Aaron Bell), 2018 discovery Both Directions At Once, John Coltrane And Johnny Hartman, Impressions, Crescent, another new millennium unearthed gem in Blue World, and closing out the year with Coltrane’s magnum opus A Love Supreme (which added Art Davis for a second day of recording, released as a second disc to the album’s deluxe edition in 2002).

In 1965 Garrison was still the main man but occasionally Davis would be alongside him: partially on The John Coltrane Quartet Plays in February and fully for June’s Ascension. Otherwise, Garrison was the sole bassist for performances and most of the other albums: Transition, Sun Ship, and Meditations. The exceptions without Davis were overdubs of Haden for the posthumously released Infinity and Garrett returning to play both bass and clarinet for Live In Seattle (as well as the 2021 archival release A Love Supreme: Live In Seattle), Om, and part of Kulu Se Mama.

1966 was even more Garrison-centric, with the only documented work including a second bassist shows in November and December with Lionel “Sonny” Johnson, the brother of Dewey Johnson, who had played on Ascension. The last year of Coltrane’s life, Garrison was there as well, with one notable absence: the Coltrane/Rashied Ali duet Interstellar Space.

Unlike Chambers or Carter, Garrison was kept so busy during his time with Coltrane that his outside discography at the time is meager, though it does include his sole leader date, Illumination! with the Elvin Jones/Jimmy Garrison Sextet. Otherwise it was sessions with Lorez Alexandria, Coltrane bandmate McCoy Tyner, Sonny Rollins, Bill Dixon, and Robert F. Pozar.

After Coltrane’s death, Garrison kept working but his documentation slowed, his two Blue Note dates with the Jones trio rounded out by Joe Farrell being the most enduring. There were also dates with Rolf and Joachim Kuhn, Clifford Thornton and Nathan Davis, and regular work with Alice Coltrane and Archie Shepp. His final recording came in early 1975 with Beaver Harris and Dave Burrell’s 360 Degree Music Experience. Garrison died of lung cancer in 1976 at 42.

items.body:
1970 (April 10th, 1970 – IBC Studios, London)

Negotiations were now underway between Sean Murphy and several labels including Deram, CBS and Harvest, the EMI sub-label that had distributed Volume Two in the UK and already had Kevin Ayers in its stable. “They are still not an attraction in the very top bracket, so it was a pleasant surprise to see major companies throwing in genuinely massive bids earlier this year when the group was looking for a recording deal,” Richard Williams revealed. Ultimately, Soft Machine signed with CBS, but Third was self-financed, taken partly from studio sessions, but also from live recordings (“Facelift”) and edits and loops of tapes made by Mike Ratledge and Hugh Hopper at the home of Bob Woolford, who had let them use his Brenell and Stellavox tape recorders. Such infringements of accepted professional practices were only possible because CBS, having acquired a finished album, were no longer in a position to force the band to comply with them.

The benefit for Soft Machine in terms of artistic freedom is easy to measure. But this has to be balanced against the fact that the production on Third is, to put it bluntly, an unmitigated disaster. IBC, at the time the studio of choice for such notorious perfectionists as The Who and the Bee Gees, are probably less to blame than the band themselves who, in spite of the issues with Volume Two, are again credited as sole producers. The sound suffers from almost constantly saturated low frequencies and extremely vague mediums, the drums are much too low in the mix, as if played behind a closed door; and the organ is deprived of much of its biting impact through overwhelming equalization. Unfortunately the 2007 remaster, while an improvement, fails to rectify this.

What is problematic is that, as well as making the album an uncomfortable listen, its sub-par production lessens the claim, widely held at the time of its release, that Third represented musical state-of-the-art. This claim was based on Soft Machine’s ability, unparalleled among their contemporaries, to draw from and amalgamate an exceptionally wide range of influences. Starting out as a rock band, and then gradually moving towards jazz to invent a uniquely personal, and absolutely valid, British answer to American fusion, Soft Machine went even further, incorporating the influence of Stockhausen’s avant-garde and Terry Riley’s repetitive minimalism. Third’s ‘total’ vision, encompassing the entire spectrum of known musical genres, placed Soft Machine at the forefront of musical “progress” in 1970. However, horizons have since expanded to such an extent, beyond the Western tradition in particular, that this concept of universality has aged considerably.

In his insightful review of Third for Actuel, Paul Alessandrini wrote of “music to really listen to, no longer aiming for a purely physical vibration, more interiorized. Soft Machine have re-thought their musical influences – Riley, Cecil Taylor, Coltrane – to really make them their own, abandoning their aesthetics of random explosion in favor of a much more thought-out approach.” There are still occasional reminders of these sonic excesses that, as Alessandrini noted, had now largely disappeared from their music. Mike Ratledge's lengthy solo introduction to “Facelift” almost sounds like an electric exorcism, as if to rid Soft Machine of what still remains of that violence in order to reinvent their music in a more controlled manner, setting formal perfection as their new objective.

Considered as a whole, Hugh Hopper's piece represents the last remnant of Soft Machine’s early days, when they still favored spirit over form - here found lacking in both sound quality and performance, with a few train wrecks along the way - and were intent on disregarding the accepted rules. “Facelift” includes free sections increasingly at odds with Ratledge’s preoccupation with structure – and while as a keyboard player, he still embodies the band’s more radical leanings, Ratledge’s own compositions reveal a much less iconoclastic temperament. Hopper described his own approach at the time as “halfway between” that of Dean, “whose thing is really total improvisation, without any structure, and on the other extreme, [that of Ratledge] who's into entirely formalized musical forms.

“Moon in June” completes Robert Wyatt’s donation to Soft Machine of the material originally intended for his first solo album in 1968. It is interesting to note that Wyatt does this at the exact point where Soft Machine had shed any remaining reference to pop in their live repertoire. Looking back, Wyatt was certainly justified in saying that his side of Third was “the last chance I had to use all the things we'd done without being a jazz band. I wanted to get twenty minutes of it down somewhere.” And since his colleagues, reluctant to act as mere accompanists, had made no secret of their lack of interest in his songs, he recorded most of “Moon in June” on his own, repeating the modus operandi of the 1968-69 demo. Hugh Hopper and Mike Ratledge’s participation is again limited to the organ solo halfway through (Hopper also plays a short melodic theme earlier in the piece). Elton Dean wasn’t asked to contribute anything – Wyatt’s unconvincing justification being that he “hadn’t yet worked out how to work on [his] stuff with the added wind instruments.”

As there was no mention of this breach of band discipline in the sleeve notes, only the most astute listeners noticed that the organ heard during the first ten minutes was a Hammond rather than Ratledge’s signature Lowrey, that the playing clearly wasn’t Ratledge’s, and that most of the ‘bass’ parts were played on an electric piano. When the truth was finally revealed, Wyatt gave contradictory versions of what had happened – in one interview claiming that Ratledge and Hopper had “refused to play [on “Moon in June”] and I had to play it all myself,” in another that he’d “almost had to force them to get them to play on it, which I thought was rather unfair as I’d done my best to get into the music they were writing.” Probably the most objective and believable of Wyatt’s rationales was that he was “terrified it’d be played wrong” if he didn’t perform it all himself.

To approach “Moon in June” as a ‘message’ song would misrepresent Wyatt’s more mundane intent, insofar as the phonetic qualities of the words often seem to matter more to him than their meaning. In other words, “Moon in June” is above all a musical composition, a suite of instrumental sections, some of which are adorned with melodies and lyrics, and others not. The singing accompanies the music rather than vice-versa. In this respect, outside of a possible rivalry with Elton Dean and Wyatt’s inability to sing while drumming, there was no theoretical incompatibility between Soft Machine’s move towards jazz and the continued presence of Wyatt’s voice (even if limited to the Echoplexed scat singing of his solitary interludes during the band’s concerts). Dispensing with vocals was the single most questionable move in Soft Machine’s entire musical evolution, not to mention one whose commercial consequences cannot be underestimated. In different circumstances, Hugh Hopper would surely have joined Wyatt in lobbying for having at least some vocals, but in addition to his increasingly strained personal relationship with Wyatt, Hopper had at this point completely lost interest in non-instrumental music. “I find that using the human voice means asserting limitations to your music right from the start”, he explained in 1972. “I am more interested in the sounds generated by instruments, or electronic devices, because the possibilities offered by songs are much more limited than when experimenting with sounds.”

Even if there was no future for singing in Soft Machine, “Moon in June” at least offers evidence that Robert Wyatt, in a voice-free context, could still be more than “a session drummer for an interesting new species of jazz groups,” as long as he contributed to the writing. When it came to extended pieces, he could stand comparison with Mike Ratledge, even though he lacked any comparable academic background. In addition to its constant melodic inspiration, “Moon in June” is very skillfully constructed (indeed, its instrumental architecture had remained intact since 1968), and confirms Wyatt’s seemingly innate talent for making a coherent whole out of ill-assorted musical ideas.

items._cn_summary: 本文为Soft Machine第三张专辑《Third》的深度乐评，聚焦1970年制作背景与音乐史定位。文章详细描述了专辑的诞生过程：乐队与CBS签约后获得前所未有的艺术自由，从IBC录音室现场录制、Mike Ratledge和Hugh Hopper的家用磁带实验素材中取材，自行制作完成。评论直言专辑制作水平糟糕——低频过饱和、中频模糊、鼓声被压制、器官失去冲击力。然而在音乐内容层面，评论高度肯定了Soft Machine的融合视野：从摇滚出发，逐步融入爵士、Stockhausen的先锋派与Terry Riley的简约主义重复手法，构建出一种跨越已知音乐类型的'总体性'美学，代表了1970年英国对美式融合爵士的独特回应。评论同时以历史视角指出，这种普遍性概念在后世视野扩展后已显陈旧。整体而言，这是一篇兼具行业史考据与美学批评的严肃乐评，详尽剖析了实验性爵士摇滚的历史意义与制作局限。

items.body: Rotterdam-based musician and designer Rutger Zuydervelt has described Re:Moving (Music for Choreographies by Yin Yue) as ‘an album with a bittersweet taste’. Rutger, aka Machinefabriek, was invited to score two new pieces by award-winning NYC choreographer, Yin Yue. Completed shortly before Covid, it was with regret that the resulting pieces never saw the light of day. The pieces have never been performed, leaving the music alone in stillness, making it ‘a soundtrack to non-existent dances’. The music should be animating and accompanying the performers, but instead find an empty stage, divorced from what should have been a special union between music and dance. As time went on, Zuydervelt and Yin Yue both agreed that the music deserved to be heard, even without its intended audience and its parental choreography, choosing to believe in it for what it was, sending it out into the world without its mother and having to rapidly take on a new life, a new form. The score is innocent and beautiful in its own right, but there’s a shadow of what if, and it hangs from every note; the kindness shown in the creative process has been a victim of cruelty beyond its control, gripped, used, and mangled by the pandemic – and the plague nearly killed off the music. The pair traded videos of choreographic sketches and calls over Skype. A Measurable Existence was the title, and it was originally planned to premiere through New York’s The Gibney Company in April 2020. With some irony, the music was intended to ‘reflect the discovery of self by interaction with others’ – an interaction lost due to enforced social distancing and lockdowns. It’s about parallel journeys that intersect, repel or collide. The dance doesn’t shy away from drama, and the music doesn’t either A collaboration between physical movement and musical experimentation, these pieces are both reflective and dynamic, active, advancing, and endlessly moving; one can feel the motion of its performers, even without their physical presence. Skirting between lighter sections and darker, synth-lit alleyways, the music is consistent in its high tempo and higher levels of activity, seamlessly segueing from one segment into the next. As well as its dense textures, the music has a fluidity to it, an unstoppable flow, gentle but very powerful. With hope, they still look forward to presenting the performance as it was intended. Perhaps, one day, the performance will be complete. One day. Re:Moving (Music for Choreographies by Yin Yue) by Machinefabriek www.phantomlimblabel.bandcamp.com
items._genre: experimental electronic / contemporary classical / ambient / modern composition
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是荷兰鹿特丹音乐人Rutger Zuydervelt（艺名Machinefabriek）为纽约编舞家尹越的两支舞蹈作品创作的配乐，原定2020年4月在Gibney公司首演，却因疫情而从未登台。音乐虽失去了与之对应的舞蹈呈现，但仍以独立形式被释放出来。Zuydervelt与尹越通过视频和Skype远程协作完成了创作，作品意图探讨自我与他者的互动关系。配乐在高密度织体与流畅动感之间穿梭，既有轻盈段落也有合成器铺陈的暗色通道，节奏活跃而连贯，呈现出持续推进的能量。乐评以'苦涩交织'形容这张专辑——音乐本是为舞蹈而生，却被迫成为一场未曾发生的演出的伴侣，独立面对听众。这种缺失本身成为作品叙事的一部分，赋予音乐一种关于等待与缺席的质地。
