items.body: Folk Tapes (Invisibilia Editions) is a dream-like selection of ambient-tinted folk songs. Composed in solitude by Maria Valentina Chirico, a singer with a long history in contemporary classical and sacred music, Folk Tapes features tape loops and field recordings, which come from frequent collaborator Andrea Penso and also includes the voice of eleven-year-old Marta Arbarello, which adds a child-like quality to the music’s fairy tale. Side A begins softly and inquisitively, with its gentle ambient sound being the song of a traditional and tranquil Sunday afternoon. Its childish innocence makes it an album of wonder and discovery, especially within and among nature. Chirico brings a youthful approach to her music, but it sounds incredibly mature in its musicianship. Side B is a musical fairy tale about a little girl who turns into a white donkey, and a mystical, enchanted mood continues on throughout its brief running time. Be it through spoken word or song, something of the fantastical is brought forth, but the sacred is also present, giving the music a balanced air between the restrained and the reverent, and meeting listeners halfway between the fantastical landscape of a child’s imagination and the sacred tones of a cathedral. Folk Tapes is a quiet record with a curious heart, and with track names such as ‘Sweet October’ and ‘Children of Water’, the purity of innocence infiltrates the music; innocence which can’t be broken or lost. Folk Tapes marks Chirico’s debut release as a songwriter, and it couldn’t be more impressive. Folk Tapes by Maria Valentina Chirico www.invisibilia.bandcamp.com
items._genre: ambient folk / field recording / contemporary classical
items._cn_summary: 这是一张由长期活跃于当代古典与圣咏领域的歌手玛丽亚·瓦伦蒂娜·奇里科独自完成的创作处女作，以磁带循环与实地录音为骨架，将民谣骨架浸入环境音色的纹理之中。十一岁女孩玛尔塔·阿巴雷洛的声音为整张唱片注入童话般的质地，A面以轻柔的氛围铺展开来，呈现宁静周日的午后意象；B面则讲述小女孩化身白驴的寓言，贯穿神秘与魔幻氛围。作品在口语与吟唱之间游走，将儿童想象力的幻想风景与大教堂般的圣咏色调融为一体，克制而庄严。曲目如《甜蜜的十月》《水的孩子们》承载着不可被摧毁的天真与好奇心，安静却拥有好奇的内核，整体呈现出纯真与成熟并存的独特张力。

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. Various Artists - L�ve L�ve (Volume1) (Review) Pedro Lima - Maguidala (Review) Ann O'aro - Bleu (Review)

items._cn_summary: 本辑为圣多美和普林西比70-80年代音乐的合集续篇，聚焦当地特有的Puxa音乐。这一流派融合了前葡萄牙非洲殖民地音乐元素，吸收merengue、Kompas、Soukouss、Benga等多种节奏，被认为具有召唤精灵或驱邪的功能。乐评指出，尽管当地仅有12个村庄，录音和发行条件有限，但这些岛屿的音乐展现出远超地理规模的丰富性。专辑收录15首作品，多吉他交织盘旋，主唱与和声相互应答，构成旋律框架，节奏律动足以让舞者沉醉数小时。Pedro Lima领衔的乐队以闷吉他与鼓组对峙，Sangazuza则在贝斯与键盘退去后展示鼓与吉他的groove张力。Africa Negra的作品呈现典型的人声让位于器乐延展的编制。这张合集由Bongo Joe发行，展现了小岛屿国家在非洲黄金时代未被充分记录的独特声音。

items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)
items.label: Analog Africa
items._cn_summary: Analog Africa厂牌推出的第44号合辑，收录贝宁传奇乐队Orchestre Poly-Rythmo在1977至1982年间为歌手兼词曲创作者Antoine Dougbé伴奏的作品。Dougbé以双腿击打Cavacha节奏而闻名，配合融合沃杜教（Vodun）元素的Sakpata与Sato律动，与Poly-Rythmo形成了其他人难以企及的化学反应。合辑中的制作因年代感而呈现出塑料质感的吉他音色与合成器铺底，同时清晰可辨古巴颂乐的影响，尤其是开篇几首作品中的牛铃与鼻音对唱。康戈拉姆巴在八十年代的冲击也渗透进音乐里，《Ma Won Min Towe Leo》以合成器音床开场，吉他在高帽主导的律动中交织。整体录音生涯虽短暂，三张专辑加数支单曲却展现了高度浓缩的跨大陆融合能量。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio
items.label: Taragot
items._cn_summary: Camilla Hole Trio 的新专辑相比前作《Eventyrferd》中科幻合成器与挪威传统素材的嫁接，转向更为踏实的探索路径，但跨越本土民乐的意图依然延续。高音萨克斯作为主奏乐器自然带入爵士血脉，开篇曲《Springleik》取材于挪威西部的传统舞曲，Hole 先陈述旋律，Kalman 与 Nesheim 分别以贝斯和鼓构建节奏骨架，随后叠加 Kalman 的模块合成器与 Nesheim 的颤音琴拓展音色层次。三人角色边界模糊，旋律在贝斯与萨克斯间流动转移，Nesheim 的鼓点逐步打开即兴空间，Hole 在曲末再次奏出主题收束，形成完整的开放-释放-回归结构。这种乐器分工的流动性与即兴张力是乐评强调的核心特征。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑诞生于新冠封锁期间的意大利法齐奥利音乐厅，古巴钢琴家Omar Sosa在空旷的音乐厅中进行两小时无脚本的即兴演奏，后期加入人声采样、打击乐、循环片段、田野录音和环境音效。Sosa明确反对风格归类，试图将爵士、拉丁、非洲、古巴传统与电子手法融为一体，同时坚守Thelonious Monk'从不重复'的精神。他重视第一遍录制的直觉与自然，关注低脉轮共振与冥想性声音，提倡'少即是多'的美学。从文章描述的曲目来看，钢琴内部琴弦被直接拨弄与延音踏板共鸣被刻意呈现，文本在探讨自由即兴、跨文化传统与现代录音手段结合方面提供了较为深入的视角。

items._cn_summary: 匈牙利作曲家Márton Illés的《Forajzok》（2021）由国际当代乐团在TIME:SPANS音乐节首演。作品结尾处，所有乐手与指挥Rebekah Heller同步在头顶摇晃硬币，金属碰撞产生细碎而稍纵即逝的沙沙声。这一细节揭示了作曲家对非常规音源与仪式化表演动作的关注——身体动作本身成为发声机制的一部分，模糊了演奏与剧场行为的边界。作为当代古典领域的实验性作品，《Forajzok》展示了欧洲新音乐场景中探索器乐边界的倾向，通过看似简单的指令激发出原始、即时且不可预测的声学现象。但原文仅为演出乐评的开篇片段，篇幅极短，对作品的结构与整体音响面貌缺乏充分描述，限制了更深层的评价。

items.body: Review by rdtprog — The band's music is described as post-rock, but I found more dynamics on this album than on mostpost-rock albums I have heard. The slow-paced songs set a melancholic, cinematic atmosphere. Thesongs contain sumptuous grooves and intense climactic crescendos. It's instrumental music with somevoices, but no lyrics. The band uses a minimalist approach with plenty of emotion in the music. Noinstrument overshadows another. The band doesn't use many notes but delivers the perfect sound andmelody that keeps you on the edge from the first note to the last. From the first song, the vocalsand the guitar remind me of the music of Ennio Morricone. Then it goes into a Tubular Bells kind ofpassage, but with an added spacey touch. Some breathtaking piano and synths continue to carry themelody. The album has to be listened to in one take, like one great song.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑虽然被归类为后摇滚，但评论者指出其在动态变化上超越了一般后摇滚作品的范畴。慢速推进的曲目营造出忧郁且具有电影画面感的氛围，饱满的律动与层层堆叠的高潮形成张力。音乐以器乐为主，虽有人声但无歌词，采用了极简的手法却充满情绪表达。各乐器之间保持平衡，不存在某件乐器喧宾夺主的情况，音符运用节制却精准到位。从开篇起，嗓音与吉他令人联想到埃尼奥·莫里科内的配乐风格，随后过渡到带有太空感色彩的Tubular Bells段落，钢琴与合成器交织承担旋律推进。整张专辑需要一气呵成地聆听，如同一首完整的作品展开。

items.body: Review by alainPP — LUNATIC SOUL, Mariusz DUDA and his desire to compose alone, a best-combination album following the saga of his seventh album, "Through Shaded Woods," released in 2020. Between life and death."Realm of the Weeping Willows," the only unreleased track, comes from the "Through Shaded Woods" recording sessions. A staccato ambient rhythm in four parts, with the aggression of the bass, the captivating organ, the mantra-like drums?in short, a sound that could easily be found on RIVERSIDE. An air from the austere Polish regions with the tambourine and acoustic guitar, an invitation to travel beyond the steppes, the flute completing the spell. The vocals fade into the distance, but RIVERSIDE is still present, the grief not yet fully processed; crescendoing prog rock sets its mid-cycle break.A Marillion-esque folk melancholy, almost angelic in the air?those already familiar with the genre will surely recognize it. This ambient passage plunges into darkness, contemplation, a shadowy, ethereal journey, with hylophobia as a backdrop. The finale, with its vibrant strings and Mariusz's choir, melts away, injecting mystery and solemnity into the long, repetitive final sound."Hylophobia," known for its sharp riff from the 2020 bonus album, still carries that unsettling feeling linked to forests. A punchy, explosive rock track with a sharp bass line; midway through, the religious, mantra-like, folk-liturgical choir appears, unchanged from the original. "Vyraj," with bass and organ, instruments of the era, is undoubtedly a nod to Dead Can Dance. A grumpy, raging folk-dance rock track; A track flirting with the great Mike Oldfield in a heavy metal version, inviting a hypnotic musical addiction. An entry into Mariusz's singular universe, his bewitching mythical paradise, beyond the Milky Way. An abrasive, percussive tempo seems to emerge from a distant past, the vocals whispered, the organ bouncing, and the bass captivating."Transition II" remixed and shorter for its LP version. Seven parts featuring an archaic flute, Mariusz narrating a story as if wandering, much like on Riverside. A slow and progressive start, linear and tribal, with an ethereal piano reminiscent of Simple Minds. Three minutes of intro before the techno bass, metallic percussion, and stereo vocals explain the encounter with the Ferryman for the transition. A pounding, contemplative experience, perhaps challenging for some, this track could easily be played in a nightclub deep in the forest, on the banks of a river like the Styx. The break from the folk atmosphere reminiscent of Oldfield, a xylophone and guitar surfing in its own world; cinematic sounds on Inspector Gadget, the music of Reich, Richter, sparkling, emerging from the melancholy inhabiting Mariusz; a way of compensating for his break with Riverside.A panting, a race to distance himself from his band, and the atmosphere shifts to a cinematic soundtrack evoking The Big Blue, airy, crystalline, on Apsaras. The light is definitely there, bringing gaiety to his notes; a little reminder of "Transition 1," about the birth of his son. The guitar suddenly leans towards Tangerine Dream before cutting to this solemn piano, ambient Pink Floyd, distant new age, stereo, recalling the album "Impressions" and snippets of Ange and Barclay James Harvest. This music is remarkable, skillfully balancing nostalgia, emotion, and sensitivity, allowing us to transcend the ending of RIVERSIDE. The final ambient, cinematic outro, reminiscent of TANGERINE DREAM, is reminiscent of Tangram and Force Majeure.LUNATIC SOUL, a musical chrysalis, metamorphoses into ambient, electronic music. An atmospheric, progressive folk sound that feels fresh and hopeful. A remix album with a beautiful unreleased track feels a bit underwhelming. (3.5)

items._cn_summary: 这是波兰音乐人Mariusz Duda的个人项目Lunatic Soul的第七张专辑，延续了前作《Through Shaded Woods》的氛围民俗路线。专辑在民谣根基上融合了前卫摇滚结构与电子节奏，将原声吉他、笛子、风琴、教堂唱诗班等传统元素与Techno贝斯、金属打击乐、简约主义重复手法并置。评论提及Dead Can Dance、Mike Oldfield、Marillion等参照系，强调黑暗森林意象与生死主题的冥想气质。终曲以电影化配乐手法收束，整体呈现为内向型的过渡性作品，介于Riverside的乐队宇宙与个人独白之间，音乐语言偏向氛围化与叙事化，但在实验性突破上较为克制。

items.body: Review by Prog Dog — I feel like I've just come out of a shopping mall, but instead of bags and shoe boxes, I'm stuffing a mountain of musical concepts and ideas into my trunk. This is my first handshake with this band, and I'm glad I'm starting my listening experience with Pure Reason Revolution's debut album "The Dark Third". This album is a really unique blending of influences. In the most general terms, it feels like indie rock, but one that ventures into the epic. Gosh, there's so much to distill here: I hear Disney on weed. I hear psychedelia. I hear progressive rock. I hear Beach Boys-style pop. I hear electronica. I hear Zeppelin. I hear Steven Wilson/ Porcupine Tree...I guess you could say this album, and maybe this band, is all about layers: heavy antique curtains, or a chiffon-layered cake.Listening to this record has brought something important to mind: you really need to listen to a band's album from start to finish. Everybody loves a good song, but it's through the full body of their work that you really start to get to know a band. You start to get a sense of their strengths as musicians, but also who they are as a creative unit?their instincts, their ideas, their chemistry. You get to hear how they move from one idea to another, how they build an album, and ultimately, you get a taste of the full wingspan of a band's psyche.This point really hit home after my first listen to The Dark Third. For example, the album finishes with an amazingly subtle musical farewell?a phrase that you can only really appreciate if you've journeyed with the band from the first song to the last. It's like skipping ahead and reading the final page of a book. You can know how it ends, but you don't have the context. You need to experience the whole journey?all the twists and turns, all the contours, to really understand where that ending takes you. And to me, that's the essence, and the fun of it. That's why I'm here, frankly, telling you all this!The core lineup is Jon Courtney on vocals/guitar/keyboards, Chlo� Alper on vocals/bass, Jamie Willcox on vocals/guitar, Jim Dobson on keyboards/guitar/bass/violin/vocals and Andrew Courtney on drums.Instrumentally, there's a lot of clean electric guitar, both strummed and picked, as well as some bottle-neck slide. That's not to say the doors don't get completely blown off the barn in bursts of classic-rock riffing and inspired sections throughout this very energetic album. There's also a good smattering of violin, both clean and distorted, along with some very full-sounding string ensemble arrangements.There are plenty of atmospheric passages too, featuring synths and echoing guitars, and piano gets its share of the spotlight. The production is dynamic and creative, handled by Paul Northfield, whose credits include Dream Theater, Rush, and Porcupine Tree. The drums are often very textural and treated or combined with electronic beats, with some interesting processing and effects applied at the mixing desk. There's some rainy and wet sounding cymbal accents from the drums.Compositionally, there are zero weak tracks or sections. The structure is often tumbling and unpredictable with ideas constantly shifting, colliding, and reconfiguring.The vocals are a highlight, often heavily layered, with contrasting vocal lines making for a rich, textured sound. Of course, the two main singers, male and female, work exceptionally well together, complementing each other nicely.Lyrically, The Dark Third is a pretty surreal album. It gets into the subconscious, dreams, sleep, and that blurry line between what's real and what's happening in your head. There's literary and philosophical influence, but the lyrics do feel like a stream of consciousness. Even the title refers to that 'dark third' of our lives?the time we spend asleep and dreaming.So really, this is a satisfying, fairly dense and rich, high calorie album. I really enjoy the time I spend with it. It's a 4.5 out of 5 dog bones (or stars on progarchives) because it does everything an album is supposed to do, and when I get to the finish I usually want to start it all over again. The songs flow into each other and it has no weak or filler tracks. It's engaging and interesting at every turn, decked out with amazing vocal layers throughout.

items.body: Review by Prog Dog — "You can't handle the truth" was a great line in a great movie, but there's something in that idea that applies to all of us. We like to imagine we're the exception, that we're ready to face whatever truth comes our way.Chasm feels like a pretty good test of that assumption.I find Chasm, by The Tea Club, to be a deep album, as deep as the title implies?but it isn't a dangerous place to go. Quite the opposite. I loved it from the get-go. It's funny how, historically speaking, artists have sometimes been deemed dangerous by overzealous governments and dictatorships. Maybe it's because art can be so individual and unique, and therefore inherently threatening to any force that demands conformity and uniformity. Art has a way of saying, I see the world differently.And it's not easy being an artist. Not that an artist necessarily has to suffer in order to create good work, but they often have to work damn hard to bring that work into the world. It's a little like giving birth to something that then needs to be cared for and nurtured until it can stand on its own two feet?and protected along the way from all the harsh elements that might keep it from surviving.That's one reason the first thing that amazed me about Chasm was how original The Tea Club sound. There are recognizable influences here, of course, but the combination feels distinctly their own. And beneath that originality is an enormous amount of raw energy and forward drive, coupled with these deeper currents of yearning, for connection, for meaning, perhaps even for wholeness.Chasm is not overly polished, and clearly isn't aiming to please the music machines so much as reach for something beyond and somewhere else. I feel like the more I dig into this album, the more it will reveal itself. It's heartfelt, often bursting with honest energy and emotion, chasing ideas but also taking the time to pause and take stock.The songwriting is strong and bold. The Tea Club's sound is reminiscent of grunge and '80s King Crimson/Adrian Belew, with hints of a youthful Sting and The Police. There's also a hint of Metric with a male vocalist. There are no long epics here?just short ones. There's lots of bending and building going on here, with a touch of madness. If this album got sucked into an AI song-creation algorithm, it would probably become confused and label the whole thing a corrupted file. There are brief moments when Chasm becomes almost anti-melodic, but purposefully so, I suspect?creating contrast with the melodies that emerge around them.You can hear this particularly well on "Vineyard". The Tea Club mostly recorded this album as a band playing live off the floor, all analog, rather than surgically piecing performances together at different times and in different places. That sense of musicians interacting in real time comes through. The drums act as the glue, while the chorus winds like a river through unexpected and beautiful chords. It sounds less like a collection of individually constructed parts and more like a proper band listening to and responding to each other in the moment.If I were a cigar-smoking record exec, I'd be yelling, "I don't hear any hits!" And this is a good thing. Long live the anti-hits emerging from the antimatter universe. There is one curiously arresting track- 'The Lunar Eclipse', a pretty and sweet piano based song that the band reports to having struggled with in the recording phase and in the album track sequencing phase. Putting it last seems the perfect cap or cherry on the top to this adventurous album, and is one of my favourite tracks along with the album opener and 'Vineyard'. So, this bold album is not for the timid traveller. It's for the vigorous and strong prog-at-heart music appreciator?the kind of listener willing to dig in and discover what's hiding in the chasm. I give it a 4.5 out of 5 dog bones (or 4/5 stars on progarchives)

items.body: Hungarian artist Csalogány releases “F3160 (Reimagined)” on August 28, 2026, a second reading of her single “Peremvidék (F3160)”. The original appeared with a video in January 2026 and went on to win Best Experimental at the London Music Video Awards and take second place in the Best Performer category at the Berlin Music Video Awards 2026. It was also selected for the music-video competition at the Odense International Film Festival, held in Denmark from August 24 to 30, 2026. The title comes from F31.60, the ICD code for a mixed episode of bipolar disorder, in which manic and depressive symptoms can be present at the same time. Csalogány builds her work around psychology and interior states, and sets herself a plainly stated aim: “I am Csalogány and my goal is to make people feel.” Rather than explaining an emotion, she said, her songs are meant to construct a landscape a listener can move through. The new version comes out of the same premise. An emotional state that contradictory, in her account, cannot be approached from one angle, so “F3160 (Reimagined)” returns to the material from a second position while keeping its emotional core intact. She describes it as the start of a new phase, widening her musical language while keeping the translation of inner experience into sound at the centre of the work. The video for the original single was directed by Péter Becz and produced by Beyond, with cinematography by Marcell Csillag. It follows a museum attendant whose routine is interrupted by a painting of a horse, after which she turns to dance as a way of building an identity. Dancer and choreographer Bettina Rose Jurák, who plays the attendant, is the performance the Berlin jury placed second. About Csalogány Csalogány is the project of Hungarian singer-songwriter and producer Tímea Pászkány. Her music combines electronic production, chanting and Central and Eastern European folk material with lyrics that work through psychological self-examination and religious thinking. She came to wider notice through Kikeltető, a Hungarian programme run by KERET that maps the country’s underground scene and connects emerging musicians with industry professionals and audiences; Csalogány took part in the 2025 edition. Her recorded output so far includes the four-track EP “The First Thing I Remember, It Is Fire”, released on September 18, 2024, and the album “Szellemzaj, Hústenger” in 2025. The single “Peremvidék (F3160)” followed, with its video published on her official YouTube channel on January 12, 2026. She has played both Hungarian and international stages, and posts under csalogany_ on Instagram. “F3160 (Reimagined)” arrives on August 28, 2026 and is the first release of what Csalogány describes as a new period for the project.

items.body: For more than four decades, Ultravox have occupied a rather unusual position in British music history. They were pioneers of electronic music, yet never quite belonged to the electronic camp. They emerged from the post-punk scene, embraced technology early, and later became one of the most successful British bands of the early 1980s. Yet their reputation has often been reduced to a handful of familiar titles, most notably “Vienna” and “Dancing With Tears In My Eyes”. Richard Evans believes the band deserves a good deal more recognition. Following his 2022 book “Listening To The Music The Machines Make – Inventing Electronic Pop 1978-1983”, Evans has turned his attention to Ultravox with “Looking Backwards Towards the Future: The Story of Ultravox”, an authorised biography published by Omnibus Press on October 8, 2026. The 400-page hardback carries a foreword by Moby; North American, Australian and New Zealand editions follow on February 9, 2027. Evans has two book events confirmed so far: the Mowlem Theatre in Swanage on October 29, 2026, and Sound Affects in Brighton on November 4, 2026, both a talk, Q&A and signing. For Evans, Ultravox was a natural subject because their story crosses several musical worlds at once. They were already active when his previous book began, and were still active when it ended. More importantly, they repeatedly moved ahead of musical fashion rather than following it. We spoke to Richard about the origins of the book, John Foxx, the transformation brought by Midge Ure, the Blitz and New Romantic scene, the band’s unexpected connection with early Depeche Mode, the reunion years, and why he believes Ultravox are still waiting for the recognition they deserve. ‘All of a sudden I was writing a book about Ultravox’ Side-Line: Your previous book covered a whole musical movement. What made you decide that Ultravox should be your next subject? Richard Evans: The exact moment was in a pub in London in 2024. I had gone into town to meet Omnibus Press, who had published my previous book, because they had got in touch to ask if I was interested in writing another one for them. “Listening To The Music The Machines Make” had sold well and they wanted to hear if I had any ideas for something else. I had a small number of ideas, maybe four in total, which I told them about over a beer. They said they liked the sound of the Ultravox one the most and that was basically it. All of a sudden I was writing a book about Ultravox. What interested me about the band was that they were one of only a small number of artists who were already active in 1978, at the start of “Listening To The Music The Machines Make”, who were still active in 1983, at the end of that book. Also, I didn’t actually know that much about them. I had a few of their singles but I didn’t know much about the band beyond that. However, I had listened to a lot of their music while I was writing “Listening To The Music The Machines Make” and I really liked it, and the idea of finding out more about them was interesting. Plus, of course, there wasn’t already a book about them. I don’t know why that was the case but it felt like a perfect opportunity. A band that never quite fitted anywhere Side-Line: Was there a particular question about Ultravox’s history that you wanted to answer? Richard Evans: There wasn’t a particular question about Ultravox’s history that I wanted to answer. It was all of their history that caught my eye: the fact that they were a rare band who were so often ahead of musical fashions, who were true pioneers, but who were almost too far ahead of those curves to receive the credit for what they achieved. They also interested me because they never made anything easy for themselves. They were always pushing themselves to explore new areas, often at the expense of easy commercial success, and I admired them for that. Side-Line: That idea of Ultravox being difficult to categorise seems to run through their entire career. Richard Evans: Ultravox are a funny band in that they never quite fitted anywhere. They were too rock for electronic purists, too electronic for rock audiences, too arty, too single-minded… all qualities that make them such an interesting band. That is one of the things that became clearer to me while writing the book. John Foxx: the beginning of everything Side-Line: Your story goes all the way back to the origins of the band and John Foxx. How important was Foxx’s original vision? Richard Evans: Incredibly important. Fundamental actually. John Foxx actually conceived the idea of creating a band in response to a lecture he attended at art school, and in fact the formation of the band was a college project of sorts. That’s where the story starts, and none of the rest could have happened without that initial impetus. Side-Line: Foxx is fascinating because his influence extends far beyond the years he spent as Ultravox’s frontman. Richard Evans: John Foxx is a fascinating character, he deserves a biography dedicated to just him in fact. He is incredibly articulate and innately curious and his career, which covers music, art, design, academia and more, is very interesting. He feels like a true maverick and a genuine innovator, but Ultravox! was the starting point for that. If that hadn’t happened then he might have gone in an entirely different direction. An artist or an illustrator perhaps, or a writer or a teacher. Ultravox! set him on a path to everything he has achieved and explored. It took a while for the world to catch up but I do think that his influence is now being realised and recognised. ‘Systems Of Romance’ and the DNA of electronic music Side-Line: The first three albums occupy a fascinating place in electronic and post-punk history, with “Systems Of Romance” in particular becoming a reference point for later generations. Did researching them change the way you heard those records? Richard Evans: They are indeed, and you’re right about “Systems Of Romance” in particular. That album represented a very special moment where creativity and technology were being explored in a new way and Ultravox were among the very first to start exploring that. My research led me to listen to those records in a different way and they contain lots of idiosyncrasies and pieces of formative DNA which pointed to everything that came next, not just for the band, but for music in general. That’s quite an achievement, isn’t it? Side-Line: Did you deliberately avoid turning John Foxx’s later solo career into part of the Ultravox narrative? Richard Evans: I don’t delve into John Foxx’s work after Ultravox in the book but I agree that “Metamatic” was a very important record. Throughout “Looking Backwards Towards the Future” I tried to give equal weight to all the members of the various line-ups as best I could. They pretty much all had other projects going on outside Ultravox and if I explored one then I would have to explore them all, which would have taken focus away from the core Ultravox story and would have made the book much too big and unwieldy. For what it’s worth though, I view “Metamatic” and John Foxx’s subsequent projects as being distinct from Ultravox rather than being extensions of it. ‘Vienna’, Blitz and the New Romantic moment Side-Line: Ultravox’s relationship with the emerging Blitz and New Romantic scene is particularly interesting. How important was that environment to the band’s success? Richard Evans: For the individual band members I don’t think it was particularly important, but for the success of “Vienna” it was crucial. That period in time, those new electronic sounds, were incredibly new and startling, but it took Blitz and the New Romantics – none of Ultravox liked that name, although at the time they said they were more comfortable with being called Futurists – to create a world around that music by adding the dance-floor, the fashions and a compelling post-punk aesthetic to hang everything on to create a scene. That scene in turn allowed all sorts of very diverse artists, Ultravox amongst them, to smuggle themselves into the mainstream under the cover of New Romanticism. Side-Line: Depeche Mode were also part of that wider environment, although they quickly tried to distance themselves from the New Romantic label. Richard Evans: It was a very fertile period and lots of bands who previously wouldn’t have been grouped together suddenly found themselves part of a movement, but the smarter artists already knew that fashions fade fast. Having used the scene as the first steps on their career ladders, they were quick to try to distance themselves from it. Even at the time very few bands identified as New Romantics even though they were thrown together under that banner. Depeche Mode could see that, I think, and didn’t want to be held back by it. I think Ultravox were the same, but perhaps they played the game a little better! When Ultravox and Depeche Mode almost crossed paths Side-Line: There is also the story of Depeche Mode being offered an opportunity to support Ultravox around the period of the “Some Bizzare Album” and Stevo’s scene. What did you learn about that episode? Richard Evans: It is something I touch on in the book. You will be unsurprised to know that I was able to talk to Vince Clarke about Ultravox for “Looking Backwards Towards the Future” and we talked about exactly that. It’s absolutely true, but although Stevo offered Depeche Mode a support slot with Ultravox as an incentive to sign with him, I don’t think that he was in a position to actually make that happen. I think Depeche made the right decision! Midge Ure and the creative chemistry of equality Side-Line: When Midge Ure joined, Ultravox didn’t simply become a more commercially successful version of the same band. The entire musical and visual identity evolved. What made that line-up work so well? Richard Evans: I think it was equality. The previous incarnation of Ultravox was John Foxx’s project and he drove it, but with this new line-up everyone was equal and that led to a real creative connection. Talking to the band about those sessions I get the impression they were having fun both creatively and personally, and they were very driven at that stage in their career, which was also an important factor. Side-Line: They also resisted the obvious commercial option. After the enormous success of “Vienna”, they followed it with something as strange and eccentric as “Rage In Eden”. Richard Evans: Initially I think they had fun with success. It’s interesting – and very typical of the band – that following the massive success of “Vienna” they made an album as strange and as eccentric as “Rage In Eden” when the safe option would have been to simply capitalise on their success and do more of the same. But I also think that as they moved forward, and as their success allowed them to explore other areas, internal dynamics did start to change and they got caught in a cycle of recording, releasing and touring album after album, which ultimately became unfulfilling and creatively challenging for them. Beyond ‘Vienna’ Side-Line: Did researching “Vienna” itself reveal anything that changed the familiar story? Richard Evans: The band have been asked about “Vienna” so many times over the years that I think everything that could be said about it has already been said. That said, I did talk to the television promotions person from Ultravox’s label at that time, Chrysalis, and his memories of the band doing “Top Of The Pops” for the first time were interesting and new to me at least, so maybe I have added a little to the story of that song after all! Side-Line: How much space did you give to the tensions behind the success? Richard Evans: I think the public face of any band is never quite aligned with what is going on behind the scenes, but yes, those tensions are part of the story and so they have been included. I was guided by the band members themselves as to how much they wanted to put in the public domain, but they were all very honest, I think. Sometimes too honest, and sometimes that honesty made it into the book, and sometimes it didn’t… Where does the classic Ultravox story end? Side-Line: The “U-Vox” period is often regarded as the end of the classic Ultravox story. Do you agree? Richard Evans: Warren Cann was already out of the band by the time “U-Vox” was released, so I would say that the end of the classic Ultravox story actually comes at the end of the “Lament” album project. “U-Vox” was a tricky moment in the band’s career though. That said, I always liked the album artwork! Side-Line: And what about the Tony Fenelle and Sam Blue line-ups? Richard Evans: I write about both of those line-ups but for me, and for a lot of other fans of the band, they aren’t true Ultravox albums. They are interesting Billy Currie projects and there’s some good music to be found from both, but attaching the name Ultravox to them just doesn’t sit right for me looking at them in retrospect. Sorry Billy… Side-Line: So was the end of the band ultimately a creative, personal or musical problem? Richard Evans: Definitely a combination of all three! An influence still waiting for recognition Side-Line: Ultravox’s reputation continued to grow through compilations and retrospectives. When did they become a genuine historical influence on new generations? Richard Evans: That’s a really interesting question. I talk to a couple of artists who claim Ultravox as a major influence on their own careers: Nick Rhodes from Duran Duran, who is a huge fan of the earlier incarnation of the band, and Moby, who is more of a fan of the later records. But despite their respective flag-waving for the band, I don’t think that Ultravox have really ever been given the respect they deserve. Hopefully the book will help remind people of what they achieved as another stepping stone towards that kind of recognition. The reunion: serendipity rather than nostalgia Side-Line: The reunion in 2008 seemed almost improbable. What brought the four classic members back together? Richard Evans: It was such an unlikely thing to happen, which is typically Ultravox in itself and I suspect that was part of the appeal for them. It was basically a case of good timing. One of Ultravox’s former managers, Chris O’Donnell, sent each of them an email wondering if they might consider doing some shows, and on that particular day, and in those particular moments, all four of them thought that there might be something in the idea. The stars just happened to align. Serendipity. Side-Line: And then came “Brilliant”. Richard Evans: The band have mixed feelings about that title, but it’s a decent album in my opinion. I think that by the end of the making of it a lot of the old tensions were back in the band, which took a lot of the joy out of the project… Writing an authorised biography without losing independence Side-Line: You had access to the surviving members, as well as former collaborators, archive material and people from the band’s wider circle. How did you build the research? Richard Evans: I was lucky on the research because I had already gathered a lot of it for “Listening To The Music The Machines Make”, so that turned out to be unexpectedly valuable. Once Omnibus Press agreed to the idea of an Ultravox book I approached the surviving band members to see if they would be comfortable with me writing about them, and also to sound them out on whether they might want to become involved. I had interviewed John Foxx, Billy Currie and Midge Ure previously for other things, so I started with them and they all confirmed they were happy for me to write the book, and also that they would make themselves available to answer questions. Billy connected me to Warren, who also agreed to be on board, and John Foxx’s manager introduced me to Robin Simon, who also said yes. Nobody was still in touch with Steve Shears though, and tracking him down took some time, and when I did he decided that he didn’t want to be directly involved. I told the band that I would only ask them about things that they hadn’t previously talked about, rather than making them go over the same things they have been asked a hundred times over the years. I think that helped my case. I’ve worked in the music industry for long enough that I knew people who had worked with the band, or who could easily connect me with people who worked with the band. And other people I talked to I just approached out of the blue, like Steve Lillywhite and Moby, or I already knew, like Vince Clarke and Nick Rhodes. Conflicting memories and uncomfortable truths Side-Line: Was there any archive material that proved particularly revealing? Richard Evans: I think the most interesting archive materials were the interviews the band did for the Ultravox fanzine “Extreme Voice”, which eventually became their official fan newsletter. Those interviews were not only very relaxed conversations with the band, but they also delved deeply into unexpected corners in the way that only true fans could have done. If I had to choose one then it would be the very honest interview that Warren Cann gave to the “In The City” fanzine after being sacked from the band, which wasn’t published at the time but later appeared in “Extreme Voice”. Aside from that, John Foxx hasn’t really talked about a lot of things I asked him about. In fact, he told me he dislikes talking about this part of his history, so there are some very interesting contributions from him and it seems I was lucky to get them. Side-Line: How do you balance honesty with fairness when different members remember the same events very differently? Richard Evans: Sometimes it was tricky. As I got to know the various band members a little over the course of the project I got to like them all, and as a result I very much wanted to represent each of them equally. Sometimes their individual recollections didn’t quite match, or were dramatically different, and in those situations I tried to present all views side by side. Did I leave some things out? Yes I did, but only if I felt that they were unfair, overly personal or unsubstantiated. Side-Line: And did the fact that this is an authorised biography ever compromise your independence? Richard Evans: Not really. None of the band members asked to see any of the book while I was writing it, and at this exact moment in time they still haven’t. As soon as printed copies are available I will send a copy to each of them and I very much hope they approve of it. Ultimately it’s my book rather than theirs, but the band were kind enough to trust me to tell their stories, so I did feel a responsibility to represent each of them properly and respectfully. I don’t recall not asking a question I wanted the answer to in any of my conversations with them though. Why Moby? Side-Line: Your previous book had a foreword by Vince Clarke. This time it is Moby. How did that happen? Richard Evans: I didn’t know Moby, although our paths had briefly crossed in the early 90s, but I did know someone who could introduce me to his manager, which is what happened. I knew Moby was a huge fan of Ultravox and when I explained what I was writing he agreed to talk to me. We scheduled a Zoom and we got along really well. His enthusiasm for Ultravox was so infectious and so heartfelt that he seemed to be the perfect person to provide the foreword. He’s another really interesting character with interesting things to say. Looking backwards, towards the future Side-Line: You are planning book events around the publication. What would you like these events to become? Richard Evans: When “Listening To The Music The Machines Make” came out I did an event for Sound Affects in Brighton. It was my first ever time doing a book event and although it went well I knew in retrospect that I didn’t do as good a job on it as I should have done, so I asked them if I could come back and do another one for this book, and they very kindly agreed. Swanage is the closest town to where I live and I did an event at the same venue for “Listening To The Music The Machines Make”, which went well, so they asked if I might like to do another one. Beyond those two I’m also having conversations with a few other people about doing talks and events at the moment. Potentially some of them will be me talking about the book, some will be conversations with other people. It’s all being worked out at the moment. Side-Line: Finally, after spending so long looking backwards towards the future of Ultravox, where do you think the band belongs today? Richard Evans: I think Ultravox are long overdue some proper respect for their achievements, and for always achieving those achievements on their own terms. If the book can help amplify that for the band then I would be very happy, and if reading it makes people discover aspects of Ultravox they weren’t previously aware of then that would be amazing. If nothing else, reminding people of the breadth and quality of their catalogue and reintroducing them to those songs feels like a successful outcome. About Ultravox Ultravox formed in London in April 1974 around singer Dennis Leigh, who took the name John Foxx, together with Chris Allen on bass, Stevie Shears on guitar, Billy Currie on violin and keyboards and Warren Cann on drums. The group worked as Tiger Lily before adopting the name Ultravox! in October 1976 and signing to Island Records. Allen had by then become Chris Cross. Steve Lillywhite and Brian Eno co-produced the debut album “Ultravox!”, released in February 1977; “Ha! Ha! Ha!” followed later the same year. Robin Simon replaced Shears on guitar for “Systems of Romance” in 1978, recorded in Germany with Conny Plank and built on synthesizers, treated guitar and drum machine. Foxx left in March 1979 after a final American date and went on to release “Metamatic” in 1980. Midge Ure, previously of Slik, The Rich Kids and Thin Lizzy, joined as singer and guitarist on November 1, 1979, having worked with Currie in Visage earlier that year. The Ure line-up signed to Chrysalis and released “Vienna” in July 1980; its title track reached number two in the UK in early 1981. “Rage in Eden” followed in 1981, “Quartet” in 1982 with George Martin producing, and “Lament” in 1984, which carried “Dancing With Tears In My Eyes”. Cann was dismissed in 1986, before the recording of “U-Vox”, released that October. Currie continued the name with two further albums fronted by other singers, “Revelation” in 1993 with Tony Fenelle and “Ingenuity” in 1994 with Sam Blue. Ure, Currie, Cann and Cross reunited in November 2008, played their first show together in more than two decades at the Edinburgh Playhouse in April 2009 and released “Brill!ant” on May 28, 2012. Chris Cross died on March 25, 2024 at the age of 71. Chrysalis issued “The Collection (Deluxe Edition)” in December 2025. “Looking Backwards Towards the Future: The Story of Ultravox” is the first full-length book on the band. Interview by János Janurik.
items._cn_summary: 本文并非传统乐评，而是对音乐记者Richard Evans所著Ultravox授权传记的访谈介绍。文章回顾了Ultravox横跨1978至1983年英国电子流行与新浪潮运动的关键地位，探讨了乐队从后朋克场景出发、早期拥抱技术、并在新浪漫主义浪潮中崛起的轨迹。访谈涉及John Foxx时期的转变、Midge Ure加入后的商业成功、与Depeche Mode的意外关联以及重组年代等话题。Evans认为Ultravox作为电子音乐先驱，长期被夹在电子纯粹主义者与摇滚听众之间，声誉被缩减为《Vienna》等少数代表作，未能获得与其历史贡献相称的认可。该书由Omnibus Press出版，Moby作序，预计引发对英国电子流行乐史的重新审视。

items.body: Frankie Rose released the video for “Return To Dust” on 21 August 2026, the second single from her album “Hila”, which arrives on 18 September 2026 through Born Losers Records outside the EU and UK and through Night School Records in the EU and UK. The Brooklyn songwriter directed the clip herself. “Return To Dust” sets Rose’s vocal high in the mix against drum machines, synthesizers and reverbed guitar, with the low end carrying most of the weight. Rose explains the song as a description of searching for the dead while asleep, and of failing at it. “In my dreams I travel the cosmos and the astral realm looking for ones I’ve lost,” she stated. “But I’m a pretty bad receiver, and I am pretty sure I keep missing what they’re trying to tell me.” The video follows that idea literally. Rose floats through star fields and planetary vistas in a homemade montage, drifting rather than exploring, and the cosmic scenery stays low-budget rather than cinematic. Frankie Rose sets ‘Hila’ for 18 September Rose announced “Hila” on 23 June 2026 alongside the first single, “Cant Be Wrong”. She describes the album as built around bereavement and the way it distorts perception. “Hila. A record about loss,” she stated. “What persists beyond the range of ordinary perception? The place mourning keeps returning to – not quite transcendence, not quite doubt. The edge of what we can see.” Rose produced the record herself at her home studio, with Justin Welch of Elastica and Lush on drums. She recorded it after touring with The Jesus and Mary Chain and Swervedriver. Night School Records describes the album as drawing on the darkness of later Coil, the production weight of Skinny Puppy and the vocal treatments associated with Cocteau Twins, with Robin Guthrie style guitar work on “Shadow Twin”. Saxophone and digital synthesis run through “Rainman” and the title track. “Hila” runs ten tracks: “Olo”, “Cant Be Wrong”, “Return To Dust”, “Shadow Twin”, “Rainman”, “Hila”, “Manifest”, “Best Of Times”, “TV Star” and “Velvet Refrain”. Born Losers Records issues it on black vinyl, on clear vinyl with a green centre, on CD and digitally, with a vinyl and T-shirt bundle also listed. Night School Records handles the EU and UK editions. HILA by Frankie Rose Frankie Rose tour dates with The Charlatans Rose opens a North American run on 5 September 2026 in San Diego, playing most dates in support of The Charlatans and headlining in Los Angeles and Minneapolis. 5 September 2026 – San Diego, CA, United States – House of Blues (with The Charlatans) 6 September 2026 – Los Angeles, CA, United States – Zebulon (headline) 7 September 2026 – San Francisco, CA, United States – Castro Theater (with The Charlatans) 10 September 2026 – Portland, OR, United States – Wonder Ballroom (with The Charlatans) 11 September 2026 – Vancouver, BC, Canada – Commodore Ballroom (with The Charlatans) 12 September 2026 – Seattle, WA, United States – The Showbox (with The Charlatans) 15 September 2026 – Minneapolis, MN, United States – Cloudland Theater (headline) 17 September 2026 – Chicago, IL, United States – Park West (with The Charlatans) 19 September 2026 – Detroit, MI, United States – El Club (with The Charlatans) 20 September 2026 – Toronto, ON, Canada – Danforth Music Hall (with The Charlatans) 21 September 2026 – Montreal, QC, Canada – Fairmont Theatre (with The Charlatans) 22 September 2026 – Boston, MA, United States – The Paradise Rock Club (with The Charlatans) 23 September 2026 – Philadelphia, PA, United States – Union Transfer (with The Charlatans) 25 September 2026 – Silver Spring, MD, United States – The Fillmore Silver Spring (with The Charlatans) 26 September 2026 – Brooklyn, NY, United States – Brooklyn Steel (with The Charlatans) About Frankie Rose Frankie Rose was born on 18 January 1979 and works out of Brooklyn, New York. She was an original member of Vivian Girls and played drums in Crystal Stilts and in Dum Dum Girls before moving to her own material. Her first single, “Thee Only One”, appeared on Slumberland Records in 2009 under the name Frankie Rose and the Outs, and the band’s self-titled debut album followed on the same label in 2010. She dropped the group name for “Interstellar”, issued by Slumberland in February 2012, and released the “Night Swim” EP and the single “Know Me” the same year. Fat Possum Records put out “Herein Wild” in 2013. In 2014 she recorded “Careers” for Kanine Records as one half of Beverly. “Cage Tropical” arrived on Slumberland in August 2017, the year Rose also released a cover of The Cure song “A Forest”. She extended that work in 2019 with “Seventeen Seconds”, a track-for-track cover of The Cure’s 1980 album, again on Slumberland. Her previous album, “Love As Projection”, came out on Slumberland in March 2023, after which she toured with The Jesus and Mary Chain and Swervedriver. “Hila” is her first record for Born Losers Records and Night School Records, and moves her writing toward synthesizer arrangements and eighties production methods. “Return To Dust” is the second track released from it.
items._genre: darkwave / dream pop / synth pop / post-punk
items._cn_summary: Frankie Rose 即将发行新专辑《Hila》，整张作品围绕丧失与哀悼展开，试图探索日常感知边界之外的领域。制作上由 Rose 独立在家中录音室完成，鼓手为 Elastica 与 Lush 乐队的 Justin Welch，融合鼓机、合成器、混响吉他与低沉低频，萨克斯与数字合成器贯穿部分曲目。厂牌描述其借鉴了晚期 Coil 的阴郁气质、Skinny Puppy 的厚重制作、Cocteau Twins 式人声处理，以及 Robin Guthrie 风格的吉他。歌曲《Return To Dust》的人声被置于混音高位，歌词描绘梦中跨越星际寻找逝者的意象。此次为独立厂牌发行，分区域由 Born Losers Records 与 Night School Records 负责，定位介于暗潮与梦幻流行之间，带有明确的实验流行色彩。

items.body:
Jeff McIlwain re-emerges from his production slumber to deliver more aural candy for the Ghostly family on this new Lusine album.

Further settling into his latter-day groove as a producer of well-polished pop-tinged electronics, the Lusine of nearly 20 years ago has not disappeared altogether, the mechanics of his early IDM, ambient and downtempo productions still drive the creative process on ‘Sensorimotor’.

There is a more introspective yearn to this album however, a sensation most apparent in the numerous vocal contributions from Jeff and his wife, Sarah McIlwain, along with Vilja Larjosto and Benoît Pioulard. The latter’s manipulated vocals feature on the sub-Burial, hushed flutter of Witness which is destined to get synced by the CSI franchise sometime soon.

items.body:
Jospehine Foster's 2016 release "No More Lamps In the Morning" available again via Fire Records.

"Foster, on nylon string guitar, and husband Victor Herrero, accompanying on Portuguese guitar, together weave intimate readings of songs spanning Foster's songwriting career including selections from recent albums "This Coming Gladness" (2008) and "I'm a Dreamer" (2013) and back to Born Heller (2004). Foster's new route is a free, chromatic music, a tuneful montana of mind--an expansive harmonic space dominated by Rif mountain on the horizon. As highwater as the music is, as broad the stylistic palette of the musicians, the music really exists in service of the lyrics. Two of the songs on No More Lamps are poems by Rudyard Kipling and James Joyce given musical settings by Foster. The rest arguably are musical settings of her own poems strengthened in a fiery crucible of guitars (and on 2 tracks Gyða Valtýsdóttir's cello) in which dissonant notes bend and quaver as wirefork embers, dying without affecting the glowing tonal fire which unites contrary forces in a Moroccan speakeasy. She and Herrero have performed, for an audience of burros, concerts of Federico Garcia Lorca poems set to music. A music of wandering and a music of roots."
items._cn_summary: Josephine Foster 与丈夫 Victor Herrero 以尼龙弦吉他与葡萄牙吉他重新演绎了她跨越十余年创作生涯的作品，包括早期专辑中的旧作。专辑中两首歌曲采用了 Rudyard Kipling 和 James Joyce 的诗作，其余多为她自己的诗作谱曲。音乐以歌词为核心，吉他作为主要乐器，辅以大提琴，在不和谐音与和声张力之间构建出流动的音色空间。整体呈现出漫游与扎根并存的音乐气质，融合了诗歌、弗拉门戈元素与室内乐编制，但更偏向艺术民谣传统而非实验性突破。Fire Records 的再版发行延续了作品的小众独立属性。

items.body:
On her third studio album, Brooklyn-based artist Frances Chang feels out the boundary between bedroom pop and lavishly orchestrated avant-experimentation, writing on a century-old grand piano and spiking her productions with jerky, unconventional electronic elements. The end result is somewhere between Aimee Mann and Cate Le Bon.

There's something unmistakably ramshackle about Chang's productions, but at the same time, it all sounds as if it's been meticulously planned. On opening track 'I can feel the waves', her voice never falters as it soars over casual phrases from her aging baby grand, but the it's the beats that immediately catch your attention, rupturing the calm with the momentum of a footwork demo. Chang's clearly an obsessive listener and it's this passion that lends her songs a breath of originality; they're classic in a sense, informed by Burt Bacharach, Chet Baker and Dionne Warwick, which actually makes sense. And where she takes the songs after they've been written is fascinating, building them out with instrumentation that's not exactly unexpected, it's just ever so slightly off-kilter. Those warbling strings on the ace 'Bad zen', or the buzzing micro-repetitions on 'Marry' - these sounds just nudge the material into a different zone and assert Chang's personality.

And as it develops, Chang's confidence grows. She's most successful when the guardrails are fully off - like on the brilliant 'No avatar'. Here, she latches her Robert Ashley-esque vocal lead to a wonky synth arpeggio that she follows with piano - or vice versa? The other instruments coolly fall into line: drums, bass and organ seem to flutter, flourish and fall at Chang's command, never quite going in the expected direction. Even advance single 'Auratones of Desire' makes more sense in context, its well-sculpted fusion of psych drum breaks, frittered farfisa organs and soft vocal affectations widening the album's reach considerably. Given it some time and attention for full reward.
items._cn_summary: Frances Chang的第三张专辑探索卧室流行与华丽编制前卫实验之间的边界，以百年古董三角钢琴为基底写作，并在制作中注入不规则电子元素与非常规节奏。开场曲中她的人声在随性的钢琴短语上稳定延展，脚下却冒出footwork式的猛烈碎拍，显示出她对多类型音乐的深度聆听。专辑整体呈现一种精心规划的随意感，既受Burt Bacharach、Chet Baker、Dionne Warwick等经典影响，又在器乐编排上微微偏离预期。颤动的弦乐、嗡鸣的微循环音、Robert Ashley式人声主导配合歪斜合成器琶音，使作品滑入独属于她的地带。鼓、贝斯、风琴在她手中起伏而不落俗套，迷幻鼓击与Farfisa风琴的融合拓宽了整体听觉范围。需要时间与耐心方能收获完整回报。

Cranky UKG bassbin permutations by a producer with form for Keysound, making his mark on Bristol-via-Berlin’s Sneaker Social Club.

Bare bones rhythms clack and swang in ‘Vintage Gilly’, where aspects of post-dubstep minimalism, electrified halfstep, dark garage and gqom tesselate with a rude UK torque. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以英国车库舞曲的骨架为出发点，融入后dubstep极简主义、电子化半步舞曲、黑暗车库以及南非gqom的切分节奏，形成棱角分明的低频质感。制作人此前在Keysound厂牌发表作品，此番转投Bristol与柏林连线厂牌Sneaker Social Club。曲目风格各异：开篇曲以简约骨架节奏展开，'Drift into Dread'呈现粗粝的grime切分，标题曲浓缩半步节拍并叠加Zomby式的旋律碎片，'Godkiller'回归El-B与Sully式的深沉车库旋转，'Glass Eater'则将UKG与gqom进行扭曲杂交。整体制作偏向实验性低频解构，节奏框架虽依循UK舞曲传统，却在音色与结构上做了相当程度的拆解与重组。

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Drumming for Yes for less than two years, having admirably taken over for the iconic Bill Bruford (who had left for King Crimson), Alan was suddenly vaulted into the limelight due to his place at la batterie for one of Prog's (and the world's) most opulent/visible/groundbreaking bands. After Yes' massive nine-month US and world-wide tours to support the release of their 1974 studio album, Relayer, the band decided to take a break to recharge. During this time each of the band members chose to express their individual ideas in solo album releases: Steve Howe's Beginnings on October 31, 1975; Chris Squire's Fish Out of Water on November 7, 1975; Patrick Moraz' The Story of I in the Spring of 1976; Jon Anderson's Olias of Sunhillow on July 9, 1976, and this album, Alan White's Ramshackled in March of 1976. To put together Ramshackled, Alan gathered his most trusted friends and collaborators of old (pre-Yes), many of whom he met while working with The Mark-Almond Band, Bell + Arc, live touring with Ginger Baker's Air Force or Joe Cocker, or an album he played on for Johnny Harris as well as a short-lived psychedelic band called Griffin back in 1969 in which White, Craddock, Kirtley, and Gibson had all played. Though I've owned this album for 50 years now, and always loved it (though I would never consider it representative of my preferences in musical styles), I am really looking forward to hearing it under the fresh spell of having gotten to know the earlier work of artistst like Alan Marshall, Peter Kirtley, Kenny Craddock, Bud Beadle, Steve Gregory, and Colin Gibson.Line-up / Musicians:- Alan White / drums, percussion, vocals, producerWith:- Alan Marshall (Riff Raff, Zzebra) / vocals- Peter Kirtley (Riff Raff, Zzebra) / guitar, vocals- Kenny Craddock / keyboards, vocals- Bud Beadle (Riff Raff, Zzebra) / saxophone solo, flute- Steve Gregory / tenor saxophone, flute- Henry Lowther / trumpet- Colin Gibson (Sanfu, Alan Hull) / bass, percussion- David Bedford (Mike Oldfield) / orchestral arranger & conductor - The Martyn Ford Orchestra / stringsAnd, special guests:- Jon Anderson / vocals (4)- Steve Howe / guitar (4)- Andy Phillips / steel drums (7)- Madeline Bell / backing vocals (8)- Joanne Williams / backing vocals (8)- Vicky Brown / backing vocals (8)1. "Ooooh Baby (Goin' to Pieces)" (5:32) an awesome funk tune from Peter Kirtley straight off the bat. It's driving, it's fun, it's funky, it's a cruisin' song! Alan's soulful LOU RAWLS-like voice (that reminds me of Arnaud Bukwald). Great album opener! Great Jazz-Rock Fusion. Really gets the blood pumpin'! (9.375/10) 2. "One Way Rag" (4:04) a great funk/R&B tune that sounds like Gerry Rafferty or Gilbert O'Sullivan singing (I'm assuming it's co-composer Kenny Craddock) and bounces delightfully with Colin Gibson's bass, percussion, Alan's drums, and, of course, Kenny's piano and organ play. Great contributions from the female background singers. (8.875/10) 3. "Avakak (aka Twelve Ways to Drink Meths)" (6:54) this is a song composed by Peter, Kenny, and Colin seen as "Havakak" on the Riff Raff album Original Man. The version the band records here starts out sounding like the intro to Roger Hodgson's "Fool's Overture" before Peter turns it with an "Awaken" opening riff and the band jumps in with a very odd funk-Yes-like syncopated chord progression over which soprano sax and guitar provide the jazzy lead melody in two revolving parts before things stop and start the song over using the full band to accompany Kenny's piano part until a quiet excursion into "Waiting Room"-like psychedelic percussive play takes over at the four-minute mark for about a minute before the odd funk-Yes-like motif retakes and Steve Gregory or Bud Beadle supply a flying treated soprano sax solo over the top of the oddly time signatured Jazz-Rock--and then a Yes-like door opens, someone lets out a scream, and it's over. An excellent, utterly exhilarating tune. I like this version (though it is very different from the Riff Raff one) very much. (13.75/15)4. "Spring - Song of Innocence" (5:00) gentle, soothing, soporific Hawai'ian-like music with some really cool and unusual instrumental sounds (thanks in part to guest stars Steve Howe and Jon Anderson as well as to Kenny Craddock's excellent keyboard contributions and Colin Gibson's expressive yet tender electric bass play) that make it sound as if it could have come from/been intended for Jon Anderson's Olias of Sunhillow album (which was to come out in July). (9.125/10)5. "Giddy" (3:11) a Jazz-Rock tune that sounds at first like Nina Simone's Sinner Man before Peter's lead guitar signals a clear Allman Brothers reference. Alan Marshall's vocal on this Kenny Craddock-Colin Gibson song is awesome, amplifying the song's Jazz-Rock elements marvelously (as does Colin Gibson's excellent bass play). So much fun! (9/10)6. "Silly Woman" (3:14) it's Reggae but it's so much more, it's Calypso, it's Ska, it's Afro-Cubano, it's fun and lively. Alan Marshall channels Joe Cocker, John Martyn, Van Morrison, and even Paul McCartney all at the same time. (8.875/10)7. "Marching into a Bottle" (1:59) acoustic guitar, flutes, orchestral woodwinds, and hand held percussion instruments create this quaint little anachronistic Neo-Baroque tune that should probably be on a GRYPHON or AMAZING BLONDEL album. (4.625/5)8. "Everybody" (3:13) Alan Marshall has really allowed his voice to evolve deep into the funky world of Soul/R&B as his Lou Rawls/Sly Stone, backed by some soulful female background singers, the song and its unusual vocal delivery remind me of something that might be done by Frank Zappa, Captain Beefheart, Eric Burdon, or Kaz Lux. I love how Alan and the girls bring it together for the choruses. And then explosion and it's all over! (8.875/10) 9. "Darkness" (5:35) yet another Gibson and Craddock composition, this one founded around a very cool swirling guitar arpeggio. The bulk of this jazzy, soulful R&B tune rests on the voice of Alan Marshall: in the first half it's anguished and insistent and then, after the orchestral break in the middle and Kenny Craddock's gorgeous classical piano play, it's Alan's achingly-emotional near-whispered vocal followed by, in the final 90 seconds, David Bedford's orchestral work over which trumpeter Henry Lowther lays down one of my favorite "goodbye" tributes of all-time. (9.125/10) Total Time 38:42A-/five stars; a minor masterpiece of eclectic Rock and Jazz-Rock compositions that are masterfully performed and rendered (with great passion and soul). Of the five Yes solos between Relayer and Going for the One, this has always been my second favorite (next to Chris Squire's Fish Out of Water.) After coming to know the background of Alan's band mates I am happy to confirm that that bias continues to exist. Highly recommended for lovers of eclectic Rock 'n' Roll and/or Jazz-Rock: just don't be looking for Yes music!
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Yes鼓手Alan White在乐队休整期间推出的个人作品，集结了他前Yes时期的旧友，包括多位曾参与Riff Raff、Zzebra等团体的乐手，并邀请Jon Anderson和Steve Howe客串。音乐以放克和节奏布鲁斯为基底，融合爵士摇滚、管乐编排与管弦乐配器，整体氛围轻松而律动感强。开篇曲目展现强劲的放克节奏与灵魂乐演唱，后续曲目在钢琴、风琴、萨克斯和铜管声部中切换，带有70年代跨界前卫摇滚的典型气质。专辑制作精良，乐手配合默契，但风格上更偏向主流摇滚与放克的结合，实验性和先锋性相对有限，适合对前卫摇滚分支中偏放克、爵士方向的听众。
